events.title: Substack’s influencer marketing era has arrived
events.summary: Anna Doré, Rothy's vice president of brand and communications, is focused on Substack. Photo Credit: Anna Doré There's a new social media platform brands are eyeing: Substack. Rothy's, a shoe brand, is tapping writers for IRL events and personal essays. Substack is welcoming brands onto its platform with open arms — and more sponsorship tools. Substack isn't just for writers anymore. It's also for influencer marketers. The newsletter platform has become an increasingly important social media tool for brands looking to find creators to work with and to reach potential customers. "Substack is one of the most exciting channels out there right now," said Anna Doré, Rothy's vice president of brand and communications. Doré is featured in Business Insider's 2026 list of 14 innovative influencer marketers. Before influencers, there were magazines and blogs. Substack, where people can write — while also sharing visual content like photos and videos — marries the media's past with its present. Rothy's, known for its comfortable, washable flats , is doubling down on the platform. Rothy's hosted an event with Substacker Denna Nazem. Courtesy of Rothy's "In this AI-driven algorithm world where we're all being served the same content on the feed, we more than ever are going to be looking to great tastemakers," Doré said. "We're looking for the gatekeepers to tell us what we should care about in this world." Here are 5 examples of how Rothy's has leveraged Substack in its marketing: Emily Sundberg , who writes the popular business newsletter Feed Me , shared on her Substack that she stashed a pair of Rothy's flats on her wedding day. Rothy's later partnered with Sundberg on sponsoring a pizza party for Feed Me's readers. Erika Veurink, who writes the fashion newsletter Long Live, wrote an article for New York Magazine featuring Rothy's shoes that went viral. Rothy's later reached out, inking a long-term relationship with the writer that resulted in a vintage pop-up experience for Veurink's readers at a Rothy's location in New York City — drawing in over 200 people and increasing the store's foot traffic by 75% that day. Denna Nazem had mentioned Rothy's in her travel-focused newsletter, Strictly the Good Stuff. Spotting this, Rothy's reached out and later worked with Nazem on an IRL event around the launch of a new Rothy's collection at Nordstrom. Doré said that Nordstrom followed in Rothy's footsteps and later partnered with Nazem again after seeing the results. To promote Rothy's 10th anniversary, the brand partnered with five Substack creators — including Veurink and others like Hunter Harris, Rose Anderson, Noora Raj Brown, and Plum Sykes — to write essays about their own personal growth. Rothy's also launched its own Substack. It isn't busy blogging, but the brand does repost its influencer partners frequently to Substack's Notes feed. Substacker Erika Veurink hosted a pop-up vintage sale for her readers at Rothy's. Courtesy of Rothy's "People follow these Substack writers because they are in the know," Doré said. It's not only Rothy's dabbling with Substack. Sophia Sesto, Poppi's vice president of culture , has been eyeing the platform as a tool for strategically partnering with creators. Substack has replaced the blog for some creators and is where they share more personal anecdotes for their most loyal followers. That helps Poppi plan future collaborations, Sesto said. "You can know more about the creators you're working with," she said, such as learning that they love to travel to a destination every year, and then coordinate a Poppi bar for that trip — planting the brand into that creator's content. Other brands are looking to Substack as a channel for their own content. The Knot Worldwide, which owns several wedding planning platforms, is "bullish" on expanding into Substack, said Kiara Kempski , the company's vice president of global consumer marketing. "We're actually starting up our own Substack from The Knot," Kempski said. "Our editors are moving over there and creating owned content for us and building that out." Substack welcomes influencer marketing Several brands have taken the same leap and launched their own Substack publications, such as Rare Beauty, The RealReal, Tory Burch, and even the dating app Hinge. Substack has its arms wide open. Bring on the brands ! Substack cofounder Chris Best announced in June that the company was launching a native brand sponsorship program, highlighting work already underway on the platform, such as Sundberg's partnership with Hinge. Chris Best is the cofounder and CEO of Substack. Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile for Collision via Getty Images This week, the platform is expanding the program to introduce new sponsorship formats. One option would allow brands to gift a one-month subscription, giving readers access to a writer's content behind the paywall. Another option is for brands to sponsor a creator's single post, making it free for anyone to read. Brands can "earn real standing instead of shouting through feeds and swipes," Dan Robbins, who joined Substack as head of brand sponsorships this year, wrote in a blog post on Thursday. Substack wants brands to see its newsletters as a "space to go deep, to say thank you, and to back communities that will grow your business," Robbins said. events.title: For the final 10% of cystic fibrosis patients, the breakthrough still hasn't come
events.summary: 10% of cystic fibrosis patients cannot benefit from today's breakthrough drugs because of underlying genetic mutations. Emily's Entourage is funding research into gene therapies and treatments for drug-resistant infections. Progress for CF's final 10% could also inform treatments for other rare genetic diseases. For the vast majority of cystic fibrosis patients, new drugs have been life-changing, transforming a debilitating lung disease into a manageable condition. But for about 10% of patients born with other genetic mutations, these treatments don't work. "We have been left behind," said Emily Kramer-Golinkoff, who founded a nonprofit, Emily's Entourage, to speed up research for what she calls "the final 10%" of CF patients who don't respond to the current treatments or experience side effects. As the cystic fibrosis community gathers this week in Atlanta for its largest annual gathering , Kramer-Golinkoff is hoping those patients will be a big part of the conversation, particularly after recent scientific setbacks. In May, Vertex and Moderna stopped a clinical trial of a drug that used mRNA, the technology behind the Covid vaccines, to treat those CF patients in the 10%, citing tolerability issues. In February, the drugmaker Boehringer Ingelheim ended a trial of a gene therapy for CF. Over four decades ago, when Kramer-Golinkoff was diagnosed with the progressive and fatal genetic disease at six weeks old, a failed clinical trial would have been where the story ends. But today, thanks largely to her nonprofit's work, there are rays of hope. Affecting about 40,000 Americans, cystic fibrosis causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs, creating life-threatening lung infections and respiratory failure. About 90% of patients with the disease have a certain genetic mutation and can benefit from Trikafta and a newer-version, Alyftrek, which are both made by Vertex Pharmaceuticals. By improving the function of a protein called CFTR that maintains the balance of salt and water in the body, the drugs thin the mucus in a patient's lungs. A 2024 article in The Atlantic, headlined "The Cystic-Fibrosis Breakthrough That Changed Everything," described how those patients can now run up stairs and take part in 1o-K races. But for patients like Kramer-Golinkoff who don't produce a fully functional CFTR protein to benefit from those drugs, the big breakthrough didn't change much. Since its creation in 2011, Emily's Entourage has raised more than $22 million and funded 51 research projects developing multiple therapeutic approaches, including antisense oligonucleotides, or ASOs, small molecules and gene therapies. Delivering a drug to the right cells presents an especially difficult scientific problem because the lung is an organ designed to keep things out. Adding to that challenge, the lung of a CF patient is filled with mucus. "It's incredibly challenging in a healthy lung," said Chandrabali Ghose, chief scientific officer for Emily's Entourage. "But it's orders of magnitude more difficult in a CF lung." One promising gene therapy developed by Spirovant Sciences could work regardless of a patient's genetic mutation. The drug is now in an early-stage clinical trial . Emily's Entourage is also investing in other approaches — phages, which are naturally occurring viruses that kill bacteria, and antimicrobials – that treat drug-resistant infections that can ultimately be fatal for CF patients. "We see these as buying-time initiatives," Ghose said. The foundation's work could ultimately help patients with other conditions, including people who suffer from joint and skin infections. Her group is also funding research into nonsense mutations, which are changes in DNA that cause the cells to stop making proteins earlier than they should, causing diseases. What scientists learn from that research could be relevant to patients with a range of rare genetic conditions. "We all benefit when there's a leap forward," Kramer-Golinkoff said. Kramer-Golinkoff sees hope in the story of Baby KJ , which has spurred regulatory changes aimed at allowing scientists to develop custom-made drugs for individual patients. There are about 2,000 genetic mutations that cause cystic fibrosis. Many are extremely rare, affecting just a small handful of people. Perhaps her biggest challenge is combating the misconception that cystic fibrosis has been cured, which stifles investment into new treatments. "Many people hear about the progress for 90% of the CF community and think we've figured it out, but that is not true," Kramer-Golinkoff said. "Those in the final 10% are still contending with the same killer disease that CF has always been." Now 41, Kramer-Golinkoff is grateful to be alive. Most CF patients at her stage are dying or receive lung transplants. But her life isn't easy.

events.title: How a college-application portal became central to the youth protests sweeping France
events.summary: France's youth protests have put Parcoursup, its college-admissions portal, under fresh scrutiny. Dimitar DILKOFF / AFP via Getty Images France's youth protests have surged over school disrepair, staff shortages, and Parcoursup. Parcoursup was meant to end admissions lotteries, but critics say it magnifies inequality. "There is no social justice," a French high schooler told Business Insider. What began last month as a protest over unfilled teaching positions at Lycée Saint-Exupéry in a working-class suburb of Paris has spread across France. Hundreds of thousands of students are protesting crowded classrooms, unfilled teaching posts, and crumbling buildings. Thursday marked the 10th day of protests. Another target has emerged on placards and in chants: Parcoursup, France's central online portal for higher-education applications. Three French students told Business Insider that the admissions system can turn underprivileged schooling, personal upheaval, and a shortage of local courses into barriers to higher education. "There is no social justice," Pierre Sourzat, a 17-year-old student in a preparatory program in Toulouse and president of the association "Les Lycéens," told Business Insider. "That's why high-school students are angry today." On Thursday, in response to the protests, the minister of national education introduced an emergency plan to address students' concerns, including a plan to mobilize substitute teachers. What is Parcoursup? Parcoursup is France's state-run, centralized website for applying to university and other post-high-school courses. The French government introduced Parcoursup in 2018 with the goal of making access to higher education fairer and more transparent than the previous system had. The Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation runs the platform. About 900,000 people use it each year to apply for first-year university courses, preparatory classes, and other higher-education programs. Most French high-school seniors seeking a first-year place use Parcoursup. Some programs, including certain live-performing-arts courses and those not listed on the portal, accept applications directly. Students in their final year of high school submit up to 10 choices on Parcoursup for specific university courses, preparatory classes, or other postsecondary programs they want to attend. Individual programs publish their admissions criteria and use committees — largely made up of teachers — to assess and rank applicants. Parcoursup then makes offers in that order. The government says the website is not a black-box algorithm deciding students' futures. But students say the criteria, and the weight given to grades, teacher assessments, personal statements, and other factors, can vary by course — leaving them with a process that can feel opaque. The Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. What do students say the issues are? Sourzat said the portal is useful as a centralized way to find and apply for courses. But he said it makes students compete on academic records built in unequal school conditions. "We don't choose our high schools. We go to the one in the area where we live," he said. "And then, when we apply through Parcoursup, we're treated as though we're all equal." Sourzat said he attended a rural high school north of Toulouse and went roughly a third of one school year without a French teacher before sitting the French baccalaureate exam. That score, in part, determines whether students can access all programs and universities. A 2021 study by researchers at Insee, France's national statistics office, and the Paris School of Economics found that, in popular courses with more applicants than places, Parcoursup allowed programs to rely more heavily on academic records to pick candidates. In the Paris region, students with stronger records were more likely to enter the most competitive courses, while those with weaker records were more often directed elsewhere, the study found. Ryad Rani, the 19-year-old president of the "Union Syndicale Lycéenne," a French high school union, called Parcoursup a "machine of social selection." After his mother died in January, Rani said he faced eviction from their social housing and missed more than three months of his final year of high school. "You're burying your mother and filling in your choices," he said. "That is the last thing on your mind — but you're put under pressure to do it." Ilies Djaouti, a 24-year-old second-year master's student at Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, said the shortage of local courses can also push students to leave home — even when they don't have the means. Djaouti said he was able to move to Paris only because of CROUS, France’s public student-support network, which provides subsidized housing and financial aid. "I had to choose programs at the other end of France," said Djaouti, who applied from Narbonne, in southern France. "Without CROUS, I would not have been able to live or study." The protests spanned the whole of France. Miguel MEDINA / AFP via Getty Images What happens now? On Wednesday, the government announced a 5-point plan to address some of the issues being raised in the protests. Those include teacher absences, issues with facilities, and the transparency of higher-education admissions. The government has also opened an online consultation inviting high-school students to share their concerns and proposals. The portal, which runs until October 23, has attracted more than 68,000 participants as of Friday; the ministry says it will publish the results by the end of the month. For Parcoursup's 2027 admissions cycle, the government says applicants will be better able to understand the criteria programs use, how heavily they weigh grades and subject choices, how files are ranked, and why they receive a given response. Speaking to lawmakers on Wednesday, Education Minister Édouard Geffray rejected calls to abolish Parcoursup. He acknowledged that the platform had "crystallised" students’ anxieties about higher education and said the government would bring forward proposals for improvement by October 20. Protests were still underway on Friday, with new school blockades and student gatherings reported in cities including Paris and Lyon, a day after tens of thousands marched nationwide. events.title: How 'The Diary of a CEO' star Steven Bartlett avoids burnout
events.summary: Steven Bartlett said staying curious about his interview subjects is critical to his success. Frederic J. Brown / AFP via Getty Images Steven Bartlett said he's setting up his company to last for 50 years by avoiding burnout. He carefully picks his podcast guests to ensure he's genuinely interested in them. He also maintains control of his holding company, Steven.com, so he can call the shots. How can I avoid burning out? That's a big question facing many creators — and other entrepreneurs — as they look to scale up their businesses. Star podcaster Steven Bartlett has thought a lot about how he can extend his business longevity. The host of "The Diary of a CEO" said he approaches decision-making with the goal of lasting for 50 years — and it comes down to how he picks guests for his show. "I say to my team all the time, 'Yes, I know this person has 150 million followers, but if I wake up in the morning and I look at my schedule, and I'm in a chair for four hours interviewing someone that I might not be interested in, and I have to do two hours of research, at some point, I'm going to get burned out,'" he told Business Insider in an interview. Bartlett, who has the No. 1 business podcast on Spotify in the US and 20 million YouTube subscribers, started out nine years ago with early guests including business tycoons like Richard Branson and Brian Chesky. He's since moved into more emotional and lifestyle territory. Recent guests have included WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann, Ivanka Trump, and the entertainer Druski. Another way Bartlett said he protects his curiosity — and avoids burning out — is by structuring his holding company, Steven.com, so he controls the board and decision-making about the business. Bartlett has also been making moves to grow the company in ways that don't rely directly on him. AI has played a big role in the company. He's used AI to clone his voice for a show, made a fully AI-animated kids show called "Steven's World," and used AI to translate "DOAC" into other languages. Company execs have stressed that they're using AI to free up employees to do more high-value work. Bartlett has said AI can help him focus on the elements that make creators irreplaceable, like in-person events. Bartlett has diversified his business by bringing other creators into his orbit through his company FlightStory, which now has five shows in addition to "DOAC." He's signaled plans to launch a paid membership program to extend his brand and those of the other creators in his network. He's also applying his diversification approach to his new tie-up with Authentic Brands Group , which will invest up to $400 million to help other creators grow their businesses. Bartlett said the goal is to help creators branch out into areas such as events, products, and animation. "We think we have a blueprint, which we think we've now proven, to help a creator grow and scale their audiences and therefore their commercial and everything else," he said in announcing the partnership. events.title: I served as the White House’s top biosecurity official. Here’s what I’m watching for with AI
events.summary: In the White House Situation Room, the hardest calls were never the obvious emergencies. What kept me up were the nights when a fragment of information came in and the debate wasn’t about what to do. It was about whether anything concerning was happening at all. In 2023, my team and I were assessing the nation’s pandemic influenza plans when the Situation Room notified me that H5N1 influenza had infected a father and killed his daughter in a remote Cambodian village. Was the virus spreading between people – the start of a pandemic that could kill millions? The national security adviser asked whether to brief President Biden immediately. If these cases were the first signs, we would need to commit billions of dollars to vaccines and treatments within days. I told him to wait. Not because I thought it was nothing, but because we had already agreed, before the alert came, on what would tell us it was something: sustained human-to-human transmission. We worked with health officials to pull surveillance data from nearby emergency rooms and compared it against prior years. The cases were not unexpectedly high. The President did not need to be alerted, I told him, and I would let him know if the ground truth changed. That trigger did two jobs at once. It kept us from dismissing a real emergency, and it kept us from escalating one that wasn’t. In almost every crisis I have worked, the decisive moment arrived before anyone agreed there was one. We are in one of those moments now. On Tuesday, President Trump and leaders of some of the nation’s largest AI companies signed the White House Accord on Superintelligence, a voluntary agreement calling on companies to strengthen internal controls around risks including biosecurity. The accord calls for internal monitoring, independent assessments and board oversight. But it leaves companies largely responsible for determining what those safeguards should look like and when a risk has become serious enough to act.  Bill Gates  is warning Americans  that artificial intelligence crossed thresholds this year, bio-attack capability among them. The threshold of most concern, he said, is whether an AI can design a bioterrorism weapon capable of killing millions. Last week, Anthropic’s chief executive urged the U.N. Security Council to back a ban on the use of AI to make biological weapons. It followed Anthropic’s disclosure of five cases of biological misuse of its models, including a researcher studying how H5N1 influenza adapts to mammals and causes illness beyond the respiratory tract. The company banned the accounts. There is almost no population immunity to H5N1, roughly half of human cases are fatal, and the virus does not yet spread efficiently between people.  Not yet. The last clause is the threshold I gave the national security adviser in 2023. It is the line between two infected relatives in a Cambodian village and a pandemic. Someone was asking an AI model how it gets crossed. Most people who read a disclosure like this come to one of two conclusions: AI has made biological weapons frighteningly accessible, or the safeguards worked and there is nothing to worry about. Neither tells us what we most need to know. Gates is right that a line was crossed, but nothing followed, because no one had decided in advance what measures crossing it should set off. The more useful question is: What could the AI help this person do, and what could it not do? The threshold Gates described is about design. The one that matters next is whether AI can carry a design from the digital world into the physical one. A model that can write a research protocol to create a pathogen is not a person who can create it. You need synthesized DNA, equipment and a lab with four walls to grow a virus in. AI has not yet dissolved those barriers. That’s not a reason to let up. It shows where we can mitigate risk, while that is still possible.  In the Situation Room, we answered that question before the emergency arrived: a specific observable trigger, paired with a specific action, agreed in advance. We have not applied this trigger-action discipline to the risks associated with AI and biology. So here is what I am watching for, and what each should set off. I’m paying close attention to evidence that someone without advanced biological expertise used AI to overcome experimental problems that previously required expert judgment. That requires independent evaluators to red-team AI models before deployment, not voluntary company disclosures. I’m looking for an AI-generated sequence of concern being ordered from a synthesis provider or run through an automated laboratory. That requires watermarking and tracing tools for biological design systems, as the Bipartisan Commission on Biodefense, on which I serve, has recommended. And I’m watching for proof that AI has substantially reduced the hands-on experience needed for dangerous biological work. DNA synthesis providers, cloud laboratories and benchtop synthesizers are where a digital capability becomes a physical one. Screening there should be expanded; a bipartisan Senate bill has not moved since January. None of these is “AI answered a dangerous biological question.” Each trigger would signal that the barrier separating AI-generated knowledge from the capability to use it in a physical lab is beginning to erode. Each has an action paired with it. Faced with a frightening new risk, we tend to ask a question that is almost impossible to answer: how worried should I be? Pre-defined thresholds are not alarmism. That is what allowed us to respond calmly when two cases of H5N1 influenza appeared in one Cambodian family. We knew what signal we were looking for and what to do if we found it. Without one, every ambiguous warning becomes something to panic about or one more thing we have already lived through.  AI is getting better at helping people do advanced biological work, and without stronger safeguards, that raises the risk of bioterrorism. The White House accord is an important acknowledgment that biosecurity belongs at the center of the AI safety conversation. But internal controls are only part of the answer. The next step is to settle two things: what evidence would show that AI has helped a dangerous capability cross into the physical world, and what we will do when it does. ‘Not yet’ is useful information. It is not a plan. The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: Foodcourt operator Singapura Heritage faces winding-up application from poultry supplier
events.summary: The winding-up application comes after several companies linked to the Lao Huo Tang Group appeared in the State Courts over unpaid CPF contributions. PHOTO: SINGAPURA HERITAGE FOOD HALL Singapura Heritage Food Hall, linked to Lao Huo Tang Group, faces a winding-up application by poultry supplier Toh Thye San Farm, filed on Sept 17 and due in court on Oct 23. The notice gave no debt amount or reason. ACRA records show the company is wholly owned by Lao Huo Tang Investments, with Thomas Hong as director. The case follows unpaid CPF issues at other Lao Huo Tang-linked firms, though several arrears were later cleared and charges compounded. SINGAPORE – The operator of Sing apura Herit age Food Hall, an eatery brand linked to Lao Huo Tang Group , is facing a winding-up application filed by poultry supplier Toh Thye San Farm. According to a notice published in the Government Gazette on Oc t 6, Toh Thye San Farm filed the application against Singapura Heritage Food Hall on Sept 17. The application is scheduled to be heard in the General Division of the High Court on Oct 23 . The notice did not disclose the amount allegedly owed or the grounds for the application. According to Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) records, Singapura Heritage Food Hall is wholly owned by Lao Huo Tang Investments. Thomas Hong is a director of both companies and the majority shareholder of Lao Huo Tang Investments. The winding-up application comes after several companies linked to the Lao Huo Tang Group appeared in the State Courts over unpaid Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions. At a State Courts hearing on Oct 6, Hong, who is also founder and chief executive of Lao Huo Tang Group, said he had personally paid off CPF arrears involving Chickita F&B, Soup Empire Holdings, Kenny Rogers (Marina Square) and Kenny Rogers F&B. Lao Huo Tang F&B received a discharge amounting to an acquittal on nine charges, while Lao Huo Tang Restaurant applied for the same outcome on six charges. According to Lao Huo Tang Group’s website, Singapura Heritage Food Hall has two outlets – at Downtown East in Pasir Ris and SingPost Centre in Eunos. Toh Thye San Farm, established in 1979, is a home-grown sole proprietorship involved in processing and distributing meat products, including poultry. The Straits Times has contacted Lao Huo Tang’s management as well as Toh Thye San Farm and its appointed law firm, Lighthouse Law, for comment. Acra/Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority

Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho has slammed criticism of star striker Kylian Mbappe, calling the attacks “ridiculous”. The French captain has come under fire for spending his time recovering from a left knee injury in France and Switzerland rather than Madrid. He suffered a hyperextension of the joint while playing in a Nations League match against Turkiye on September 25. list 1 of 4 What Man City charges anger Liverpool before Premier League game? list 2 of 4 French giants Bordeaux relegated to sixth tier for financial irregularities list 3 of 4 Prosecutors in Maradona death trial seek sentences up to 12 years list 4 of 4 NBA star Wembanyama to French students: ‘I hear you’ The 27-year-old was also pictured at the entrance of a Parisian nightclub and photographed on a bicycle when he was in Switzerland. Some fans claimed it was a deliberate snubbing of Mourinho, who only days before had said players should avoid skiing or riding bicycles to avoid injury. “Are these criticisms over the top? They are ridiculous,” Mourinho said at a news conference on Friday on the eve of Real’s La Liga home match with Villarreal. “All the players who were obliged to be present every day for their recovery were here. “Mbappe came, like the others, to undergo scans in order to be diagnosed. “He then went to see a specialist in France because he has history with his knee, which we cannot ignore.” Mourinho, whose side lost to Atletico Madrid in their last match and already lag six points behind bitter rivals Barcelona, is never one to shy away from a confrontation and tackled each of the criticisms against Mbappe. “Problems involving football are not sufficient for you,” the 63-year-old Portuguese coach told reporters. “Therefore, you have raised the issue of the discotheque, which in fact was not one because it was used for a private event for Fashion Week. “As for the bicycle in Switzerland, it was in a hotel made up of small houses which makes them available so guests can ride to the communal areas, and you would have us believe he was competing in the Tour of Switzerland.” Mbappe, who returned to training on Wednesday, could feature on the pitch as early as Saturday. Mourinho shrugged off the potential of a hostile reception for Mbappe against Villarreal, reiterating that he was “certain” the all-time World Cup record goal scorer has fulfilled “his obligations to Real Madrid”. It is not the first time this season that Mbappe has been subjected to attacks by fans. The Ultras Sur, a Real Madrid supporters group linked to the far right and banned from the Santiago Bernabeu, took issue with him last month. They were furious that before a Real Madrid match, Mbappe, alongside Vinicius Jr and fellow Frenchman Ibrahima Konate, partially rolled up T-shirts bearing the words “ We are all Ceutans “, which was intended to be a message of support for people in the Spanish territory bordering Morocco. Ceuta, a Spanish North African exclave, has been grappling with a migration crisis . Mbappe was also criticised earlier this season over his choice of a location for recovery from a previous injury, which led to an online “ Mbappe Out ” campaign by some Real fans.

They likely face a severe points penalty that could lead to relegation or even expulsion from the Premier League if they fail to overturn the verdict. “The reason why I joined this club is because I completely trust 100 percent the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don’t have any doubt about that,” Maresca said. “I spoke with the club for sure, and we all [have] trust, and the right moment to speak about that is when we win this appeal.” Since an Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008, City have become the dominant force in English football. They have won eight Premier League titles, the Champions League and multiple other trophies over the past 15 years. Maresca, whose side have won all five of their Premier League games this season, rejected the suggestion that those previous successes were now tainted. “Absolutely not,” the former Chelsea boss said. “I know the effort from the players, from the club, from the manager in that time that was Pep. “So I know exactly the effort that the club put to achieve that kind of target.” Maresca to welcome Guardiola’s first return to Man City Guardiola stepped down at the end of last season after a trophy-laden decade at the Etihad Stadium. City travel to Liverpool on Sunday for their first outing since the guilty finding, and Guardiola is set to attend their next home game against Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday. “After 10 years here, he can come at any time he wants,” Maresca said. “I think it would be nice for him. It would be nice for the fans, for everyone.” Maresca had spoken to City’s in-house media on Thursday and said the current players “ don’t care too much about the noise ” currently surrounding the club. The new head coach and his players, however, are set for a hostile reception when they travel to Anfield, the home of their fierce rivals, but Maresca said his players would stay focused on the match. “Probably [it] will be even more warm in terms of environment. But the reason why I decided to be manager is for this kind of game,” he said. “I’m not worried at all. Again, the environment is from the players. It’s nice. “In this moment, we are top of the league, so the players have all the reasons to be happy and excited.”

events.title: Why US support for Riyadh in Yemen matters
events.summary: Faisal’s view Two statements by US Senator Chris Murphy and Secretary of State Marco Rubio signal that Washington takes Gulf security seriously. They have come at a critical juncture for Saudi Arabia and the region. Senator Murphy’s comments carry weight because he has long criticized Saudi policy. Yet he traveled to Riyadh, spent two hours discussing his concerns with the kingdom’s leadership, and publicly stated that Washington can’t achieve its goals alone. This has brought him closer to Riyadh’s view: If the US aims to enhance regional stability, contain Iranian influence, and advance a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, it must work with its regional partners. Secretary Rubio — who is also the US national security advisor — affirmed Saudi Arabia’s right to defend itself against Houthi aggression and Washington’s intention to honor its defense and security agreements with the kingdom. Together, these statements matter at a time when some in Washington advocate a narrower role for the US. They show that American leaders recognize that threats against the Gulf have global consequences. While Saudi Arabia has considerable military capabilities, experience in Yemen, and powerful allies like Pakistan and Türkiye, active US backing remains crucial, both strategically and politically. I write this as a Saudi citizen whose country supports Yemen’s legitimate government. The military operation there aims to restore sovereignty and confront the Houthi militia that’s attacking not just Saudi Arabia and Yemen, but the arteries of the global economy. The Houthis are sometimes misrepresented as a Yemeni faction vying to share power with others in the state. But their slogan — “God is the greatest, Death to America, Death to Israel, A Curse Upon the Jews” — is clear about their objectives and ideology. Allowing them to consolidate control risks turning Yemen into a permanent breeding ground for international extremism and handing another Arab state to Tehran. We need only look at the painful legacy of Iraq to understand the disastrous consequences of allowing Iranian influence to swallow state institutions unchecked. Beyond security, the economic risks are acute. An Iran-backed force dictating traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threatens another chokepoint in the region, a scenario the global economy can’t absorb as it deals with disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Keeping these waters open, which can only be achieved through Saudi-led deterrence, benefits the kingdom, but also serves US and global interests. Some observers may question why Riyadh has turned up the heat now. The answer is simple: It was the Houthis who shattered years of goodwill and unilaterally escalated against the Yemeni government. Saudi Arabia was always clear that it wouldn’t tolerate attacks in the Red Sea or inside its territory. To truly understand Saudi foreign policy — which, at its core, balances diplomacy with resolve — I recently spoke to HRH Prince Turki Al-Faisal, the kingdom’s former intelligence chief, on the debut episode of the Arab Views podcast. Prince Turki traced Saudi Arabia’s engagement in Yemen through the eras of King Abdulaziz and his father, King Faisal, describing a policy shaped by strategic restraint within limits. With the kingdom now facing persistent provocations on multiple fronts from regional proxies, “that restraint is no longer operable,” he said. The Houthis appear to have mistaken Saudi restraint for an inability to act. With the militia stretched thin, Riyadh sees an opportunity to defeat it or force it back to negotiations. Washington’s support isn’t a favor to the Gulf, but rather a clear-eyed assessment of its own strategic interests. By standing firmly with Saudi Arabia, the US is helping protect global trade, confront state-sponsored terror, and ensure that diplomacy in the Middle East is backed by unyielding strength. There is a question of responsibility, too. Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries have suffered severe damage from the US and Israeli war against Iran. Yemen gives Washington a chance to show that they won’t be left to manage the regional consequences alone. Notable Saudi Arabia has been fighting the Houthis in Yemen for almost two decades. This Council on Foreign Relations backgrounder explains the history of the conflict and examines the latest escalation.

events.title: I love spending time with my friends, but it's hard to catch up in a loud restaurant or bar. Enter: saunas.
events.summary: The author says going to saunas with friends is now her preferred social activity. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith Time with my friends is precious, and I never feel like I can truly catch up in a restaurant or bar. I started going to saunas with friends, and it's much more relaxing. Now, it's my preferred social activity. As a working mom of four, I have limited and precious time with friends. For years, I typically met friends for brunch or coffee, and the occasional Mom's Night Out. By default, these get-togethers always felt rushed. Even a long, lingering brunch rarely lasted much more than an hour. At most restaurants, the constant din of conversation and utensils clanging against porcelain dishes made it difficult for me to truly relax and have a heart-to-heart. Yet, there didn't seem to be a viable alternative, so I stuck with the status quo. Things changed when I realized I could access European-style sauna culture in the United States. Travel showed me a different way to socialize As a dual citizen , I travel to Europe frequently. I've known about European sauna culture my entire life. As a child, my grandfather would often disappear to the local bathhouse, which he called "the schvitz." He talked about the perceived health benefits of going to saunas regularly, but even as a young child, I could tell the real appeal was spending time with friends since he rarely went to the schvitz alone. Nevertheless, I initially found saunas too hot and decided they weren't for me. But because saunas and bathing culture are such a big part of European wellness and social culture, I kept encountering them everywhere and begrudgingly tried again, because I didn't want to miss out on enjoying the experience with others, from Iceland to Romania . I picked up some tips that helped me enjoy myself more, like sitting on a bottom bench near the door and covering my head to avoid overheating. Slowly, I realized that I actually was actually enjoying my time in saunas, and I always enjoyed the company. I started seeking out saunas on my own I knew my relationship with saunas had permanently changed during a visit to Oslo with my children. During that trip, I suggested visiting a sauna because I knew it would be a lot of fun and would likely be the highlight of our trip. I was right, and we all had a great time. When I got back home, I started looking to see if there were any nearby I could go to with friends. Social time in saunas shouldn't be reserved just for travel, I reasoned. I looked into gym memberships, but using saunas for recovery with a bunch of strangers wasn't the vibe I was going for. Instead, I booked a massage with a friend at a hotel that had a sauna in its spa. The experience was nice, and I continued to invite friends to join me for an occasional massage and a sweat in the sauna . The author has grown to love going to saunas over time. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith I found what I was looking for near a suburban mall not far from my home Eventually, I found a better solution. A deep dive one night led me to the Balian Springs, a wellness facility inspired by Bali's wellness practices. Although the huge facility near a suburban mall had been open for a few years, I had never heard of it. I couldn't get there fast enough. I found it very similar to a Therme, a wellness facility with several locations in Europe that I had already fallen in love with during my trips across the Atlantic. Both have multiple saunas with different themes, along with other wellness amenities such as thermal pools and hot tubs. On my first trip, my friend Nicole and I jumped from sauna to sauna searching for our favorites — like bar-hopping, but sweatier and non-alcoholic. I loved the pink Himalayan salt sauna and also enjoyed the chromotherapy and charcoal saunas. We also spent time in the facility's warm thermal pools, hot tubs, and rooftop infinity pool, although I decided to skip to the cold plunge and igloo room. Nicole and I were shocked to realize five hours had flown by. "This is so much better than brunch," she said. "Why haven't we done this before?" Although we text daily and regularly grab coffee, I felt as though we hadn't had the chance to truly catch up on a deep level the way we had in the sauna. During our visit, we saw other groups of women celebrating birthdays together by doing cold plunges in swimsuits instead of dressing up and eating cake across a table. Couples were lounging in tranquil pools rather than hitting bars. Moreover, going to the sauna leaves me relaxed in a way brunch never does. I still go out for coffee and brunch with friends, but saunas are now my preferred social activity whenever possible, whether it's a sauna in a hotel spa or a full-day wellness experience. It's not lost on me that I now have my own version of "the schvitz" I once associated with the old way of life my grandparents left behind in Europe. I only wish I had paid attention to my grandparents' ways of spending time with friends sooner. It turns out they were onto something much better than brunch all along. events.title: Zambia agrees health deal with US after resolving dispute
events.summary: The News Zambia signed a $1.5 billion health financing agreement with the US after separating it from a critical minerals deal that is still being negotiated. The health pact had been jeopardized by privacy concerns over sharing citizens’ data. Zambia is among several African countries that have signed bilateral health deals under the Trump administration’s America First Global Health Strategy, but Africa’s second largest copper producer stands out for having publicly resisted key provisions and winning changes. Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe said at the signing ceremony that the two memorandums of understanding “ needed to be decoupled and this has been done .” Washington said the deal was worth $2.49 billion , with Zambia committing $975 million in “new funding” and the US putting up $1.5 billion. Global aid tumbled at its steepest rate on record last year as the US cut its budget by 57% when it dismantled the USAID model of unconditional funding, which researchers say has had an impact on health programs. A Lancet Global Health study published this week found that HIV testing dropped by more than 60% at four providers in Uganda and Zimbabwe, while treatment, which Washington had promised to protect, fell by about one third. “The safety net that was supposed to preserve life-saving treatment did not hold,” lead author Henry Cust said. Know More President Hakainde Hichilema, who secured a second five-year term in August, held out for months against the US demands requiring it to hand over biological specimens and patient data in exchange for the funding. The deal strips out the specimen clause and restricts data sharing to monitoring and evaluation of US-funded programmes. “The government will not be sharing any specimens with the United States,” Health Minister Roma Chilengi said. Zambia joins 35 countries, including several in Africa, which have signed the Trump administration’s America First Global Health Strategy that replaces the old USAID and PEPFAR system. Kenya was among the first to agree, but its courts suspended the deal last December, first due to the data clauses and then because of privacy issues and a lack of parliamentary approval. Ghana and Namibia refused to sign up over concerns about data and specimens, while Zimbabwe lost all US health aid last month. Notable Think Global Health, published by New York-based foreign policy think tank Council on Foreign Relations, found total health spending falls in most deals as the US steps back, by about 14% by 2030 in eight countries, including Mozambique, Lesotho, and Eswatini.

events.title: AI vs. the rest of the economy
events.summary: Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: Data center construction includes construction costs, such as labor, materials, profits of contractors, architectural and engineering work and miscellaneous overhead, interest and taxes. Does not include servers, racks, chips or memory. More and more, it seems as if there's the AI economy — and everything else. Why it matters: The growing chasm between the breakneck growth of the AI world and the slower pace of the economy where most Americans work and live has huge implications, especially for the markets. Zoom in: The most recent numbers on U.S. construction spending through August — shown above — paint the picture remarkably clearly. Zoom out: The same divide is an important theme in the markets as well. In corporate bonds, AI-related offerings accounted for more than half of net investment grade issuance for the year through the end of August, according to data from Apollo and Bloomberg. Data: Apollo, Bloomberg; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips And of course, excitement over all things related to AI has supercharged the market values of Nvidia, the hyperscalers and other AI-related tech stocks. Stunning stat: The weighting of the S&P 500 technology sector in terms of market capitalization is now roughly 40%. That's higher than during the peak of the dot-com bubble. But that actually underplays the impact of AI. If you throw in the hyperscalers Meta and Amazon, which S&P doesn't include in the tech sector, the share of the AI-pilled part of the blue-chip index climbs closer to 50%. Data: FactSet, Axios; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips The bottom line: The growth gap between AI and everything else means the U.S. economy and the markets are increasingly yoked to AI — and all the risks that come with it.

events.title: ‘Indentured servants’: US green card move will hit thousands of IT workers
events.summary: The US is suspending top tech firms, including Microsoft, from a key programme to sponsor foreign workers’ green cards. The United States government has moved to exclude some of the world’s top tech companies from a programme that allows them to sponsor skilled foreign workers for permanent residency. Vice President JD Vance said the action was a response to companies abusing the system to hire lower-paid foreign workers at the expense of US workers. list 1 of 3 Trump’s approval hits new low among Hispanic voters ahead of midterms list 2 of 3 US Supreme Court agrees to take up Trump’s ICE detention policy list 3 of 3 Trump launches midterms campaign blitz amid record low approval ratings It comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration continues efforts to clamp down on immigration – both legal and undocumented – and make it harder for immigrants to get residency or citizenship. But the latest move also potentially impacts thousands of foreign workers, many of whom have spent years waiting for a backlog in applications to clear. Here’s what to know about the latest policy: The suspension concerns the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, which enables a US-based employer to sponsor a foreign worker’s green card — as the permanent residency is commonly known. To qualify, the employer is supposed to demonstrate that there are insufficient US workers for a needed job role and that bringing a foreign worker will not impact the pay or conditions of US workers in the industry. PERM is a key step in the green card process for many skilled foreign workers. Major tech companies often hire workers on temporary visas, such as the H-1B, before they transition to permanent residency through the PERM process. Vance on Thursday accused major companies of fraudulently using the current visa regime to displace US employees and bring in lower-paid foreign workers who amount to “indentured servants”. “The programme has become rife with fraud,” said Vance at a White House news conference. He claimed that many workers who start off on temporary H-1B visas and later apply for permanent residency under the PERM programme are “being mistreated by their employers” and “used to undercut the wages of American workers”. “You’ve got to hire great American workers,” the US vice president said. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.” Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling used similar language, saying the US would “shut down the pipeline of systemic fraud that has flooded our country”. “The fraud doesn’t end with getting the job,” said Sonderling. “That job becomes a pathway for foreign workers and their families to stay in America permanently and eventually (become) US citizens.” “And who pays for it all? The American worker,” he said. Vance singled out Microsoft as a major offender and said it would be suspended from the PERM programme. Other companies whose PERM applications will no longer be processed include US software firm Adobe and some of the world’s top IT firms, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. Of these, Capgemini is French, Microsoft and Adobe are American, and the rest — Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL — are all Indian. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” said Sonderling. Vance said the suspensions would continue “as long as it needs to”. Other companies that rely heavily on H-1B visas such as Meta, Amazon or Alphabet’s Google will not be affected. Have tech firms been abusing US immigration rules? Critics of the H-1B visa and PERM green card process argue that some employers use the system not to fill legitimate skills shortages, but to reduce labour costs, gain leverage over workers and make it harder for US employees to compete for jobs. They say companies do this by hiring foreign workers at lower wages and manipulating recruitment conditions to keep out qualified US workers. Vance said Microsoft last year let go 6,000 US workers, while also securing 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” said Vance. Sonderling said companies being suspended from PERM had received more than 230,000 H-1B visas and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications since 2009. “That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said. The H1-B visa system has also emerged as a lightning rod for many of the most vocal backers of Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, some of whom have married criticism of the programme with anti-immigrant stereotypes — particularly against Indians — to demand that the scheme be scrapped. Microsoft disputed the implication that its visa filings represented new hires replacing US workers.

events.title: The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age
events.summary: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s release When The Social Network came out, Mark Zuckerberg organised a staff viewing of a film he described as “fun” . A group corporate outing to the sequel is unlikely. The Social Network hardly portrayed the Facebook founder and his company in a hagiographical light (Zuckerberg later described the film as “hurtful” ), but there was at least an element of the plucky upstart to the rise of Zuckerberg as he takes Facebook to 500 million users and a valuation of $25bn (ridiculously small numbers now – Meta has 3.6 billion users and is worth $1.8tn). By the end of that film, though, a steely CEO is emerging and his company is on the brink of global hegemony. The Social Reckoning picks up from there, with a clear perspective that both the founder and his company – as well as the industry they represent – are corporate villains now. This is set to be underlined by the release of the OpenAI drama, Artificial, where its CEO, Sam Altman, is reportedly given a deeply unflattering portrayal. Elon Musk completes the villainous trilogy by appearing as himself – aside from the odd deployment of an AI avatar – in Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary, Musk, about the world’s first trillionaire. Tech is the obvious thread joining these films, but another is the scathing portrayal of the company leaders in them. Film villains used to be hoodlums, ex-deep state operatives, people with posh British accents. Tech execs are the new Darth Vader. This is underlined by the casting of Jeremy Strong , who looks a touch on the old side to be playing 2019-2021 era Zuckerberg (the Meta CEO was in his mid-30s at the time of the film’s events whereas Strong is 47), but is embedded in our minds as the tortured Roy family scion Kendall in Succession. Strong also brings a straitjacketed simmer to the role here, one that breaks slightly at the end as he backtracks on being a “free speech absolutist” under intolerable pressure. It is the most human Zuckerberg moment in the entire film. Peter Bradshaw describes Strong’s performance as a “very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet”. It is much less sympathetic than Jesse Eisenberg’s in The Social Network and is a sort of corporeal representation of Meta as the monolithic, corporate bad guy. Elements of the portrayal chime with some former Meta employees, including a whistleblower, Arturo Béjar, who describes it as “accurate” . Another former employee tells the Guardian that Zuckerberg was “unemotional” in meetings (perhaps what you’d expect from a $1.8tn company CEO, admittedly). Well, Strong’s performance certainly is that. There had already been a turning point in public perception of Facebook before the Haugen leaks , with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which raised questions about the privacy of account holders’ data and how it is used. Haugen’s revelations in 2021 compounded this disquiet. By the time of the 2022 inquest for British teenager Molly Russell , who took her own life after watching harmful content on Instagram, regulation of social media around the world was inevitable. The tone of The Social Reckoning and Strong’s performance reflect this shift. In the UK, screenings of the film are carrying an advert for the online safety charity established by Molly’s family, in which her father says : “ ‘ Instagram helped kill my daughter”. Responding to Russell, Meta says it has worked to improve the safety of its platforms. The regulatory, legal and political backlash against social media – as well as the release of The Social Reckoning – reflects a lack of trust in such statements. Strong’s Zuckerberg says in the film that “the debate is over”. If it is, The Social Reckoning portrays a world where Meta is on the wrong side of it.

events.title: New status symbols are taking over this fall. Here's what you'll see everywhere.
events.summary: Maison Margiela; KHAITE; The Row; Getty Images; BI The fall fashion status symbols are loud and luxurious. Think oversize tote bags and sunglasses that look like ski goggles. If that's not your thing, there are also more subtle options — like $640 Khaite jeans. Leaves are falling, the air is crisp, and fashion is expensive. That's the 2026 fall season in a nutshell. When it comes to the latter, you might notice a few trends from fashionable folks as we make our way through autumn. Loud, luxurious pieces are at the forefront again. Sunglasses are statement-makers, bags are bigger, and shoes are distinctive. These are the fashion status symbols men and women are loving right now. This fall, you'll see everyone carrying extra-oversized designer bags. The large Margate bag from Burberry. Edward Berthelot/Getty Images Apologies to anyone who purchased a Coach Brooklyn bag or a Chloé Paddington purse in recent years. In 2026, we're going bigger. Fashion houses like Bottega Veneta showcased massive totes on fall runways, and search interest in "oversize bags" is up more than 5,000% compared with this time last year, according to Google Trends. Some popular options include Burberry's $1,395 large Margate bag , The Row's $3,900 Jean Shoulder Bag , and Bottega Veneta's $5,100 Jodie bag . The most coveted jeans cost between $590 and $820 per pair. Elsa Hosk at a 2026 Khaite runway show in New York City. Aeon/Getty Images Khaite jeans have been around for a while — 10 years to be exact. If you've scrolled through TikTok in the past month, though, chances are that you've heard people rave about Walmart's $30 jeans that some say are a dupe for the brand's luxury pairs. Naturally, that's brought the New York City brand that's loved by celebrities and models — including Elsa Hosk, Hailey Bieber, and Dakota Johnson — back into the spotlight. Khaite jeans are no longer a quiet-luxury staple. Owning the real thing is the ultimate display of wealth and style. The brand's jeans cost between $590 and $820 per pair. The fragrance for fall goes to Dries Van Noten. The Velvet Violet perfume from Dries Van Noten. Dries Van Noten Perfumers told Business Insider that the best scents to wear this fall are woody, gourmand, nutty, and floral. The $350 Velvet Violet perfume from Dries Van Noten is all of those things. It includes notes of violet leaf, grilled tonka bean, and vetiver, among others. The unisex fragrance received rave reviews on TikTok when it was released in July, with many fans saying they'd be wearing the scent throughout the fall. New fans are also discovering the perfume. Google search interest for the scent peaked in late July, but it began rising again at the end of September. Collared shirts are being elevated with script monograms for an expensive feel. Nicole Kidman at the 2026 US Open. Jean Catuffe/Getty Images Nothing says luxury like a monogram. The classic embroidery, which typically features a name or initials in script, has been a staple of menswear for generations. Once a practical feature on clothes, monograms now serve as subtle status symbols . The detail is having a moment this fall, thanks to Chanel. Instead of initials, people are wearing tops featuring the fashion house's monogram prominently on the bodice. Nicole Kidman, for example, wore a striped, collared blouse with Chanel embroidered in red at the 2026 US Open in September. Variants of the top have also been worn by Jessie Buckley and Jacob Elordi this year. One version, from the Métiers d'art 2026 collection, retails for $3,950 . Move over, classic ballet flats. It's all about tabi styles this year. A woman wears Tabi flats during Copenhagen Fashion Week 2026. Edward Berthelot/Getty Images Flats have remained the supreme fall shoe for a few years now, and that's not changing in 2026. The trending style, however, is. Rather than wearing the classic ballet silhouette, people are opting for tabi styles in both flats and sneakers . The most famous split-toe shoes, of course, come from Maison Margiela, where its men's and women's flats cost between $1,050 and $1,750 per pair. Sunglasses look a bit more like ski goggles this season. Mirja Klein wears Phoebe Philo sunglasses in Germany. Moritz Scholz/Getty Images As photos have emerged from fall fashion weeks around the globe, one accessory has made a consistent appearance: chunky sunglasses resembling ski goggles. The oversize silhouette has also been named one of the trending styles for fall across TikTok, where people have showcased their designer dupes from brands like Jimmy Fairly. The real things, though, are the Phoebe Philo Bombé sunglasses. The oversize shades cost $750 and are sold in four shades of brown. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: AI and the climate crisis pose existential risks. The law offers a way to reduce them | Robert Reich
events.summary: AI and the climate crisis pose existential risks. The law offers a way to reduce them Liability lawsuits have held tobacco, oil and pharma companies to account in the past. AI investors won’t ignore this threat The most basic function of government is to protect people from harm. Two growing phenomena – the climate crisis and AI – pose escalating risks of extraordinary harm. The climate crisis is already causing floods, wildfires, drought and record heat. AI agents are already escaping super-secure environments to hack into systems they’re supposed to avoid. Yet Donald Trump and his Republican enablers, backed by big money from big oil and big AI, refuse to do a thing about either risk. In many ways, they’re worsening both. But there’s another way to reduce these risks: through liability law. I have no more faith in the supreme court than you do, but I was struck by the responses of at least half the justices who will be considering an important case that opened the supreme court’s new term, Suncor v Boulder. The case was brought by several Colorado localities against Suncor and ExxonMobil – one of about three dozen filed around the country in which cities and states are demanding that big oil reimburse them for the escalating costs of climate disasters brought on by the burning of fossil fuels. On Monday, at least four justices (Samuel Alito has recused himself) expressed skepticism about big oil’s argument that the Clean Air Act explicitly prevents such lawsuits against polluters. “It’s like, wow, like, where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” asked justice Elena Kagan. Chief justice John Roberts drew parallels between Boulder’s claim and prior lawsuits against the tobacco and opioid industries in which states and localities won significant damages. “I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we’ve allowed them to proceed in state court,” said Roberts. In 1998, the leading US tobacco companies agreed to pay $206bn to cover public health costs and smoking-related expenses. When translated into current dollars, this is more than $423bn. And recall the $20bn paid by BP in 2010 to cover environmental and economic damage to the Gulf Coast after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Or the $7.4bn paid by the Sackler family and Purdue Pharma to resolve liability for the opioid crisis. Such liability lawsuits – the last resort when the public is harmed by corporate malfeasance or nonfeasance – are also relevant to the risks posed by AI. If AI agents escape super-secure environments to release dangerous toxins, or destroy critical water, electricity, transportation, or health infrastructure, AI companies and the tech giants behind them could be on the hook for tens if not hundreds of billions of dollars in payments to those who are harmed. No way major investors in AI – or the insurance companies backstopping AI – are going to ignore this potential liability. The current dollar value of the tobacco settlement – as I said, $423bn – is comparable to what the tech giants spent on AI chips, servers, and datacenters last year. This gigantic financial risk will weigh on the values of AI companies and the tech companies unless or until they become far more serious about protecting the public against such harms. I expect political demands from the AI industry to limit such liability through federal laws that set caps on it and that establish industry-funded “trust funds” to pay for big liability judgments. A sane Congress (we may yet have one) wouldn’t agree without specific industry steps to dramatically increase safety. In all likelihood, the AI industry will also seek government regulations it could use as partial defenses against such massive liability, just as pharmaceutical companies use certification by the Food and Drug Administration that their drugs are safe and effective to defend against lawsuits claiming their drugs cause harm. The big AI investors and insurers will force this issue. More than 200 cases already in the courts involve cyber-liability and AI-related product liability. Follow the money. Insurers are already demanding more effective means of controlling AI risks, and big investors are demanding better means of limiting them. Both the climate crisis and AI pose existential risks to human life on this planet. Liability law is hardly an easy or perfect fix, but it’s an important start. The fact that liability for the climate crisis is already in the supreme court and that four justices seem sympathetic suggests how significant a role liability can play as an incentive for both fossil fuel and AI giants – and their insurers and major investors – to clean up their acts. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com .

events.title: Current price of oil as of October 9, 2026
events.summary: At 6:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil was priced at $105.72 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s a drop of $2.61 compared with yesterday morning and around $40 higher than the price one year ago. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $108.33 -2.40% Price of oil 1 month ago $101.01 +4.66% Price of oil 1 year ago $65.58 +61.20% Will oil prices go up? It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business. Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks. It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks: Brent crude oil , the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) , the main benchmark of North America Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as lower demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with increased global demand, but it soon plummeted alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before—bringing prices below $20 per barrel. All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: Trump’s red-dyed diesel plan is more midterms appeal than gas price solution Economists say Trump’s red-dyed diesel order could raise prices for farmers Iraq devalued its currency as the Iran war squeezes its oil exports Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: Labour fends off the Green party in closely watched UK by-election
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Sagal Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the UK as child refugee from Somalia, won 3,300 more votes than Zack Polanski, leader of the Greens. UK by-election: Labour holds Starmer’s former seat The Labour Party has won an election for a parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer, fending off a challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for the British prime minister. Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali , the leader of the local council, won the seat in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras with 12,292 votes, compared with 8,928 for Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader who came second. list 2 of 4 UK Greens are wrong – Zionism is not racism list 3 of 4 Before UK Greens, who else has equated Zionism with racism? list 4 of 4 Pro-Palestine Greens challenge Labour’s grip on Starmer’s former seat The victory, which had been expected, will buoy Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was recently installed by lawmakers fearful that Starmer’s unpopularity was opening the way for a challenge by the populist Reform UK party at the next national election. After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour looks to have won many voters back, a result that triggered more questions about Polanski’s leadership. There are now five Green MPs, compared with one in 2023. But Polanski, 43, recently came under fire after party members passed a motion declaring that Zionism is racism at their annual conference. The move, which called for “the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine” was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party lawmakers. Polanski did not vote on the motion. Labour has held Holborn since the seat was created in 1983. Labour’s Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the United Kingdom as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for “those who seek to divide us”. “We have a responsibility to defend what we’ve built and pass it on,” she said. After conceding defeat, Polanski, who is not an MP, answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader, and described the result as part of “Andy Burnham’s honeymoon”. Polanski congratulated Abdi-Wali, but said, “One in three voters backed us here, and we know that many more considered it.” Al Jazeera’s Sonia Gallego, reporting from London, said, “The constituency has been going through what some people have been calling ‘ the Burnham bounce ‘ … so far there is a deep sigh of relief (among Labour) that they’ve managed to hold on.” Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has changed voter habits during the past three years. The Greens, far more critical of Israel’s conduct than any other party, got a boost in the 2024 general election. Back then, Starmer won the seat with 49 percent. Andrew Feinstein, a pro-Palestine independent candidate, came second, with 19 percent. Polanski has raised the “progressive vote” while “reducing the Labour vote”, Feinstein said.
