AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters New usage policy cracks down on cruelty to chatbot, alongside slightly more pressing matters of weapons development, surveillance, and election interference Microsoft and Anthropic play invoice tennis with startup's $17,600 Claude bill 1 hour ago AI company moves to defend critical infrastructure and open-source projects from AI 11 hours ago Rust upstart reveals 'reimplementation' of Microsoft Office – with Claude on coding duty 21 hours ago Anthropic reconfigures its cool kids security program 2 days ago Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says 2 days ago Anthropic has updated its rules to stop people being mean to Claude, apparently deciding that its AI chatbot needs protection from the humans paying to use it. The AI developer's latest usage policy prohibits "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its models. The rules take effect November 12, giving users just over a month to get any lingering insults out of their systems. "The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose," Anthropic said. "It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research." So you can still tell Claude it is wrong, but repeatedly berating it for the sheer pleasure of doing so could land you in trouble. It's not clear how Anthropic intends to distinguish between legitimate frustration and gratuitous cruelty, though it says Claude's existing ability to end abusive conversations will remain its primary enforcement tool. Anthropic gave Claude the ability to end certain conversations back in August 2025 as part of its research into what it calls "model welfare." The feature lets some versions of Claude cut off users who persistently subject the models to abuse. It’s worth remembering that Claude is software, not a person, and there's no established evidence that it experiences distress. That hasn't stopped Anthropic from telling paying customers to mind their manners around its chatbot. The etiquette rules are only one part of a broader overhaul covering rather more consequential matters, including election interference, weapons development, and surveillance. Anthropic has tightened its restrictions on deceptive influence campaigns after observing state media outlets, government propaganda offices, and commercial organizations using Claude to operate fake accounts and fabricated news websites. At the same time, it has dropped its blanket ban on personalized political targeting, arguing that the restriction also caught legitimate activities, such as nonprofits translating voter information. Deceptive targeting and misuse of personal information remain prohibited. The company has also clarified that its weapons ban extends to software and components after observing attempts to use Claude to develop guidance and control systems for weapons, including armed drones and autonomous vehicles. Meanwhile, Claude cannot be used to recommend which people police should investigate, arrest, or charge, nor to develop tools for surveillance. Tracking people without their consent is also prohibited, whether in real time or retrospectively. Anthropic says these changes clarify existing restrictions rather than introduce new ones. There are also new requirements for customers connecting Claude to physical equipment capable of causing injury. A qualified human operator must be able to monitor and stop the hardware, which must remain in a safe state if the AI connection drops. The policy overhaul comes as Anthropic tries to address some of the security risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems. The company has also launched a new cybersecurity initiative aimed at helping critical infrastructure operators and open source projects find and fix vulnerabilities using its AI models.

events.title: Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
events.summary: US media reports suggest he may be weighing strikes before the vote but the president has ruled that out. United States President Donald Trump has said that he does not intend to bomb Iran again until the November midterm elections, even though several US media outlets have reported that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to relaunch attacks before that vote. Trump has been accused of misdirection on the issue in the past. The US launched its initial attacks on Iran on February 28, as talks with Iran were ongoing and despite Trump saying just the day before that he had not made any decision. One year previously, the US struck Iran towards the end of Israel’s June 2025 12-day war, despite Trump saying he would announce a decision about attacks “in two weeks”. list 1 of 4 Trump says US will not strike Iran before midterm elections list 2 of 4 US stocks slide as oil prices fluctuate over renewed Iran war fears list 3 of 4 October 7 redrew the map of the Middle East, opening new faultlines list 4 of 4 The Hormuz bonus: Sailor salaries soar for transits amid Iran war Still, striking Iran ahead of the midterm elections would be risky for the administration as the war remains deeply unpopular with Americans. Resuming the war afterwards may have less of a negative impact on Trump, who is not eligible to run for another term as US president anyway. Here’s what we know about Trump’s plans. What has been reported by US media? In the past two days, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and other publications have reported claims by unnamed officials that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to attack Iran before the midterms, if authorised to do so. On Wednesday, US publication Axios cited US and Israeli officials saying the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command (CENTCOM) to prepare for imminent major combat operations. The Atlantic also reported along similar lines. On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social media platform that he will not order a resumption of strikes on Iran before November 3, when the US midterm elections will be held. “I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition…we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” he said. The president added that the US is presently “having productive discussions” with the Iranian side. However, that was also the case on February 28, the day the US and Israel first struck Iran, triggering the war. Trump did not make any reference to preparing for potential military operations, nor did he provide more details on the state of talks. Why might Trump be hesitant about resuming bombing before the midterms? Trump and Republicans are worried about a voter backlash against the war at the polls. The US war on Iran is intensely unpopular domestically as Americans have had to grapple with surging prices of gas, food and other basic commodities because of the crisis in the Middle East. Since the start of the war, surveys have shown that large numbers of Americans did not approve of striking Iran. Now, about 65 percent of Americans say they “disapprove” of the way in which Trump has handled the Iran war overall, according to a Pew Research Center poll released on Thursday. Trump stated at the start of the war that it would go on for just a few weeks, however, it is now into its eighth month. According to Pew, most Americans now believe the war will continue for at least another year. Even Republican or more conservative-leaning voters are growing more negative about the war, its poll found. The conflict has also severely affected Trump’s personal ratings and eroded support for Republicans. A Reuters/Ipsos poll on Thursday found that only 30 percent of his supporters were enthusiastic about voting in the midterms, compared with 48 percent of Democratic voters. About 13 percent of those who voted for Trump in 2024 say they are not sure who to vote for in the congressional elections. Delaying attacks until after the elections could potentially shield Republican candidates from voter backlash, analysts say. While analysts say Trump will see a good performance at the polls as approval for renewed strikes, a Republican defeat at the polls could equally further incentivise him to hit Iran again as he will calculate that he has little to lose at that point. While that could further affect Trump’s ratings, the president is not eligible to run in the next presidential election in any case. Will the US restart the war after the midterms? In recent weeks, the US president has threatened to “end” the war with force after the elections as talks with Iran have dragged on. At a Republican convention in September, he accused Iran of trying to affect the outcome of the midterms and said that conflict “is going to end immediately after the elections”.

events.title: UAE economy grew in first half of 2026 despite impact of Iran war
events.summary: The UAE's real gross domestic product grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to the GDP during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said in a statement on Friday. The results "reflect the continued diversification of the UAE's economic base and the growing role of non-oil activities", the FCSC said. Trade topped contributions to non-oil GDP at 16.2 per cent, followed by financial and insurance (15.2 per cent), construction (13.1 per cent), manufacturing (11.8) and real estate (7.9 per cent). Meanwhile, activities in the financial and insurance sector posted the highest growth rate in the six months through the end of June, rising by 14.8 per cent, the FCSC said. That was followed by information and communication (7.3 per cent), health and social work (6 per cent), construction (5.1 per cent), government (3.6 per cent) and real estate (2.3 per cent). The non-oil sector's "expanding contribution to economic activity demonstrates the diversity of growth drivers and supports sustainable and balanced growth across a broad range of economic sectors", the FCSC added. The UAE's GDP last year grew 6.2 per cent year-on-year to hit Dh1.9 trillion, as non-oil GDP jumped 6.8 per cent to Dh1.5 trillion. In the second quarter of the year, the UAE's real GDP hit Dh476.9 billion, a decline of 2.1 per cent annually. Non-oil activities also contracted by 1.1 per cent, as several economic sectors, particularly tourism, transport and trade, were affected by regional developments and disruption to travel. However, the non-oil sector has started to rebound. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index remained stable at 55.3 in September, the same as August, and well above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. That reading is “another indication that the non-oil economy has moved past the midyear slowdown linked to the Middle East conflict”, S&P said. Business activity in September increased rapidly and higher output requirements encouraged companies to expand purchasing activity and employment, with staffing numbers rising modestly last month, the index found. Demand conditions in the UAE non-oil private sector also continued to improve markedly in September, boosting pricing power and enabling companies to raise their selling prices at the fastest pace in more than 15 years, in response to higher input costs, the report found.

events.title: Ex-OpenAI staff say they were fired for raising safety concerns
events.summary: Three former researchers pen open letter warning of ‘chilling’ effect on company culture. Three former OpenAI employees say they have been fired due to their efforts to ensure the safety of artificial intelligence. Safety researchers Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang levelled the accusations on Thursday after their dismissals last week. The trio warned of a “chilling” effect on other staff concerned about the frontier technology’s risks. list 1 of 4 ICE shooting of New York man in car with five-year-old sparks protests list 2 of 4 Northern Ireland’s Sinn Fein faces police probe as protest tensions fester list 3 of 4 Uproar in NY after ICE shoots man with child in the car list 4 of 4 Mexico prison clash in strife-torn Sinaloa state leaves 10 dead OpenAI said they were let go due to misconduct involving the mishandling of company information. “I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation,” Balesni said in a post on X. Korbak voiced a similar sentiment, expressing his belief that he had been terminated for raising concerns that OpenAI was “losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave”. In an open letter published in tandem with their social media posts, Balesni, Korbak and Wang expressed concerns that their dismissal would make their former colleagues “afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI”. “We could raise safety concerns and disagree openly, and were encouraged to draw on the expertise of independent safety organizations,” they said in the letter. “This is part of what made OpenAI special, and why we are immensely proud to have been part of the team.” The three added that “if the people closest to the risks can no longer work in high-trust, high-bandwidth ways with each other and with third parties”, then AI could not be developed safely. “It is that culture we are writing to defend,” they stated. The trio denied violating company policy, saying any engagement with external safety experts had been in line with the mandate of their roles. “Given the significant safety concerns surrounding the development of AI, employees must not be left working in an environment where fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work and weaken third-party accountability,” they said. “Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.” In a statement, OpenAI said it had uncovered “a significant breach of trust” by the former researchers that went beyond what was described in their letter and said it stood behind the decision to fire them. “We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out,” the San Francisco-based company said. “Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust. We will continue to be extremely forgiving of our team making good-faith mistakes.” OpenAI added that it was saddened by the outcome. “We appreciated Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek’s contributions to AI safety at OpenAI and their willingness to speak up and challenge ideas,” the company said. “We championed their voices, supported their work, and placed enormous trust in them. These decisions were not about them raising safety concerns. We have always encouraged that and always will.” The ex-employees’ intervention comes as OpenAI and other AI companies are at the centre of intense debate about how to ensure the rapidly evolving technology does not expose humanity to catastrophic harm. The risk of cutting-edge AI models escaping human control has been in the spotlight since July when it emerged that autonomous agents generated by OpenAI had hacked the software start-up Hugging Face. OpenAI and its chief rival, Anthropic, have urged the international community to work together on a coordinated slowdown in AI development. However, that suggestion has been rebuffed by the two leading AI powers, the United States and China. Last month, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceXAI and Nvidia endorsed a voluntary accord calling for stronger internal safeguards and the engagement of external auditors to better manage safety risks. The accord, announced by US President Donald Trump, drew a mixed response from AI safety advocates, many of whom criticised its nonbinding nature. OpenAI has announced a number of steps to mitigate risks in the absence of formal regulation, including scrapping the planned release of its latest-generation model, GPT-6.1 Astra. The ChatGPT creator said it decided not to go ahead with the release after its model failed to meet company standards for acting in accordance with human wishes.

events.title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Just before the genocide, 15 Gaza schoolgirls posed for a photograph. Three years on, Al Jazeera went looking for them. Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work. For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems. Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years. Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems. She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities. Asked about the girls she taught before the October 7 genocide began, Maha pauses before reaching for her phone. While scrolling back to find a photograph taken in June 2023, she speaks softly, so as not to disturb the girls in the classroom. “I was proud of them," she says. "I could see that they had bright futures ahead of them. They were very special in their personalities, even before it came to their studies. But October 7 changed the course of their lives.” In the photo, 15 teenage girls in navy school robes and white scarves crowd around Maha in the schoolyard. Some have their arms around one another; others lean towards the camera. All are smiling. They had just finished their mock exams and wanted a photograph together. Sara Rayan took it, holding out the phone so everyone fit in the frame. The girls were 17 and 18. Like many teenagers their age, they worried about exams and university places, talked about what they wanted to become, and imagined the lives that lay ahead. Four months later, Israel's war on Gaza began. Three years on, one of the girls in the photograph has been killed in an Israeli air strike. Four have left Gaza. Others have been displaced - their education interrupted and their plans for the future upended. Al Jazeera set out to find the 15 girls, to discover what had happened to them and the futures they once imagined, and to see whether they could be brought together again for a photograph in the same schoolyard. Muscat Secondary School is still standing, although it was struck by artillery in February 2024 and became a shelter for displaced families. Some classrooms still bear the marks of the war: holes left by quadcopter gunfire, windows damaged by shelling and soot stains where families cooked over open fires. On the walls, children have drawn kites, flowers and a Palestinian flag. Some have written their names: Haya, Marah, Mohammed and Khaled. Displaced families still shelter in parts of the school, while a tent at the edge of the yard serves as a makeshift classroom for younger pupils whose own school can no longer accommodate them. It's just past 10am on a Thursday in late September when Yasmin Abu Zaid arrives. Then Aya Adnan arrives, quickening her pace when she sees Yasmin and pulling her into an embrace. “I haven’t seen you for three years,” she says. “Where have you been? You never show up.” Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader arrives a few minutes later, carrying a plastic bag of books for Aya’s younger sister, who is preparing for the Tawjihi, Gaza’s national secondary school graduation exams. Aya and Lina have seen each other since leaving school. Their families have been friends for years, and they still live in the same neighbourhood of Nuseirat. But Yasmin, who once lived nearby, was displaced early in the war. With the fighting making it difficult to meet, neither has seen her for three years. The three have also kept in touch with Ghaida Zaqout, who now lives in Egypt. Together, they have a private WhatsApp group where they chat regularly and check on one another. When Maha finishes teaching, she greets "my girls" with arms wide open. They erupt into chatter, talking over one another and trying to catch up. In time, Maha pulls up the old photograph on her phone. The girls huddle around her, then point at the tree behind them, recognising it from the photograph. Now, they begin recalling the school days they shared. There were the ordinary intimacies of teenage friendship: who would lend you a pen, who would explain homework you didn't understand, who whispered through lessons and who worried for days about an exam. "These are my girls," she says again. Ghaida was the girl whose laughter could be heard before she entered the classroom, and who rarely stopped talking, even when teachers moved her to another desk. Sara and her twin sister Fatima were forever taking selfies, while Lina al-Hour was quieter, often bringing novels to read during breaks. The girls talked about clothes, television programmes and football. They bought food together during breaks and wondered aloud about university and what they might become. Some dreamed of studying medicine; another wanted to design buildings.

events.title: Power firms cut waste and modernize systems to meet surging demand
events.summary: Power-focused engineering firms are increasingly trying to cut down waste and optimize current systems as they position their commercial offerings for the huge demand growth of the coming decades. ABB has in recent weeks rolled out a portfolio of products aimed at addressing the needs of AI data centers, while Schneider Electric acquired a US industrial software firm for $22.6 billion. Some of these solutions are not entirely new, but the energy demand surge from AI data centers, industrial electrification, and the need for more climate-resilient infrastructure is creating momentum to improve current systems. “There is an opportunity to utilize existing assets more than we are today,” Schneider Electric’s CEO of digital grid Ruben Llanes told Semafor. ABB’s DC-powered data center solutions have been in development for over two decades, electrification president Giampiero Frisio said, but “the business and the market were not ready to do it” before. — Eugenia Perozo

events.title: Octopus looks to buy software startups to manage data center demand
events.summary: Octopus Energy US is looking to acquire more software startups that can help utilities manage the influx of data center power demand, its CEO told Semafor. In March, the company bought the technology firm Uplight, which utilities can use to free up more power in the grid by subtly modulating their customers’ consumption. The company also recently rolled out a battery for homeowners in Texas that can release power to the grid at moments of high demand. “We’re just beginning to scratch the surface of how consumer flexibility can help solve the problem of data centers,” which have an economic disincentive to curb their own power demand, Octopus US CEO Nick Chaset said. Startups like Uplight “are batting above their weight in terms of solving the problem, but that value is not yet reflected in the companies themselves,” he said. “So we’re very much looking for interesting opportunities in that space.”

events.title: Rates for oil tankers hit record high, as more crude passes through Hormuz
events.summary: Charter rates for oil tankers hit a fresh record, driving a larger wedge between the nominal price of crude futures and what it costs to actually receive barrels. Crude oil exiting the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 10 million barrels per day over the past week, despite a rising number of attacks on tankers. But the time required for the largest tankers to rest outside the strait waiting for crude deliveries from smaller vessels has effectively created a tanker shortage. It now costs up to $77 million to hire a large tanker to move crude from the US to Asia, up from less than $10 million last year. Crude futures, meanwhile, fluctuated based more on traders’ perceptions of Trump administration statements than by the flow of physical barrels, which has made them “increasingly unreliable as a proxy for genuine supply,” analyst Amrita Sen wrote in the Financial Times ; the gap between the “dated” and futures prices for Brent is now the highest since the war started . And because emergency crude stocks have already been drained, if Gulf exports fall again, “you do have that $200-a-barrel scenario,” the CEO of trading house Vitol warned . Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency clarified that last week’s G7 commitment to release diesel from strategic supplies will be drawn from the volume originally authorized in March, and not represent any new barrels; European diesel prices jumped 8% on the news . — Tim McDonnell

events.title: A’ja Wilson wins her third straight WNBA MVP and record fifth overall
events.summary: Former US Vice President Kamala Harris among those to hail Wilson as Las Vegas Aces centre continues record run. A’ja Wilson fine-tunes her shooting touch after every practice. That extra work has defined her greatness since being drafted first overall in 2018. On Thursday, she received a voice message from former Vice President Kamala Harris congratulating her on redefining greatness leaguewide after she was named the WNBA’s MVP for a third straight year and for the fifth time overall. list 1 of 4 What Man City charges anger Liverpool before Premier League game? list 2 of 4 French giants Bordeaux relegated to sixth tier for financial irregularities list 3 of 4 CAS promises Senegal-Morocco AFCON title decision within days list 4 of 4 UEFA details FIFA presidential candidate criteria in bid to oust Infantino “Obviously, that is an honour,” Wilson said. “A woman of our history, and I’m so appreciative to be able to share that moment with her through the phone call and the message of her delivering that I won my fifth MVP.” In addition to becoming the first player to three-peat, Wilson won the award in 2020 and 2022. Commissioner Cathy Engelbert, Aces owner Mark Davis and team President Nikki Fargas accompanied Wilson’s mother, Eva, who presented her daughter with the trophy. “Each one of these has not been taken lightly,” Wilson said while flanked by all five of her MVP trophies. “In my heart, they’ve always been so special. But this one here, I cried a little bit harder. This one here is just a little bit different. … When you dream as a young girl, you dream so big and you write your goals out, and you just never imagine that you were able to just check them off. “And when you’re able to check them off – small wins, big wins – it truly means a lot. And so I think that’s why I cried a little bit harder on this one, because 15-year-old A’ja wasn’t sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP. She wasn’t dreaming about being a three-time champion. She was dreaming about surviving this world.” The 30-year-old Wilson once again led the league in scoring with an average of 26.2 points per game while shooting nearly 53 percent from the field. She averaged 9.4 rebounds per game, a career-best 3.2 assists and 1.9 blocks. Wilson has the defending champion Aces back in the WNBA semifinals for the eighth consecutive season although Las Vegas is down 2-0 in the best-of-five series against Golden State. Game 3 is on Friday. “This is great. I love it, not going to take for granted, shine her up, let’s do it,” Wilson said on Thursday. “But tomorrow, when it comes to hoisting it in front of the fans, I love the fans, … but I doubt I will be doing that. I’ll be warming up with my team. … Everyone in this room knows the competitor that I am. Everyone knows what my main focus is, and that is to get a game.” Wilson received 65 first-place votes and nine second-place votes for a total of 713 points from a national panel of sportswriters and broadcasters. Minnesota’s Olivia Miles received six first-place votes and 40 second-place votes (442 points) while Indiana guards Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark followed with 287 and 212 points, respectively. No WNBA player besides Wilson has more than three MVPs. Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson each have a trio. On the NBA side, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar has six, and Michael Jordan and Bill Russell each have five. “A’ja Wilson is one of one,” Fargas said. “She’s now standing in a category that no other WNBA player in the history of the league has accomplished. She’s in the conversations with the Michael Jordans and the Wayne Gretzkys of the world – where she belongs.”

events.title: As U.S. blocks DJI, Insta360 races to win American creators
events.summary: Regulatory clarity and market timing are a boon for smaller Chinese smart-camera maker Insta360 and its independent Antigravity drone brand. Chinese camera maker Insta360 is hoping to gain U.S. market share while market leader DJI remains hampered by national security restrictions. Insta360 is benefiting from the clarity of 2024 regulatory rules while DJI’s new products are barred from FCC approval. Insta360 launched Antigravity as an independent drone brand in 2025, which was incubated in collaboration with third parties. On a Saturday morning in September, dozens of people lined up in New York City’s Times Square to check out pocket-sized cameras made by Chinese camera maker Insta360. YouTubers flew in to promote the products. As part of the marketing campaign, cyclists prepared to bike around the city in bright yellow shirts emblazoned with the Insta360 logo. The Shenzhen-based company was opening its first flagship store in the U.S., a high-profile push to market its smart cameras to content creators, travelers, and sports enthusiasts. It was also a statement of confidence in a market where Chinese technology companies are facing growing scrutiny. There are restrictions, but it’s better to have a clear no than maybe in business.” Chris Pereira, founder of consultancy iMpact “The U.S. is a super high potential market for us,” Max Richter, Insta360’s co-founder, told Rest of World at the store opening. The U.S. accounts for 30% to 40% of the company’s revenue, he said. “You have an amazing outdoor sports community, you have a huge influencer economy, and I think Insta360 really gathers both of these audiences.” Insta360’s optimism and U.S. expansion stand in sharp contrast to the experience of DJI, the dominant Chinese player it’s trying to challenge in the global drone and handheld camera market. DJI dominates the global civilian drone market, while Insta360 last year announced a separate company to make drones. In handheld smart cameras, DJI accounted for 73% of the global shipments, while Insta360 accounted for 20%. California-based GoPro, the pioneer of action cameras, has been largely pushed out of the market . Washington has increasingly treated DJI as a national security risk. The U.S. Department of Defense has labeled DJI a Chinese military company, a decision the company has been fighting for years . The Federal Communications Commission has blocked DJI from selling new drones as well as cameras in the U.S. In the meantime, Insta360 is racing to win American consumers. Both companies are based in Shenzhen, but they took different paths to becoming rivals. DJI was founded in 2006 and quickly became the global leader in consumer drones, with most of its sales coming from overseas. It expanded into handheld stabilized cameras in 2016. Insta360 was founded in 2015 as a camera company. Its early success came from 360-degree cameras, which capture a panoramic view, before the company expanded into stabilized cameras and microphones. Its founder JK Liu had said the company aimed at the global market from “day one,” with a particular emphasis on America. Richter, a German native, first moved to China with a German company. He then worked for DJI before joining Insta360. Insta360 recently entered the drone business. The company announced the launch of an independent drone brand, Antigravity, in 2025, which it said was incubated in collaboration with third parties. The move could help insulate Insta360’s camera business from any future restrictions targeting Chinese drones, Chris Pereira, founder of consultancy iMpact, which helps Chinese companies sell abroad, told Rest of World. The FCC has banned new foreign-made drones from entering the U.S. market, though companies can apply for waivers if they plan to move manufacturing to America. Antigravity obtained FCC’s approval for its drone, A1, just before the rule took effect. Michael Shabun, the Los Angeles-based chief executive of Antigravity, told Rest of World at the store opening that the company was planning to move its manufacturing from Asia to the U.S. in the coming years. Antigravity is positioning the A1 drone, with a 360-degree camera, firmly as a consumer-facing product. Shabun said the company stores all U.S. user data locally and has designed the drone so that it cannot carry more than 50 grams of additional weight, a restriction intended to prevent misuse of the drone for purposes beyond leisure. “They’re built for fun; they’re built for content creation; they’re built for exploration,” he said. events.title: Ken Paxton’s Security for Travel Cost Taxpayers Millions. Just 1 in 6 of His Trips Had a Stated Business Purpose.
events.summary: Illustration by Joel Kimmel for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune. Reference image: ZUMA Press Wire/Reuters Connect. In the summer of 2023, after he was impeached on charges of abusing his office for personal gain, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was suspended and barred from conducting any official business for more than three months while awaiting trial in the state Senate. So, he traveled. Paxton, a Republican who is now running for U.S. Senate, took at least 17 trips over three months, including to resort destinations Park City, Utah, and Vail, Colorado. He visited the Oklahoma town where he owns a vacation lodge and a Utah community with a golf resort, where he later bought four condominiums. State police joined him each time, costing taxpayers tens of thousands of dollars for trips unrelated to his job as attorney general. The Texas Senate ultimately acquitted him on the impeachment charges. But Paxton’s use of the taxpayer-funded detail did not begin or end there. In fact, it stands out compared with his predecessor, fellow elected officials in Texas and other state attorneys general, ProPublica and The Texas Tribune found. Paxton has traveled frequently out of state while listing little on his official calendar, The Associated Press reported last week . ProPublica and the Tribune’s analysis, which included reviewing every publicly available document Paxton’s office says it possesses about his travel, discloses for the first time how few of his trips had a listed business purpose: just 1 in 6. It also found Paxton’s security has cost taxpayers far more than has previously been reported. Since assuming office in 2015, Paxton has taken nearly 1,000 trips with a state-funded security detail, costing $3.3 million. The newsrooms’ review of Paxton’s travel records, obtained through the state’s Public Information Act, could only connect 138 of those trips and $553,000 in security costs to state business. Records detailing the purpose of Paxton’s visits to 36 states and 19 countries do not appear to exist in most cases. These include a trip to a small town in Hawaii months before his family’s blind trust bought land there; 24 trips to Utah, where the trust owns five properties; and 53 trips to Florida, where Paxton and the trust have two houses and a townhome. “If you’ve got all these extra trips, it becomes ethically and morally problematic,” said Chris Toth, former executive director of the National Association of Attorneys General, who has also criticized Paxton’s conduct on other issues. “The ethical question is whether a legitimate security function has effectively become a taxpayer-funded subsidy.” Texas law allows the Department of Public Safety to provide security for key state leaders, including the attorney general, but does not require officials to use it. In fact, Paxton himself hasn’t used it in at least two dozen cases while traveling on official business. Paxton has dismissed opponents’ attacks that he has used the perks of office to benefit himself and has not answered questions about how he vastly increased his wealth as a public servant. He also did not answer detailed questions for this story. ProPublica and the Tribune sent Paxton a spreadsheet detailing travel for which there was no record that he was on state business and asked him to provide additional information if the trips were not personal. Neither Paxton nor his office provided such records. Instead, his office provided a general statement. “Throughout his career, Ken Paxton has faced numerous security threats stemming from his courageous work as Attorney General fighting on behalf of the people of Texas,” his office said in the statement. “Those threats are a direct result of him taking on the cartels terrorizing Texans and some of the nation’s most dangerous violent criminals.” Paxton’s office directed additional questions to DPS. A DPS spokesperson declined to answer the newsrooms’ questions, saying the agency does not comment on its security arrangements. Logs from the Texas Department of Public Safety security detail assigned to Attorney General Ken Paxton show multiple out-of-state trips while he was suspended from office in 2023. Obtained and highlighted by ProPublica and The Texas Tribune An Outlier Among Peers To analyze Paxton’s travel, ProPublica and the Tribune reviewed DPS logs for his security detail and records from the attorney general’s office, including airfare and lodging receipts, per diems and his daily calendars. The records available for his predecessor, Greg Abbott , show a stark difference: Abbott traveled mostly within the state as attorney general, and his security cost $203,000 during his last three years in the office. Adjusted for inflation, Abbott’s security detail cost $7,400 per month. Paxton’s has averaged $24,300. Because the state keeps records only for a limited time, Abbott’s travel expenses and his daily calendars as attorney general no longer exist, so the news organizations could not determine how many of his trips were for business. Records are available, however, for Abbott’s security costs as governor and for Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick . Both are also offered state police security and have been in their current roles as long as Paxton. When compared, the records show Paxton has taken 82 more out-of-state trips with a security detail than Abbott and nearly as many as the governor and lieutenant governor combined. Though DPS security detail records are available for state leaders’ full tenure, Abbott’s office only provided calendars that document business-related activity for his first six years in office. More than two-thirds of the governor’s international trips during those years had a listed business purpose, compared with just two of 25 for Paxton during his full tenure. The governor’s office said it planned to release the remaining five years on Tuesday but only provided five months, saying it needed more time. The attorney general’s records do not show a business purpose for travel to Albania, Aruba, Australia, Costa Rica, the Czech Republic, the Dominican Republic, England, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Malta, Mexico, Poland, South Africa or Taiwan. The share of Paxton’s travel with a documented business purpose peaked early in his tenure, in 2018 and 2019, at 30%, the newsrooms’ analysis found. That aligns with the governor’s share of business travel during that period. Since then, Paxton has taken fewer trips that are documented as state business while increasingly traveling out of state. Last year, just five of Paxton’s 91 trips with the security detail had a listed business purpose. Forty-one were outside Texas. In some cases, Paxton has taken business trips without a DPS detail, an analysis of records from the department and the attorney general’s office shows. events.title: At the movies, tech founders like Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk are in their villain era
events.summary: Movies about Sam Altman, Elizabeth Holmes, Mark Zuckerberg, and Elon Musk are all coming out in 2026. Neon; Philip Pacheco/Getty Images; Sony; BI "The Social Reckoning" leads a wave of new films about tech founders like Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman. Hollywood's obsession with this subgenre reflects our anxiety about who holds power. Get ready for some techno-pessimism at the movies. When David Fincher's Facebook origin story "The Social Network" premiered 16 years ago, it delighted critics with its witty dialogue and nuanced character work. Aaron Sorkin was awarded the Oscar for best adapted screenplay, and Jesse Eisenberg was hailed for his portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg as an aggrieved yet triumphant prodigy. Playing a rising tech titan earned Eisenberg an Oscar nomination and made him synonymous with Zuck — not a bad thing in 2010, when Zuckerberg was crowned Time's Person of the Year . A lot has changed since then. These days, Eisenberg would rather not be associated with the tech wonder whose wealth, influence, and impunity have more in common with that of an oligarch than a scrappy college kid. Eisenberg declined to reprise the role for Sorkin's new pseudo-sequel, "The Social Reckoning," and Jeremy Strong took on the part instead. "He simply did not want to be conflated with Mark Zuckerberg anymore," Sorkin told Vanity Fair of Eisenberg. "He doesn't like kids coming up to him in airports with business cards that say 'I'm CEO, bitch' for him to sign." "The Social Reckoning," out Friday, reflects Eisenberg's change of heart about Zuckerberg on a macro scale. Gone is the smug, impish charm of Eisenberg's hoodie-clad Harvard dropout . Now, Strong's Zuck has tailored suits and the severity of a tyrant. Facebook — now Meta — is no longer the dorm-room startup that launched a billion friend requests; the company is depicted as a sinister and relentless force, a tool that kids use to bully each other and extremists use to spread hate speech. The movie's climax dovetails with the January 6 insurrection , which Zuckerberg watches unfold from his "war room." It's far from the only movie this season to paint a tech titan's rise to power as a sobering sign of the times. "The Social Reckoning" premieres the same day as "Musk," Alex Gibney's super-sized documentary about Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, an incisive, nearly four-hour affair that Musk has decried as a "hit piece." Next week, there's " You Can See Everything ," a genre-bending documentary that locks co-director Nathan Fielder in a chilling tete-a-tete with Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes as he probes her psyche before she reports to prison. On Christmas, you can enjoy Luca Guadagnino's "Artificial," a biopic that depicts OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as amoral, manipulative , and Machiavellian , according to early reviews. Don't count TV out, either: Graham Moore's "The Altruists," a Netflix limited series that tracks the rise and fall of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried , is coming in November. Unlike the movies that defined the 2010s wave of techno-optimism, like "The Social Network" and the 2013 Steve Jobs biopic "Jobs" — both Sorkin-penned stories that map a founder's rise onto the classic beats of a hero's journey — this new wave of tech movies courses with an undercurrent of dread. If the 2010s proved tech companies have great power, these new movies are reaching for their subjects to recognize that they also hold great responsibility. The next act of a billionaire's origin story is about consequences — or lack thereof Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Reckoning." Sony During the climactic insurrection scene in "The Social Reckoning," flickers of guilt and panic pass over Strong-as-Zuckerberg's face as he hears the news. The Facebook CEO's infamous "free-speech absolutism" is being put to the ultimate test, as President Donald Trump shares a slew of posts cheering on the rioters. Although Zuckerberg ultimately agrees, at the urging of his inner circle, to suspend the president's account amid the violence, the movie ends with a reality check: Meta has since abandoned fact-checking , not just for politicians and political ads, but for everything. Trump's Facebook account was restored in 2023. It's a bleak postscript to the far more triumphant final title card of "The Social Network," which is presented as a kiss-off to Harvard's then-president scoffing at Facebook's earning potential: "Mark Zuckerberg is the youngest billionaire in the world." The end-credits song is "Baby You're a Rich Man" by The Beatles. While "The Social Network" wasn't entirely kind to Zuckerberg, it reflected a sense of wonder about what he'd accomplished, and all the bigwigs he had to piss off in the process. There's a reason "I'm CEO, bitch" became a cultural touchstone — that precocious, defiant swagger felt revelatory at the dawn of social media's imperial age. For a generation of millennial founders, it was downright inspiring. As a companion piece, "The Social Reckoning" is forced to grapple with the positive PR its predecessor gave Zuckerberg, whether intentionally or not. The real Zuckerberg has undergone his own evolution (or, some might argue, devolution) during his reign as CEO, accelerating his free-speech-at-all-costs rhetoric and cozying up to Trump in his second term as president. Zuckerberg's portraiture in pop culture has become more caustic and ominous to match. In "The Social Reckoning," Strong-as-Zuckerberg insists that Facebook should not be a referee for hate speech and misinformation, but a "public square" for all self-expression to coexist. "It's a business," he declares in one scene. "You know why we don't fact-check ads? Because we don't have to." The movie makes the consequences of this policy clear. Most of the action centers on the whistleblower scandal of 2021, when former Facebook employee Frances Haugen leaked tens of thousands of internal documents. The trove included evidence that Facebook's algorithm was designed to spread inflammatory content, push its users into extremist groups, and prioritize "profit over safety," in Haugen's words. "Mark has been surrounded by people since he was 19 years old who told him he was doing a great job," Haugen later told Bloomberg , calling for him to step down as CEO. She added, "We can demonize Zuckerberg, but it's not going to make him heal faster." "The Social Reckoning" makes this point, too, dotting Zuckerberg's orbit with preening yes-men, crisis PR experts, and wardrobe specialists. Still, the film doesn't let him off the hook. In one scene, when he's presented with an initiative to improve safety measures for 38% of Facebook users — in exchange for losing about 1% of engagement — Strong plays the CEO's reaction with icy indifference. He opts to keep the engagement. Big Tech's promise is starting to look like a threat Elizabeth Holmes in "You Can See Everything." events.title: Dell pledges $1,000 to Trump Accounts of employees' kids, and says it will become a standard benefit in corporate America
events.summary: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images Tech giant Dell is planning to put a $1,000 in its employees' children's Trump Accounts. CEO Michael Dell said this week that such donations will become a standard corporate benefit. Dell is closely linked to the program as his family foundation has donated $6.25 billion. Dell is joining the list of companies paying into the Trump Accounts of its employees' children. "We plan to provide a one-time $1,000 contribution for eligible children of our team members, in addition to any government seed contribution for which the child qualifies," a Dell company spokesperson told Business Insider. The company is still working through the logistics and guidance from the US Treasury, the spokesperson added. Employees can apply for and contribute to their children's Trump Accounts and receive the government's one-time contribution in the meantime. Trump Accounts , launched on July 4, are a new investment program designed to help children grow their wealth. If your baby is born between 2025 and 2028 and is an American citizen, the government will deposit $1,000 into the account. Companies, including Goldman Sachs, Micron, and Chipotle, have also announced plans to match the government's $1,000 contribution for their employees. On Wednesday, Michael Dell, the founder of Dell Technologies, told Fox News that he believes donations to Trump Accounts will become "a standard benefit" at many companies. Dell is closely tied to the Trump Accounts scheme . His family foundation, which he leads with his wife, Susan, has donated $6.25 billion to the program, and he has made regular appearances alongside the president over the last year to promote the investment program. The Dells' donation is set to land in Trump Accounts this week as a $250 contribution for eligible recipients. To qualify , recipients must be born between 2016 and 2024, and live in a ZIP code with a median family income of $115,000 or less, based on US Census data. By the end of the week, 25 million accounts will have received the $250 lump sum, Dell told Fox News on Wednesday. Have a tip or story to share? Contact this reporter via email at pthompson@businessinsider.com or Signal at Polly_Thompson.89. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely . The Dell Foundation has long focused its philanthropic efforts on children, education, and economic opportunity, aligning with the mission of Trump Accounts. "We did research in our foundation and found that, when a child has even a small amount, they're much more likely to have greater life outcomes," Dell told Fox News. Being close to the president has also brought Dell's company some free publicity. On several occasions, Trump has told reporters to "go out and buy a Dell computer." In April, following one such endorsement , Dell's shares popped by as much as 9%. Since the Dell Foundation announced its donation in December, the president has purchased more than $1 million in Dell stock. In April, he sold at least $50,000 worth of Dell shares and possibly as much as $100,000. Read the original article on Business Insider

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Vegalabs says $21,168 in unused Azure credits expired as separate Marketplace charges piled up Anthropic asks users to stop being mean to Claude 3 hours ago India’s tech giants shrug off changes to USA’s skilled visa program 10 hours ago AI company moves to defend critical infrastructure and open-source projects from AI 13 hours ago Rust upstart reveals 'reimplementation' of Microsoft Office – with Claude on coding duty 23 hours ago Windows Search learns to take orders 1 day ago A Norwegian startup says it ran up a $17,600 bill using Claude in Microsoft Foundry after assuming its Azure credits would cover the cost. We reported a similar case in March , involving third-party model charges that weren't covered by Azure sponsorship credits. This time, the customer says Microsoft and Anthropic each directed it to the other to resolve the charges. Vegalabs AS says it received $25,060 in Azure credits through Microsoft for Startups and deployed Claude in August, expecting its analysis workloads to use that balance. However, Microsoft's sponsorship rules exclude Anthropic models purchased through Azure Marketplace. Vegalabs says Microsoft attempted to collect $16,500 from its card, with the invoiced total subsequently reaching $17,600 before tax. Vegalabs says it monitored the sponsorship portal, which continued to show available credits while separate Marketplace charges accumulated. Microsoft's Claude deployment guide says credit-only sponsored subscriptions aren't supported, but accounts with a card on file will have that card charged instead. The company says it deleted the deployment within an hour of discovering the charges. Its card issuer declined the attempted payment over suspected fraud, and $21,168 in unused sponsorship credits expired on September 8. Vegalabs acknowledges it did not read the credit exclusions or configure a budget alert. It disputes neither the usage nor the documented rule, but says the deployment interface failed to make the separate billing clear. Its request for a waiver then bounced between Microsoft and Anthropic support. The Register has seen communications from Microsoft directing the user to Anthropic. "Marketplace transactions are processed through a separate billing pipeline associated with the third-party publisher. As a result, Azure Support does not have the ability to directly waive, refund, or adjust these Marketplace charges on the customer's behalf." "If Anthropic approves the request, they can initiate the appropriate refund authorization through Microsoft." Anthropic support, however, said Microsoft did not require its authorization to process a refund and directed Vegalabs back to Microsoft. Vegalabs says four of the seven support replies it received were AI-generated, including both responses from Anthropic. It says those responses incorrectly described its account as an "Azure Student Sponsorship." We asked Microsoft on October 6 if it had any comment on the situation, but beyond an acknowledgment and a request to let us know what Anthropic had to say, the company had nothing further to share. We also asked Anthropic for its take on the situation, but the company did not respond. Microsoft's rules distinguish between credit-covered services and separately billed models offered through the same platform. Vegalabs' experience suggests that distinction needs to be clearer where customers deploy them. For now, the company has a bill and two support teams directing it elsewhere.

events.title: McKinsey top exec: AI is making workers, not companies, more productive
events.summary: McKinsey's Eric Kutcher said AI has increased workers' productivity more than that of the organizations they work for. Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Fortune Media McKinsey's Eric Kutcher says AI is boosting workers more than organizations as a whole. The firm's North America chair said companies must rethink how they work to achieve broad gains. Software is a bright spot: AI has helped developers generate more code and release features faster. AI is helping workers get more done, though not necessarily delivering broad benefits for the organizations that employ them, according to a top McKinsey & Company executive. Eric Kutcher , a senior partner and chair of McKinsey North America, told reporters at the company's media day on Wednesday that outside specific areas such as software development, many of the hoped-for productivity increases have yet to materialize across companies. "You have people that are getting more productive as individuals, but they're just changing some of the work that they're doing," he said. Until companies look at the scope of work across an organization and identify inefficiencies in the system, it's hard to generate sweeping increases in output , Kutcher said. "We have not gotten enterprise-level productivity, with the exception of a few areas," he said. Early on, he said, many companies' attempts to supercharge workers' productivity meant giving them access to tools like Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT and, in some cases, telling them to use them as much as possible. Kutcher said that some companies even ranked who was using the most AI tokens "without realizing those tokens cost money." That gap between workers' and companies' results shows up in McKinsey data. In August, the consulting firm's AI division, called QuantumBlack, reported that in a survey, eight in 10 respondents said AI had increased their productivity. At the same time, the survey found that the share of respondents who said that AI had contributed to their organization's profits from core operations — before interest and taxes — was essentially flat from a year earlier, at 37%. Kutcher said the technology's benefits have materialized in areas such as software, where developers have used AI to generate more code . That can translate, he said, into quicker releases of new products and features. More businesses appear to be trying to turn the productivity boost software developers have seen from AI into broader results. McKinsey's survey showed a six percentage-point increase from 2025 to 2026 in the share of organizations using AI that were moving beyond experimentation and pilot phases into "scaling" mode. Many organizations, Kutcher said, "are trying to figure out right now, 'How do I shift from this individual productivity into the institutional?'" To make that shift, Kutcher said, some companies are rethinking a key part of their business, from end to end. For a life-sciences company, that might mean considering how AI could remake research and development; for an oil-and-gas company, it might mean new approaches to drilling. "You pick the area and say, 'How would I do this profoundly differently?'" he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I've been with my boyfriend for two years and don't know his salary
events.summary: Watch: How soon into dating do you talk about your salary? We ask New Yorkers and Londoners You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns? Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all. We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries. Willa says she doesn't know what her partner earns even though he knows her salary Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all. "It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says. Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return. He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does. "He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'" Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees. "It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills." Vik says if someone brought up salary and spending on a first date they probably wouldn't be the right person for him For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple. Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone. Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make". Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship." He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy". "If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me". Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates. "I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me." For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily". Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think". "In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility." Emily's been in a relationship for two years and has not discussed salaries yet Becoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though. Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make". She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask. "Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it. events.title: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
events.summary: Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm. "I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X , external alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees. On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures". OpenAI repeated these claims , external on Friday morning in a note from research leaders. "We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said. "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment." The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society. The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company. Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value. The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI". Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote , external : "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave. "I believe that was why I was fired." OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks. "We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X , external . "Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last." events.title: Scoop: AI companies plot "day after" scenarios for public revolt
events.summary: Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies are privately gaming out scenarios for a public and political revolt after a catastrophic AI event . Why it matters: These officials anticipate a large-scale event, most likely a cyberattack, that shuts down access to financial services, internet connectivity, or even power and water. The first example of significant real-world harm caused by unsafe AI would turn an already wary public further against the technology and its leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, as well as President Trump for reluctance to regulate it. The risk: While scenario planning is common within many companies and national security settings — the Pentagon has been running war games for decades — the difference is that many top AI researchers and executives believe a major incident is inevitable . "OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," a company spokesperson said. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable, but are meant to help us prepare for a variety of circumstances." Anthropic declined to comment. Zoom in: The blame game will start whether a rogue-agent swarm breaks containment from an internal testing environment or a bad actor finds unexpected ways to use available models. A recent campaign targeting South Korean financial organizations — including reported breaches at two banks — shows the damage one person can do. A hacker from China allegedly used AI tools from China-developed models, including DeepSeek, to steal data from tens of thousands of bank customers. The attacker used Claude Code to ask for help finding places to sell the stolen data, according to cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike . Top AI planners assume Democrats, ascendant after the midterms, will move fast to shut down AI but will face significant challenges. An aging Congress, out of touch with the AI revolution, could find itself out of its depth. The global economy is now heavily intertwined with an AI infrastructure buildout. Slowing it down could hit an already fragile economy hard. Too many open-weight models exist that can already be freely downloaded and used to cause harm, a problem most cybersecurity pros see as solvable only by using AI to fight rogue AI . Between the lines: The planning involves red-teaming for worst-case scenarios. It focuses mainly on racing to educate members of Congress. Company executives know regulation has no chance of passing right now, but still want to shape the legislation and policies U.S. leaders will turn to after a first catastrophic event. What we're watching: Many AI industry insiders told Axios they believe a major event will occur in the next six to 12 months. Even with Democrats in control of the House and Senate, the companies see fractured politics as the norm, including within the Democratic Party. Some of the most heavy-handed Democratic proposals include banning superintelligence or pausing advanced AI development. Others have bipartisan support and even some industry buy-in, including a required kill switch on advanced AI. But experts have questioned the viability of trying to turn off all AI systems. The bottom line: In a real crisis, Washington can set partisan differences aside. One Democratic aide pointed to cooperation during COVID and the 2008 financial crisis.

events.title: 3 rules for making money on Airbnb, from a short-term-rental owner who built a business by optimizing revenue
events.summary: Real estate investor Mike Savage and his family reside in South Carolina. Courtesy of Mike Savage Short-term rentals can earn more than long-term rentals, but they require a business mindset. Mike Savage, cofounder of SynergyStays, shares strategies that can help Airbnbs perform better. Pay attention to the median booking window, and focus on weekdays, not just weekends. Mike Savage has owned both long-term and short-term rentals — and he sees a fundamental difference between the two. With a long-term rental, investors can improve a property and potentially raise the rent, but the market largely determines what a comparable home can earn. A three-bedroom, one-bath house will generally command something close to what similar homes in the area rent for. A short-term rental offers more room to influence revenue, but it also requires more work. "You're choosing to open a business" when you buy a short-term rental, Savage told Business Insider. Investors need to think beyond the purchase price and location to operations, maintenance, guest communication, hospitality, marketing, photography, and listing descriptions. Savage started buying short-term rentals in South Carolina in 2017. At the time, he said, simply leaving guests a nice note and a bottle of wine could be enough to earn five-star reviews. Today, with stiffer competition, that's no longer enough. Savage, who quit his day job as a firefighter to invest full time and grow SynergyStays , a revenue-management business for short-term-rental owners, shares three strategies he uses to help properties perform better. 1. Pay attention to the median booking window Short-term-rental owners often focus on occupancy and average daily rate, or ADR. But Savage thinks an equally important metric is the median booking window: how far in advance guests typically book a given date. Knowing that number can help owners decide whether to hold their rates or lower them. Savage added an accessory dwelling unit, or ADU, to his South Carolina primary residence, creating another source of rental income. Courtesy of Mike Savage If guests in a market typically book about 30 days ahead, for example, an owner trying to fill a date 60 days out may be able to hold rates relatively high. There is still time for demand to materialize. Once a property enters its typical booking window, however, it may be time to consider lowering rates. Owners should try to avoid relying on last-minute bookings, which can force them to offer deeper discounts to fill empty nights. Savage called falling into that last-minute cycle "probably the No. 1 flaw" among owner-operators who manage their own properties. 2. Focus on weekdays, not just weekends It is relatively easy to fill Friday and Saturday nights, Savage said. The bigger opportunity is often Monday through Thursday. That means owners should review their calendars for nights that aren't earning money — then make it easier for travelers to book them. One common mistake, Savage said, is setting overly restrictive minimum-stay requirements. An owner may require a four-night booking for a high-demand summer period because they want to avoid short stays and maximize revenue, but that can also keep the listing from appearing in searches by guests who want a two-night trip. Instead of blocking those shorter stays entirely, Savage suggests giving guests the option to book them at a higher rate while offering discounts to travelers who book longer visits. The same thinking applies to cancellation policies. A strict policy may seem like a way to protect a property owner from last-minute cancellations, but it can also discourage potential guests looking for flexibility. "Removing as many restrictions as possible" can increase a listing's visibility, Savage said. Owners can then use pricing and discounts to encourage the booking behavior they want. 3. Don't try to appeal to everyone For Savage, one of the biggest shifts in short-term rentals is the move toward more personalized search results. Instead of asking how to get a listing onto the first page for every traveler, he thinks owners should ask: "Who am I going to show up on page one for?" Savage is a former firefighter and EMT who now invests in real estate and runs SynergyStays full-time. Courtesy of Mike Savage Airbnb can use a guest's search and booking history, past reviews, and stated preferences to surface homes that fit their needs. A traveler who has previously highlighted family-friendly features, for example, may be more likely to see listings that clearly promote a fenced backyard, a quiet cul-de-sac, or a pack 'n play. That makes specificity more valuable than trying to create a generic home that appeals to everyone. "It's counterintuitive. We just want as many people as possible to want to book our home," he said, but a property designed around a distinct guest profile — such as families with young children, remote workers, or pet owners — can draw guests willing to pay more and leave stronger reviews because the home met their particular needs. "We don't need everybody to want to book our home," he said. "We just need a specific avatar that we can speak to better than everybody else — and that's how we win the game."
