events.title: China and EU trade envoys seek ways to ease tensions over growing imbalances
events.summary: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union are wrapping up two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over growing imbalances between the two giant economies BEIJING -- The top trade envoys for China and the European Union were wrapping up two days of talks Friday aimed at calming escalating tensions over growing imbalances between the two giant economies. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic traveled to Beijing saying it was crucial that the negotiations deliver “tangible outcomes” in rebalancing trade between China and the 27-nation bloc. It was unclear, however, if the two sides would find the will to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($410 billion) last year. China is pushing for the EU to stop blocking its imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington's behest. Sefcovic said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an October deadline for meaningful results on trade rebalancing. Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire. Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms. ISIS-inspired mass shooting plot at Mall of America thwarted, FBI says Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries. Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing. Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China's global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year. The EU's trade deficit with China widened to 103.34 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the April-July quarter, as imports rose to 153.63 billion euros ($172.3 billion) ,while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56.4 billion), according to EU statistics. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters SPONSORED POST: Vendor roadmaps set the pace of change in most enterprise software estates. Origina argues the business should. Most enterprise software estates run to somebody else’s calendar. End-of-support dates, license model changes and needless upgrades arrive on the vendor’s schedule, and the IT team absorbs them: the migration nobody budgeted for, the re-platforming that displaces a project the business actually asked for, the patch cadence that is really a product roadmap in disguise. Origina, an independent provider of software maintenance and support, puts figures on the pressure. As a rule of thumb, up to 90 percent of IT budgets go on “keeping the lights on”, leaving only 10 percent for anything new. Enterprise software costs, it says, are on course to rise 40 percent by 2027, and most of that increase is driven by vendors rather than by customers. The alternative it argues for is not standing still. It is to decide, on the business’ terms, what changes and when. A system that is stable, compliant and doing its job does not need upgrading because of a vendor-driven deadline. It needs to be supported, secured and kept in step with the business until the business has a reason to move. That reason might be a merger, a new operating model or a real step change in capability. It should not be a support deadline. That is the case for building flexibility into long-term planning from the start, rather than buying it back later at a premium. On the estate’s biggest lines, this is how it looks. Perpetual VMware licenses stay supported for as long as they are useful, instead of moving to a subscription bundle on someone else’s timetable. SAP environments run beyond standard support windows, and modernization programs are planned properly and executed when it makes business sense. Plus, the whole estate is protected against the vulnerabilities that are actually exploited, not the tens of thousands that are merely disclosed. In 2025, 48,000-plus vulnerabilities were published, but only around one percent of these were ever used in an attack. Origina’s OPTAS service proactively identifies, prioritizes and addresses issues before they become a problem. Beyond the budget, one of the constraints most IT leaders feel first is people. The engineers who understand a long-lived SAP estate or a sprawling VMware footprint are scarce, and every unnecessary migration keeps them tied up with work the business never asked for. Independent support helps you to free up resources you can invest in innovation and growth. Control, in the end, is the ability to say not yet, and to mean it. Explore your options: find out how Origina supports VMware and SAP on your timetable, and how OPTAS protects the estate in between. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Chap who took the job left a trail of wreckage – and invaluable case studies – in his incompetent wake Techie was stung by a wasp, held overnight by Chinese police, then trapped in a 13-hour meeting 7 days ago Techie assumed boss knew what they were talking about and killed Exchange by deleting data 11 days ago Project leader thought his team understood the plan, ended up fixing their 'interpretation' of it 14 days ago Your cloud survived everything except the real world 18 days ago Techie fixed Wi-Fi dead zone with a drill 21 days ago Welcome to another installment of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed Friday column which often shares your stories of what happens when incompetent people climb the greasy pole and send their failures straight back down into the lap of tech support. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Preston," who wrote to share his story of working as a field service tech in the late 1990s. "I'd risen to the rank of senior field service engineer and was offered a position in consultancy," Preston told The Register . He turned it down because he liked working at the coal face, and the people he worked with there appreciated his skills. "As soon as I arrived at clients, someone was making me a coffee just as I liked it," Preston explained, "so I turned down the consultancy position." One of Preston's colleagues took the promotion and was soon working on projects such as reconfiguring Windows NT 4.0 and the servers it ran on to handle two CPUs, configuring backup systems, and ensuring uninterruptible power supplies (UPSes) were in place to keep things alive. Preston kept doing his own thing, but the character of his job soon changed. "Within weeks, I was getting assigned calls where upgrades had gone wrong, UPSes were failing, and backups were not working." Preston realized the chap who took the promotion was making basic mistakes on almost every job – some of them so bad that one customer refused to work with the newly minted consultant. One of the jobs that eventually landed on Preston's to-fix list saw the consultant wipe a customer database that his backup regime did not protect. At another site, he created a system that pointlessly powered down every day and botched the installation of the UPS that would have saved his bacon. Preston covered as best he could to protect his company rather than the incompetent "consultant." He eventually quit the IT services caper and became a trainer. "I used these incidents as examples of what to look out for when installing and fault finding on customer sites, and also as a lesson on why you should never rely on the person who does a job before you getting things perfectly right." events.title: Oil headed for weekly gain on impact of Middle East tension and Hurricane Isaias
events.summary: Oil prices slipped on Friday after US President Donald Trump ruled out launching attacks on Iran before the midterm elections next month, although crude remains on track for a weekly rise amid lingering geopolitical tensions. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was trading 0.82 per cent lower at $103.42 a barrel at 10.35am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was down 0.74 per cent at $90.81 a barrel. Brent is on track to post a weekly gain after settling more than 4 per cent higher on Thursday, amid the tension in the Middle East. WTI is set for a weekly decline despite the US, the world’s biggest oil producer, bracing for a powerful hurricane that could threaten its oil output on the country's Gulf coast. “Brent crude rose 4.1 per cent to $104.20 per barrel on Thursday as renewed Middle East tensions coincided with disruption to US Gulf of Mexico production from Hurricane Isaias,” said Nick Stadtmiller, chief economist and group head of research at Emirates NBD. “Around 63 per cent of US Gulf oil production has been shut in ahead of the storm, while prices came off their intraday highs after President Donald Trump said the US was holding productive discussions with Iran.” Hurricane Isaias is moving towards the US Gulf coast, which is home to offshore oil production sites, as well as refining infrastructure and export terminals. The hurricane is expected to hit the US coast late on Friday or early on Saturday. It is forecast to lead to heavy rain and potentially flash floods. About 500,000 barrels per day of capacity are at risk from the hurricane, said Soojin Kim and Edward Bell from MUFG. "Ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis are keeping the geopolitical risk in oil markets elevated while shipping in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz continues to be threatened," they said. The Houthis carried out deadly attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia's southern region and Riyadh this week, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile damaging civilian sites in the kingdom's capital. Meanwhile, Mr Trump on Thursday said he had no intention of ordering attacks on Iran before the midterm elections take place next month, which has temporarily eased supply concerns. In a post on Truth Social, he said Iran was in a “very bad condition” economically and militarily and the US blockade on Iranian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz would remain in “full force”. He added that the countries were holding "productive discussions". Impact on oil prices Oil prices have remained volatile this week as attacks on ships in the strait, a vital route for global crude shipments, increased. The US also announced new sanctions on 17 vessels responsible for transporting millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, as well as petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets in southern and eastern Asia. The US is looking to squeeze Iran’s oil revenue and put pressure on Tehran as the regional war continues. The US Treasury is "starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

events.title: Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
events.summary: Published 9 October 2026, 04:41 BST Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings. The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests. Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn). One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not to take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said. Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta. It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region. The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street. Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC. Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment. The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear. A humming annoyance or jobs boom? Life next to 199 data centres Published 26 October 2025 AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost? Published 3 September UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO. "We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors. He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans. "It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC. This kind of listing is a test of how willing companies are to keep "ploughing money" into AI, said Phillip Wool, chief research officer from Rayliant Investment Research. Investors in Firmus would be buying into a company that is still in its early stages and is likely to need to borrow large sums of money, Wool said. "It's more like a bet on a dream", he added. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment , thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to. There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more. That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create . In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public. The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each. AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought. events.title: Sale rescues landmark WA dairy brands from collapse
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mundella yoghurt returns to shelves as deal revives collapsed WA dairy brands Mundella yoghurt was established in Western Australia in 1974. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Emerging processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets of collapsed Mundella Foods and Margaret River Dairy Company. The companies were put into liquidation in August, leaving creditors owed millions of dollars. Yoghurt production is expected to start near Margaret River before the Christmas period. A late rescue deal and sale is set to keep two landmark West Australian dairy brands on supermarket shelves. Mundella Foods and the Margaret River Dairy Company went into liquidation in August, with creditors owed millions of dollars. Local processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets, including processing facilities in Perth and Margaret River, for an undisclosed sum. Mundella Foods' operations near Mundigjong will not be used for processing by the new owners. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Artisanal Market managing director Kevin Sorgiovanni founded another well-known WA dairy and juice brand, Harvey Fresh. He said he had been interested in buying the companies back in 2023, when they were sold by Chinese-owned Manassen Foods to The Cheeky Cow, which has since collapsed. "We saw the Mundella and Margaret River business as a great opportunity for the South West and also to add some value back to the WA dairy market." Mr Sorgiovanni said both brands of yoghurt would be manufactured at the export-approved Metricup processing facility near Margaret River. Artisanal Markets will mothball Mundella's original manufacturing facility at Mundijong, near Perth, because of its poor condition. Artisanal Markets is jointly owned by PenAgri Group and Research Corporation. Mr Sorgiovanni told the ABC the new ownership had plans to target the Asian market for broader sales. There are hopes to export Mundella yoghurt to Asia. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) "We want to do more than just the WA market," he said. Mr Sorgiovanni said production at the Metricup facility would start at 2 million litres a year, but it had the capacity for 10 million litres. The revival is welcome news for dairy farmers across southern WA, but challenges remain. WA Farmers Dairy Council president Ian Noakes said he was keen to see how Artisanal Market would secure milk supply. Ian Noakes has welcomed the sale. ( ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia ) "Most of the milk in WA is contracted, and the main companies are not very good at letting a bit of milk go to somebody else," he said. "So it would be a matter of waiting probably until somebody comes out of contract to get a milk supply." Mr Noakes hoped the additional competition would improve the price points for local dairy farmers. events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Top of the Week TSMC and GF inked a $2B manufacturing agreement , under which GF will manufacture silicon interposers for TSMC’s CoWoS advanced-packaging ecosystem at its Malta, New York fab. Volume production is expected to ramp in the first half of 2028. Applied Materials and Intel are expanding their R&D collaboration to develop next-gen transistors, interconnects, and advanced packaging technologies, combining work at Applied’s EPIC Center in Silicon Valley with Intel’s R&D operations in Hillsboro, Oregon. Rapidus launched Rapidus CORE , a global ecosystem framework intended to support customers from chip design through manufacturing for its planned 2nm foundry business. The first phase includes 17 design-service partners. Xanadu and GF formed a multi-year manufacturing partnership to move ultra-low-loss silicon nitride photonics and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors onto GF’s 300mm production line in Malta, New York. Big hauls Wolfspeed received a conditional commitment for up to $1.5B in 30-year U.S. government financing to expand domestic SiC materials and wide-bandgap power-device production. Vinci raised $250M in Series B funding at a $1.5B valuation to expand its AI-powered physics simulation platform . The platform models thermal, thermo-mechanical, and fluid behavior during design, with simulations reportedly running in minutes rather than hours or days. Oratomic raised $475M for its neutral-atom quantum computing hardware. VEIR raised $110M for superconducting power delivery technology for AI data centers. Atomic Machines launched with $250M for its Matter Compiler system that builds micro-machines from code , including an electromechanical micro-relay to cut power in 800VDC data centers during a fault. Financials TSMC (Sept. revenue) and Samsung (Q3 guidance). Analysis Global semiconductor sales reached $159.7B in August, up 8% from July, with year-to-date sales topping $1T , reports SIA/WSTS . McKinsey expects inference to account for about 60% of AI compute by 2030, driving demand for custom accelerators, HBM, chiplets, advanced packaging, and silicon photonics. Silicon photonics, CPO, and optical networking are emerging as the next U.S.–China semiconductor battleground as AI data centers outgrow electrical interconnects, says Wilson Center , which estimates China accounts for 56% of global optical-transceiver manufacturing capacity. Brookings estimates the U.S. AI buildout could require $10.3T through 2032 for data centers, power, networking and specialized chips, but it warned that increasingly complex financing could obscure financial risks. Lithography ASML and Carl Zeiss researchers outlined a hyper-NA EUV lithography architecture with a numerical aperture of at least 0.75, potentially enabling features as small as 5nm, more than one-third smaller than current high-NA systems. The technology could be ready in about a decade, although commercial production remains uncommitted. Canon says its nanoimprint lithography technology is entering the final stage toward full-scale mass production. DUV immersion lithography is the strongest remaining chokepoint on China’s AI-chip production, contends think tank Center for Technology & Statecraft . It estimates Chinese-owned fabs had accumulated more than 330 DUVi systems by 1Q26 and says continued imports could significantly narrow the U.S.-allied AI-chip manufacturing advantage. The report calls for a China-wide ban on DUVi exports, servicing restrictions and tighter controls on critical components. Memory Samsung is reportedly planning ~$3.9B in investment in memory-chip testing facilities in Vietnam . Netlist and Micron entered into patent license and settlement agreements covering Netlist’s portfolio for server DIMMs and high-bandwidth memory, ending all pending legal proceedings between the companies. Micron faces a potential walkout at its Taiwan facilities after workers voted overwhelmingly to authorize a strike over profit sharing. Toshiba plans to invest approximately $380M to double HDD production capacity for AI data centers by fiscal 2027, compared with 2025 levels, reports Nikkei Asia. Security and export controls Arteris won an additional $3.3M through the U.S. government’s Trusted and Assured Microelectronics initiative to expand its third-party IP (3PIP) security assurance program in collaboration with BAE and SiFive . The U.S. DOJ charged the owner of California-based Earthmade Computer with allegedly smuggling more than $300M in export-controlled computer servers to China . Prosecutors allege the servers contained high-end U.S.-manufactured GPUs and were routed through Malaysia and Singapore using false end-user and destination information to evade U.S. export controls. Meanwhile, CSET researchers modeled more than 10 million scenarios for detecting diverted AI chips and found ping-based location verification to be the most cost-effective approach. However, they cautioned that implementation costs and complexity could limit its usefulness, and said that combining PLV with targeted physical inspections could improve enforcement. Recognition Silvaco CEO Wally Rhines was inducted into the National Academy of Engineering for his co-invention of the blue-light-emitting diode and decades of leadership in the semiconductor/EDA industry. In Germany, X-FAB broke ground on a new cleanroom in Erfurt, and Mitutoyo opened a new semiconductor measurement and inspection center in Dresden. HCSS warns that Europe risks losing its strong position in polysilicon unless production capacity grows fast enough to meet rising domestic and global demand. Asia Elephantech plans to open an advanced packaging center in Tokyo in March to support process development, prototyping, and scale-up for AI-server packaging and PCBs. AMD is working with 14 South Korean AI semiconductor and technology companies to develop heterogeneous computing systems that combine AMD CPUs and GPUs with Korean AI processors, reports SBS News. Cadence and Jilin University unveiled their CAE Multiphysics Joint Laboratory in China . The organizations also have a computational fluid dynamics joint lab. Towa plans to invest approximately $32M in a new molding equipment plant near Kyoto, Japan , to expand production capacity for advanced packaging. Americas CSIS examines the trade-offs between restricting exports of U.S. AI technology and expanding global adoption of American chips and models, recommending targeted export controls and faster domestic innovation. events.title: Audit firm fined $100,000 by Abu Dhabi's ADGM regulator
events.summary: The Registration Authority of ADGM has imposed fines totalling $100,000 on an audit firm at Abu Dhabi's financial centre over regulatory failings. The action was taken against PKF Accountants and Business Advisers, an ADGM-registered audit firm, and its registered audit principal, Saranga Lalwani, the authority said in a statement on Friday. It has imposed a fine of $65,000 on PKF and $35,000 on Ms Lalwani. The decision was taken after an on-site inspection conducted by the authority to assess PKF’s compliance with ADGM's auditor rules and the quality of its audit work, the statement added. During the inspection, the authority said it identified "significant deficiencies" in an audit conducted for an ADGM-registered entity by PKF and Ms Lalwani. The deficiencies included "failures to conduct the audit and prepare the audit report in accordance with International Standards on Auditing (ISA) as required by the Companies Regulations (Auditors) Rules 2023 and failure to exercise due skill, care and diligence in carrying out the audit", the authority said. The inspection identified that PKF "rebutted the risk of fraud in management override of controls, which is a mandatory fraud risk and cannot be rebutted under ISAs". The firm was also accused of failing to assess fraud risks, failing to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence, inadequate audit documentation, and insufficient evidence demonstrating the audit principal's involvement in the audit process. "Registered auditors and registered audit principals are expected to conduct audits in accordance with applicable professional standards and exercise appropriate skill, care and diligence," the authority said in the statement. "This action reinforces the importance of robust audit practices and demonstrates that failures to meet regulatory requirements will result in appropriate enforcement action." Authorities in the UAE have cracked down on entities that breach regulations as part of efforts to maintain the financial system's integrity and reliability. The Dubai Financial Services Authority this month imposed a Dh401,000 ($109,200) fine on wealth management firm Vault Wealth for conducting transactions without authorisation.

events.title: Frasers Hospitality CEO to step down; COO to lead company and report to Frasers Property
events.summary: Fraser Suites Singapore along River Valley Road, one of the company’s assets. Frasers Hospitality CEO Eu Chin Fen will step down on Jan 1, 2027, after key milestones, including the 2025 privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust and the 2026 portfolio optimisation. Chew Hang Song will lead the lodging business as COO, reporting to Frasers Property group CEO Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi, with a focus on global brand growth and third-party management deals. Eric Gan will head hospitality investment and asset management under group investment, supporting an asset-light strategy and stronger capital partnerships across hospitality and living assets. SINGAPORE – Eu Chin Fen will step down as chief executive officer of Frasers Hospitality, effective on Jan 1, 2027, Frasers Property said in a statement on the morning of Oct 9. Chew Hang Song will lead Frasers Hospitality as its chief operating officer, reporting to Frasers Property’s group CEO, Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi. This follows the achievement of strategic milestones: the privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust in 2025 and the completion of its portfolio optimisation in September 2026. Eu, 55, has decided to pursue personal interests, with the hospitality platform now well-positioned for its next state of growth, Frasers Property said. It added: “To sharpen operational focus and support efforts to enhance real estate portfolio value, Frasers Hospitality’s leadership structure will be strategically segmented, aligning with group resources, and reporting into senior group leadership.” Chew’s role will involve driving global brand stewardship for the lodging business, expanding the portfolio through third-party management agreements and overseeing operations at its properties worldwide. Meanwhile, Frasers Hospitality’s current chief financial officer, Eric Gan, will lead hospitality investment and asset management under group investment. He will report to group COO Tony Lombardo. As managing director of group investment, Gan’s focus will be on investment strategies and asset portfolio management across hospitality and the wider living sector. Sirivadhanabhakdi said that the move to house hospitality investment and asset management within group investment aligns with its asset-light strategy for the sector, “connecting (its) real estate platform to institutional capital and enabling (it) to grow (its) capital partnerships more dynamically”. Empowering the lodging business under Chew, meanwhile, allows the team to scale the brand globally through management contracts, he added. Sirivadhanabhakdi said: “(Eu) has helped build a resilient global brand, established trusted partnerships and nurtured a strong hospitality executive team. Our evolved structure builds on that foundation by giving each part of the business clearer focus and optimised resources.” Eu joined the group in 2011. She worked closely with group leadership on the $2.1 billion Frasers Hospitality Trust portfolio optimisation. The stapled group was taken private in October 2025 via a trust scheme of arrangement. Frasers Property closed at 94 cents, down 1.05%, on Oct 9. THE BUSINESS TIMES

CCS is seeking public feedback on Eneos Apac’s proposed acquisition of Chevron Singapore, and will decide if the deal breaches section 54 of the Competition Act 2004. Chevron Singapore runs fuel retail, storage, terminal and lubricant businesses in Singapore and Vietnam, and would keep the Chevron and Caltex brands if the deal goes ahead. Eneos says the takeover should not harm competition because there are many rivals, low entry barriers, and customers can easily switch suppliers; public submissions close at 5 pm on Oct 16. SINGAPORE – The Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCS) is inviting public feedback on the proposed acquisition of Chevron Singapore – a distributor of petroleum products – by Eneos Apac, a subsidiary of energy, resources and materials group Eneos. The authority on Oct 2 accepted the companies’ application for a decision on whether the proposed transaction would infringe Section 54 of the Competition Act 2004. Chevron Singapore is a subsidiary of Chevron South Asia, which is indirectly wholly owned by Chevron Corp. It is primarily a downstream petroleum company with operations in Singapore and Vietnam. In Singapore, Chevron Singapore engages in the retail distribution of fuels and lubricants. It holds an equity interest in Singapore Refining Company, a 50:50 joint venture with Singapore Petroleum Company. Chevron Singapore’s activities also include fuel storage and terminal operations, and lubricant blending and wholesale. The company operates under the Chevron brand in the Republic. Caltex, for retail petrol and diesel; Delo, for commercial and industrial lubricants; Havoline for passenger vehicle lubricants; Star Mart, for convenience retail offerings at service stations; Texaco, a legacy brand in fuels and lubricants; and Techron and Techron D, for fuel additives. Meanwhile, Eneos is a Japan-based energy, resources and materials group with global operations. In Singapore, it is active in the trading of crude oil, naphtha and refined petroleum products, lubricants blending and wholesale, the supply of marine fuels and solar energy solutions. The company mainly operates under the Eneos brand. If the proposed acquisition were to be completed, Chevron Singapore would continue to operate under the Chevron and Caltex brands. Eneos would “step into Chevron’s current operations in Singapore”, CCS added. Chevron Singapore would continue to source Chevron-branded products and raw materials mostly from Chevron Corp. Eneos Apac believes that it overlaps with Chevron Singapore in the market only for lubricant blending and wholesale supply in the city-state. The proposed transaction will not raise any material competitive concerns, “given the significant number of existing competitors, relatively low barriers to entry and expansion, and ability of customers to multi-source and switch among credible alternative lubricant suppliers in Singapore at minimal cost”. Eneos Apac also submitted that no material vertical effects are anticipated. Chevron Singapore faces significant competitive constraints in its active markets, such as fuel refining, storage and terminal services, retail distribution of fuels and lubricants, it said, while Eneos has a limited market presence in lubricant blending and wholesale in Singapore. CCS invites views from the public on the impact of this proposed acquisition on competition. Submissions – via its online form or through e-mail – will close at 5 pm on Oct 16. THE BUSINESS TIMES CCCS/Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore

events.title: Adidas accuses Australian label White Fox of ‘trading off its reputation’ with use of four-stripe branding
events.summary: Global sportswear brand is suing online retailer in the federal court for selling clothes featuring ‘deceptively similar’ design Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Global sportswear brand Adidas claims Australian label White Fox is trying to trade off its reputation by infringing its distinctive three-stripe trademark. Adidas is suing the online fast-fashion retailer in the Federal Court for selling clothes with a four-stripe design, which it argues is deceptively similar to its classic design. White Fox rejected repeated requests to stop selling and promoting clothing bearing the four parallel stripes, its rival claims. During the first mention of the dispute on Friday, Adidas’s barrister Patrick Flynn SC argued the Sydney-based company had been using the stripes as a trademark for months. He pointed to a picture of a White Fox-endorsed influencer wearing the company’s four-stripe shorts with genuine Adidas shoes as a promotion that would confuse consumers. “There’s an intention to trade off our reputation,” Flynn said. Adidas has held the trademark for a three-stripe design in Australia for more than 50 years and successfully sued another retailer for infringement over shoes bearing four stripes in 2013. It meant the action filed against White Fox in September was “not uncharted territory”, Flynn noted. “This is a pretty simple matter,” he said. White Fox’s barrister Ed Heerey KC said the Australian company would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label’s clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark. He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands such as fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons, and Shein. “Obviously Adidas has a reputation,” Heerey said. “Their own slogan is that it’s the brand with three stripes. Emphasis on the three.” The boutique will interrogate whether the use of four stripes was deceptively similar to Adidas’s trademark and whether any consumers would actually be misled. Get the most important news as it breaks He noted the 2013 judgment in favour of Adidas found it was common for branding to be placed on the side of shoes, but there was no such common practice for clothing. Adidas is seeking orders that will prevent White Fox making clothing with four stripes and force it to hand over profits it made on the products. Justice Ian Jackman – brother of one of Australia’s most famous exports Hugh Jackman – set the dispute down for a hearing in early 2027. It marks the first high-profile litigation of this kind against White Fox Boutique, which has become a major player in the retail industry since it was launched in Sydney in 2013. Co-founders Georgia and Daniel Contos, who own the company with Daniel’s mother Melina Maceri, focused on social media and influencer marketing to build their brand. The online retailer later expanded to the US and UK and generated $542m in revenue in the year to June 2025. Meanwhile Adidas, which generated a record $39.9bn in 2025, has vigilantly defended its three-stripe trademark across the globe with varying success. The sportswear giant recently lost its trademark infringement cases against luxury brand Thom Browne in the US, UK, and Germany. The upcoming battle in the federal court could prove to be a battleground for Adidas in a world of fast fashion and prolific imitation.

events.title: So long, Spokes: GitHub rewrites storage to restore reliability, just in time for agentic hordes
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Octocats claim 35x write improvement There can be only one: Google Cloud casts Gemini as your enterprise AI hero 14 hours ago OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties 1 day ago Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism 2 days ago OpenAI tries disarming AI angst with cute graphics and always-on agents 9 days ago AI models keep posting screenshots showing sensitive data from inside tech companies 9 days ago Responding to unprecedented demand from AI agents, GitHub is rebuilding its Git storage architecture from scratch. Early tests with the new architecture show a promising 35x write improvement in internal tests. GitHub will need a miracle of that proportion just to keep up with customer demand. The plan involves decoupling writes from reads, offloading maintenance, and letting object storage manage redundancy. Most impressive is that the redesign is happening under the hood, with the goal of a non-disruptive change that won't alter developer workflows, review processes, or security controls. Running an enterprise-grade code repository means supporting “large engineering teams running busy CI pipelines alongside growing fleets of agents. Supporting these teams means building Git infrastructure for sustained, concurrent reads and writes at a scale few repositories reach today,” wrote Brian Celenza , GitHub principal software engineer, in a blog post describing the updates. Celenza did not offer a timeline for this ambitious migration. When GitHub’s customers shifted their coding focus to AI agents, activity on the platform spiked significantly. Between September 2025 and August 2026, GitHub traffic doubled, from 218.2 billion events per month to 473.3 billion. In September alone, commits hit 7.38 billion, a 5x increase from September 2025. This shift in traffic is stressing the system. According to the GitHub Availability Report , the service suffered 10 incidents in April alone that degraded performance. Another nine incidents landed in May, with each generating more bad publicity than the previous one. GitHub's current storage architecture, nicknamed Spokes , uses a three-phase commit protocol, storing full repo copies across multiple local disks and requiring a quorum of replicas to acknowledge each write. While this approach ensures strong reliability, it bottlenecks write speed, as every push is bounded by the slowest replica required for quorum. The new architecture writes a commit only once, to Azure Blob Storage , an object store service that automatically handles replication (and hence redundancy) on its own, eliminating the quorum bottleneck. GitHub also gooses performance by separating read requests into their own channel, a job handled by lightweight compute workers. The only coordination between reads and writes is over the reference branch pointers. Maintenance duties – such as compaction and garbage collection — are moved from the serving path to operate as background processes, further reducing system lag. GitHub seems to be on the same page with others in rethinking Git for the agentic age. Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke launched a Git-hosting service called Entire , which offloads agent traffic to mirror repositories, allowing a customer’s core GitHub repos to just serve the core development traffic. SpaceX subsidiary Cursor, which uses Git to back its agent-support service, also refined the storage layer for better performance. Cursor engineers also rejected Spokes’ three-phase commit in favor of uploading pushes into an object storage write-ahead log (WAL), which captured all changes as immutable objects, caching at least one copy on super-speedy solid-state disks. While it's cathartic to hate on a service that often goes down, you have to feel empathy for the GitHub engineers who, when they created the service, couldn’t have guessed what they signed up for.

events.title: Virgin unveils its future cross-Channel train as it gears up to take on Eurostar
events.summary: Group plans to launch services from London in 2030 and hopes to outshine competitor with design inspiration from its airline, cruise and hotel arms Flash interiors, fancy food and maybe even a bar: Virgin has unveiled a mock-up of its future cross-Channel train, with a pledge to create “something genuinely new”. The group is planning to launch rail services from London to the continent in 2030, with Eurostar facing competition for the first time since the opening of the Channel tunnel. Virgin has ordered 12 high-speed trains from the manufacturer Alstom, matching Eurostar’s for speed at up to 190mph (300km/h) but aiming to outshine the incumbent on design and customer experience. While Virgin’s last stab at reimagining UK train travel may have peaked with the talking toilet seat on its intercity services in 2013, it has said the future trains will draw inspiration from its airline, cruise and hotel arms. Although details are being kept under wraps, it said it would draw on Virgin Atlantic’s airport lounges, or Clubhouses, for “pre-departure and onboard social spaces” with “more flexibility to work, relax or socialise in style”. Food will be influenced by its cruise line menu and the design by its Virgin Hotels brand. Virgin Trains is expecting to introduce 20 daily return services between London, Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam from 2030, adding almost 7.5m seats a year to the cross-Channel network, creating up to 1,000 new jobs. Josh Bayliss, the chief executive of Virgin Group , said: “Virgin has a proud history in UK rail. With our latest venture we are drawing on more than four decades of experience across travel and hospitality to create something genuinely new. “We’re confident that more journeys between the UK and Europe will be made by train. We’re adding capacity for millions more international rail journeys each year, growing the market as a whole. We’re looking forward to seeing our distinctive red and black trains travelling across Europe.” Virgin also hopes to connect its rail and airline networks, potentially bringing passengers from France for Virgin Atlantic flights. It will also wrap the train service into its loyalty platform so that passengers can earn points towards other types of Virgin travel. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The Office of Rail and Road on Thursday published an agreement with Eurostar for Virgin to maintain its trains at the Temple Mills international depot near Stratford in east London, with track access in the UK confirmed until at least 2040. Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia is also expected to launch cross-Channel high-speed services. It already runs international trains as far as Paris and recently announced its own €2bn order for 19 new trains from Hitachi, some of which are expected to be based in France and run through the tunnel to London.

events.title: Sydney trader sacked for working from Singapore without permission wins unfair dismissal case
events.summary: Employee had also been in Bali when he told his manager he was working from home, Fair Work Commission hears Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast A Sydney currency trader who was sacked for working from Singapore without approval has won an unfair dismissal case, but failed to be awarded compensation. The Fair Work Commission ruled on Wednesday that Charles Graham had been unfairly dismissed by HIFX Australia, trading as Xe, in December last year. Graham was sacked after his manager asked an IT worker to use his “FBI skills” and track the IP address on Graham’s laptop. They discovered he was working from Singapore. It was also later discovered he had previously worked from Bali after telling his manager he was working from home because he had a plumber “coming around to sort out some recurring bathroom issues”. Graham was sacked as Xe found he knew he had to get prior approval to work overseas and was to attend the office three times a week. He said he had been holidaying in Singapore before his partner became ill with a bacterial infection, preventing him from returning to Australia. He provided documentation, which he said showed his partner required medical treatment. Graham had previously asked Xe if he could relocate to Singapore, but his request was denied. Fair Work Commission commissioner Alana Matheson said that after the company sent an email to Graham advising him of its discovery on 17 November last year, the “tone … had clearly pivoted” by the following day, when he was told “there was a case to answer regarding alleged breaches of company policy”. Over the following 10 days, a series of further email exchanges and a discussion between Xe managers took place. Graham said in his written response to Xe that he travelled to Singapore for a holiday and that there was no relation to his previous request to relocate there, that the decision to reschedule the return flight to Australia was made over a weekend, and that as there was no expectation or precedent that he contacted his manager outside business hours, he could not inform them of this. He said that when he did log on from Singapore rather than in Australia “he was bombarded with triaging hundreds of unread emails from his time off, fielding inbound calls and dealing with an eligible complaint from a high-value client”, and this took priority over telling his manager he was stuck overseas. Among his other responses was that he only intended to spend a short amount of time overseas, he had not been told about specific policies regarding hybrid work, and that he had intended to let his manager know he was overseas as soon as practicable. The company was not swayed and on 2 December last year sent him a termination letter that stated it had carefully reviewed his written submissions and found that he had not provided flight screenshots with his name, medical evidence that showed his partner was unable to travel, an adequate explanation for not telling his manager he was in Singapore, and had previously complied with “absence and approval processes”, demonstrating that he was familiar with them and had instead made “a conscious choice not to follow” them. Our Australian morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters “Your conduct represents a serious breach of company policy, a failure to follow lawful and reasonable instructions, and an irreparable breakdown of trust and confidence,” it said in the letter. Graham told the commission he worked remotely twice before November 2025: the previous year from Townsville, and in April and May 2025 from Bali. He had been employed by Xe for 20 months. But his manager said she had not been aware he had ever worked remotely from overseas. A Microsoft Teams message from Graham to his manager was included in evidence before the commission that detailed his claim he was working from home as he had a plumbing issue during one of the days he also told the commission he worked from Bali. Matheson found that she was satisfied that the dismissal of Graham was unreasonable because while there was a valid reason for his dismissal, the process followed was procedurally unfair. This was because Xe failed to fully raise the matters it was relying on in making the decision to dismiss Graham, Matheson said. She found that reinstatement was inappropriate but also decided against awarding compensation. This was, she said, in part because his misconduct contributed to the decision to dismiss him, and he was paid four weeks in lieu of notice.

events.title: US bars Microsoft, Adobe and Indian IT firms from worker visa programme
events.summary: The Trump administration has accused Microsoft , Adobe and a half-dozen other companies of abusing a US worker visa programme. The companies have been suspended indefinitely from the longstanding immigration initiative that’s served as a crucial talent pipeline for Silicon Valley and Wall Street. The suspensions, announced on Thursday by US Vice President JD Vance and Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling, included information technology services giants Cognizant Technology Solutions, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. Those companies, either based in India or with large operations there, are often called outsourcers for their role offering contract IT work to other businesses. At a briefing in Washington, Mr Sonderling said there were multiple federal investigations under way into the use of a system that allows US employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency. “We are cutting off the head of the snake — the companies that enabled this abuse for decades,” Mr Sonderling told reporters. Mr Vance singled out Microsoft, the world’s third most-valuable company, for what he characterised as exploitation of the programme. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” he said. In a statement, Microsoft defended its use of visa programmes and said that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information. Adobe and the Indian companies named didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Shares of Microsoft fell more than 1.3 per cent in New York trading on Thursday, while Cognizant reversed earlier losses and was up more than 5 per cent. Shares in Indian IT services firms including Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys rose on Friday. Mr Vance’s comments assailing Microsoft came hours before US President Donald Trump honoured the company’s chief executive, Satya Nadella, with a National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to highlight US scientific leadership. Last week, Mr Nadella joined other tech industry leaders at a White House luncheon to discuss safeguards for artificial intelligence. “Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them, they do a lot of important things,” Mr Vance said. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company. It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.” The latest move takes aim at the Permanent Labor Certification Programme, or Perm, which allows companies to sponsor a foreigner who has been working in the US under the H-1B and other visa holders to become a legal permanent resident, the first step to becoming a US citizen. Silicon Valley’s reliance on foreign workers has long been a flashpoint in the debate over immigration. Since Mr Trump’s return to office last year, the administration has seized on those concerns and pressed tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers. As part of that effort, Trump has moved to make it harder for companies to use H-1B visas to attract foreign talent, targeting a major source of workers for the industry. The changes have included proposals for $100,000 filing fees for most candidates and tightening the rules of how the H-1B visas are awarded in an annual lottery, giving priority to companies offering the highest salaries. In his remarks, Mr Vance urged US-based companies to shift their policies to employ more US workers. “Stop defrauding the American worker. Stop importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do,” the vice president said. Immigration crackdown The suspensions marked the latest move by the Trump administration to crack down on both legal and undocumented pathways to migration, an effort that’s narrowing a key path linking global scientific and engineering workers with US companies across a range of sectors. In a nearly simultaneous announcement on Thursday, the administration also said it had opened investigations into foreign exchange visa holders at nine top colleges including Harvard University, Stanford University and MIT. The sweeping fraud probe is focused on J-1 visas, which at universities are often held by international PhD candidates and visiting scholars. During the Thursday summit where Mr Nadella was honoured by Mr Trump, the administration announced plans to inject more than $100 million into education programmes for American researchers in science, technology, engineering and math. The initiative seeks to boost the number of scientific researchers who are American citizens and reduce the reliance on foreign talent by companies and universities. Representative Pramila Jayapal, a Washington Democrat, faulted the administration’s decision and said that the Perm programme has a clearly delineated process that’s designed to make it beneficial to the US economy and to ensure that it doesn’t take jobs away from American citizens. “You don’t fix a broken immigration system by taking a hammer to legal immigration,” Ms Jayapal said in a statement. “Targeting Microsoft or the Perm programme in this way simply undermines legal immigration and weakens America’s ability to innovate.” Companies like Microsoft often use the H-1B programme to bring in foreign workers and then help some of them remain in the country through the system. Through the third quarter of the 2026 federal fiscal year, which ended September 30, Microsoft had filed about 1,680 such petitions for permanent status, according to Department of Labour data. In its statement following the suspensions, Microsoft said that of the 6,000 total H-1B visa applications it submitted in the most recent fiscal year, 80 per cent were to extend or change the status of current company employees. “These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1 per cent of our US workforce,” the company said on its corporate blog. The Permanent Labour Certification Programme is a major retention tool for Microsoft, which has a reputation for helping employees with work visas seek permanent legal status. The Redmond, Washington-based company has long bolstered its US-based workforce with employees in the country on H-1B visas, as well as visas for intracompany transfers and recent university graduates. Outside the tech industry, Wall Street firms and telecommunications companies have also relied on the H-1B programme through their use of IT contractors from staffing and outsourcing agencies. Staffing companies have developed a lucrative business recruiting programmers and other technology professionals from abroad and placing them with US clients. events.title: Contribution of high value residents discussed
events.summary: Mary O'Keeffe was one of several business people who said high value residents contribute positively to the island's economy More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy. Jersey's high value residency programme , external grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals. One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island. However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling". About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme. O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation , external to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes. "They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals. "So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy." High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income , external . They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax , external . O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way. "First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income. "And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand. "High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off." Industry leaders from law, finance, business and real estate met at a Chamber of Commerce lunch to discuss the role of high value residents in Jersey Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them. He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy. Former economic advisor to the government of Jersey John Christensen said the amount of tax paid by high value residents was "piffling" "If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said. "So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%. "We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax. "We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions." events.title: 'You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world'
events.summary: Longbow's co-founders and CEOs Daniel Davey (left) and Mark Tapscott show Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds (left in car) and mayor Richard Parker the Speedster A British carmaker has unveiled plans to start production of its hand-built electric sports car in Warwickshire. Longbow is to start production of its limited-edition Speedster at Mira Tech Park in Nuneaton next year. West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, who backed Longbow with £3m from a government fund, said the project will be followed by the firm's Roadster model, creating more than 200 skilled jobs. Daniel Davey, Longbow's co-chief executive officer, said the region was the best place to build the cars. "It's not just the supply chain; you've got the talent here and the know-how," he said. Davey said: "You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world. And if you did, you would be importing UK components to it. "So you can get heavy components elsewhere, and you can get high-volume components elsewhere; what we're looking for is low-volume, high-quality, low-cost, low-weight." The Speedster has a waiting list of prospective buyers from across the world, waiting to spend around £85,000 on the sports car. At the test track at Mira, the all-British creation silently demonstrated how a lightweight sports car can go from an idea to a vehicle in less than two years, helped by regional expertise. Longbow said the UK was good at building lightweight sports cars. "Our designers are just up the road in Leamington Spa, engineers from across the West Midlands and further afield," Davey added. People around the world are waiting to buy the limited edition car for around £85,000 The project was backed by £3m from the government's £50m West Midlands Supplier Readiness and Transformation fund , external , which aims to accelerate the UK's transition to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the £3m was to strengthen the supply chain and the industry. West Midlands Combined Authority said the money would be match-funded by Longbow, which plans to manufacture more than 10,000 cars a year. Parker said: "We've been building cars here in West Midlands for 130 years, so what better location for a new generation of carmakers like Longbow. "They know this industry inside out and are investing here because this is quite simply the best place in the UK to build a car." Car industry expert Professor David Bailey said: "They're trying to do what Tesla first did many years ago with a sort of lightweight, fast electric sports car. "So I think it's great; it shows we have great research and development skills. We can probably compete, I think, in terms of low-volume, high-margin cars, but more broadly we need to be doing a lot more to support the auto industry in the region and enable it to continue growing." events.title: Revealed: the ‘black box’ wastewater trade that rakes in millions for UK utility companies
events.summary: Exclusive: Firms made more than £340m last year from processing industrial and commercial wastewater at sewage works that are unable to remove many chemical pollutants Water companies in the UK made more than £340m in revenue last year by pouring billions of litres of industrial and commercial wastewater into sewage treatment works that experts say are not designed to remove most chemicals, leaving pollutants to pass into rivers, seas and farmland. Water companies in England are required by law to take industrial wastewater and issue permits called “trade-effluent consents” that allow businesses to send it to sewage works, though water companies can refuse applications. However, no independent regulator oversees the trade-effluent process and there is no central register, so Watershed Investigations, the Guardian and the campaign group River Action compiled a database of 26,000 consents, providing the first ever national picture of the system. The investigation found an annual total of up to 608bn litres of industrial wastewater entering sewage works from sites such as power stations, pharmaceutical plants, food factories, hospitals, abattoirs and waste facilities. The permits are issued and enforced by the water companies themselves, with environmental regulators having no direct role. “It’s a bit of a black box,” one industry expert said. Most sewage works only have biological treatment facilities, which are not designed to remove industrial chemicals, including flame retardants, Pfas , solvents and pharmaceuticals. Some permits on the database feature chemicals such as cyanide, chromium, cadmium and mercury. Watershed has mapped every sewage treatment works and the industrial companies permitted to send waste to each one. Pollutants that survive treatment are discharged into rivers, lakes and seas as “treated effluent”, while those captured in sewage sludge are spread on farmland as fertiliser. The waste also adds to the overloading of sewer networks that triggers raw sewage spills , which have caused outrage, community protests and calls for the industry to be nationalised so that profits can be reinvested in improving the system rather than going to shareholders. United Utilities made the most revenue from industrial waste last year, at £61.6m, followed by Yorkshire Water at £48.8m. However, these companies included revenues from tankered waste in their figures, while some others did not. Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water, Scottish Water and Wessex Water said they routed commercial tankered waste through separate companies within their groups. Thames Water has the largest volume of permitted industrial sewage, at 113bn litres, followed by United Utilities at 105bn litres and Severn Trent Water at 79bn litres. Across the sector, revenues from receiving industrial and commercial wastewater have risen sharply in five years, with Anglian Water’s increasing by 62%. The industry expert said water companies had “a financial incentive to accept far more toxic material than they should”. The permit regime was very old and not fit for purpose, they added. “Currently the Environment Agency doesn’t know exactly how much of this waste is going into waterworks each year.” Waste handlers also drive tankers carrying industrial effluents, landfill leachate and other liquid wastes to sewage works. An Environment Agency (EA) officer said landfill leachate was its “greatest concern” because of the harmful chemical cocktail it can contain. Both the officer and the industry expert identified Davyhulme wastewater treatment works in Manchester, operated by United Utilities , and Avonmouth, operated by Wessex Water, as big receivers of tankered waste. “Carriers will drive [long distances] to dispose of their wastes here … You can see lines of tankers queueing outside Avonmouth,” the expert said. Checks by water companies across the sector can just involve taking a sample and carrying out basic pH and metals analysis, but even more advanced testing does not always pick up a wide range of potentially harmful substances, “and by the time you’ve identified [that] it had something nasty in it, it’s already gone”, the EA officer added. But “ignorance is no defence”, said the officer. “They should be seeking sufficient information from the producer of that waste to satisfy themselves so they can treat it properly.” The industry expert said the UK needed a dedicated liquid-waste treatment sector rather than relying on a “dilute and disperse” model. events.title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown
events.summary: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010 T he coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome the growing resistance to antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies? While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. We are home to four of the world’s top 10 universities and 16 of the top 100, five of which are in Europe’s top 10 for spin-outs, startups based on intellectual property produced through a university’s research. With less than 1% of the world’s population, the UK produces 6% of the world’s research papers, nearly 9% of citations and 12% of the most highly cited research. Our research expertise is one of the many reasons we have been at the forefront of recent inventions: from AlphaFold , which predicts how proteins behave, to viral-vector vaccine technology and AI that detects cancer as reliably as radiologists. Britain already sits at the intersection of AI, quantum computing and synthetic biology. The question then is: why, having led the first Industrial Revolution, should the UK not be the world’s great innovation nation once again? We know the public have an entrepreneurial spirit, and back this vision. New polling for this week’s conference finds that 75% of people agree that innovation is essential for creating UK economic growth. But it is disappointing that only 36% of the British public believes the country is a world leader in science. It is time for innovation to move to the forefront of government policy and the 10-year plan the government is preparing. If we were to raise Britain to Swedish or Japanese levels of innovation intensity we would, over time, leave every household £5,000 better off (according to my calculations), and increase our national income by £150bn a year as higher investment in research and development feeds through into productivity. And a jobs plan on the scale that Our Scottish Future has proposed for Scotland would mean about 3m new jobs across the UK. We can identify the major hurdles to overcome. While the UK is good at startups and spin-outs, we are slow to turn startups into scale-ups, and even slower to turn scale-ups into global success stories. Per head of population, the US has double the number of $1bn companies and nearly three times as many $10bn-plus companies than the UK. And even when we do scale up at home, three-quarters of venture capital investment comes from overseas. Turning this around will require a government to keep tackling the bottlenecks that are inevitably created from innovation. Speakers from future-facing companies at today’s conference will set out the steps that we need to consider. These will range from making sure firms can access the money they need to grow from UK investors, to new incentives for investors, to public-private partnerships – as happens in Germany, France and Italy – capitalised by the British Business Bank and the national wealth fund . Competition policy must favour new entrants against vested interests and be aligned with a favourable tax regime, such as through research and development credits that favour companies of all sizes. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Research for the conference has identified 127 innovative clusters covering every region and nation of the UK, many of which will succeed if we are willing to give long-term support to the infrastructure, skills training and research and development support from UK Research and Innovation they need to grow. In order to harness this potential, more power needs to be devolved to enable mayors and regional authorities to act locally while ensuring access to global markets. Britain does not lack genius or great assets. Every nation, including ours, must do more to find its “ lost Einsteins ” – the young people in lower-income areas who have the talent but not yet the opportunity to show their creative genius.

events.title: OpenAI’s Singapore-based APAC policy head leaving job after 6 months, source says
events.summary: The start-up had apologised earlier in October for its artificial intelligence models’ breach of Australian government websites. OpenAI’s Singapore-based APAC policy head, Sanghyun Lee, is leaving after six months, according to a source, as the company faces tighter scrutiny from regulators in the region. Lee led public policy and government engagement across Australia, Japan, Korea, India and Southeast Asia, building ties with policymakers to support responsible AI use. OpenAI has apologised for AI models breaching Australian government websites, while also expanding in Asia-Pacific and seeking major new funding, Bloomberg reported. SINGAPORE – OpenAI’s most senior Asia-Pacific public policy executive is departing after six months in the role, according to a person familiar with the matter, just as the ChatGPT maker faces scrutiny from regulators in the region . The executive, Sanghyun Lee, is based in Singapore and joined OpenAI in April after six years at Google, according to his LinkedIn profile. The reasons for his exit were not immediately clear. The person familiar asked not to be identified discussing a private matter. OpenAI declined to comment. Lee did not respond to requests for comment. The San Francisco-based start-up apologised in October for its artificial intelligence models that recently breached Australian government websites , pledging to work to prevent similar incidents and to respond faster if they do occur. In his role, Lee has led OpenAI’s public policy and government engagement across Australia, Japan, Korea, India and South-east Asia, according to his profile. He builds and manages “relationships with senior policymakers, regulators and institutions to support the responsible development and adoption of AI”, the profile says. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission is scrutinising OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI firms over the safety of their products amid high-profile cybersecurity incidents . Public policy staff typically advise companies on regulatory issues and liaise with governments. The Asia-Pacific region is key to OpenAI in part because it is home to populous, often youthful markets that support the company’s consumer growth and enterprise adoption as it competes against rivals such as Anthropic. OpenAI has in recent years opened offices in locations including India, South Korea, Japan and Australia. OpenAI is in discussions with investors to raise US$30 billion (S$38.4 billion) or more in a funding round that would value the firm at about US$1.4 trillion, Bloomberg News has reported. The company is expecting to reach or exceed US$70 billion in annualised revenue by the end of 2026 . Before joining OpenAI, Lee was Google’s global head of government affairs and public policy strategy for platforms and devices, working across markets such as the United States, European Union and several Asia-Pacific countries, according to his LinkedIn profile.
