events.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq end lower as crude prices jump, chip stocks weigh
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Oct 5, in New York City. - US stocks fell as crude prices jumped on Middle East tensions and lower US output, raising inflation and rate-hike fears. - The Nasdaq dropped most, while chip stocks slid after a report on OpenAI revenues and wider worries over tech debt and funding. - Energy stocks rose, but the S&P 500 and Nasdaq ended lower; investors now await third-quarter earnings and more Fed policy signals. NEW YORK - US stocks dipped on Oct 8 as crude prices surged on a spike in Middle East tensions and a cut in US output that stoked inflation and rate-hike fears, while semiconductor stocks slumped. Of the major US stock indexes, the Nasdaq closed with the steepest percentage loss, two days after the tech-heavy index reached a record closing high. The S&P 500‘s loss was more modest, while the blue-chip Dow eked out a nominal gain. Chipmakers, which have soared over 80% so far this year, were clear underperformers on the day, falling 3.4% in the wake of a report from the Financial Times that OpenAI’s annualised revenues were US$20 billion (S$25 billion) less than the company previously signalled. “The market’s going sideways in anticipation of third-quarter earnings season, which begins next week, and then there’s the ongoing conflict in Iran that’s pushing oil prices higher,” said Terry Sandven, chief equity strategist at US Bank Wealth Management in Minneapolis, Minnesota. “What’s equally telling is that year-to-date, the path of least resistance for equities has been up.” Oil prices jumped on supply concerns after a spate of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, combined with a cut in US output due to hurricane activity. Front-month WTI and Brent settled up 3.6% and 4.1%, respectively. Tight global crude supplies during the Iran war have sent US crude soaring more than 60% so far this year, stoking inflation pressures. In response to those pressures, the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in September for the first time since July 2023. Financial markets currently expect the central bank to leave rates unchanged this month, while the probability of a December hike is 69.2%, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. That mirrors the expected rate hike path of the European Central Bank, and was affirmed by Fed Governor Christopher Waller, who said additional rate hikes will probably be necessary, but the timing of those hikes is “flexible.” The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 51.77 points, or 0.10%, to 51,231.64, the S&P 500 lost 36.41 points, or 0.47%, to 7,765.36 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 345.35 points, or 1.25%, to 27,193.34. Among the 11 major sectors in the S&P 500, energy stocks led the percentage gainers, while technology, weighed by chips, suffered the steepest loss. Memory-chip giant Samsung Electronics’ record quarterly profit forecast failed to lift sentiment, with its shares closing lower in South Korea. Rival Micron Technology dropped 4.8%. On Oct 7, the Wall Street Journal reported that Broadcom is lining up US$50 billion in financing for OpenAI, with Oracle also seeking an unspecified sum, spurring fears that massive debt issuance by technology companies could intensify the competition for capital. Broadcom and Oracle fell 4.4% and 5.5%, respectively. PepsiCo shares gained 3.7% after the beverage company said it would pursue additional spending cuts while lowering its annual core profit forecast. Starbucks dipped 0.4% following reports that the coffee chain was exploring a purchase of Chipotle Mexican Grill, whose shares jumped 6.2%. Palantir climbed 2.4% after Goldman Sachs upgraded its rating on the data analytics software provider to “buy” from “neutral.” Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.28-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 110 new highs and 416 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,050 stocks rose and 2,734 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.33-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 4 new 52-week highs and 12 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 33 new highs and 319 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 18.81 billion shares, compared with the 17.74 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania, but most of its planned centres are not built yet. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) The mega float of data centre operator Firmus has been pulled. It follows poor interest from investors amid concerns about the company's debt and a lack of detail. The company says it will pursue private funding. AI data centre company Firmus has withdrawn its application to list on the ASX, scrapping what was set to be one of Australia's biggest share market floats. The company cited recent market volatility and conditions, saying the offer would not appropriately reflect its long-term growth prospects. Firmus said it would now pursue private market funding while considering other options. "We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said in a statement. Firmus, the AI factory builder backed by chip-making giant Nvidia, was set to be the biggest float in the Australian share market since Telstra in 1997. The company's founders, co-chief executives Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield, targeted a $44 billion valuation, but prospective investors pulled back based on the high sale price of $11 a share and concerns over an AI bubble. Yesterday, reports emerged that Firmus and its advisors were considering reducing the size of the initial public offering (IPO) and lowering the per-share price from $11 to $8.25. Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield at Firmus's St Leonards, Launceston site. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Many investors were also focused on Mr Curtis's criminal background — he is a former investment banker who served one year in prison a decade ago for insider trading. With AI infrastructure demand accelerating across the Asia-Pacific, Firmus's website says its broader portfolio spans seven AI factories across four countries: Australia, Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia. It said two sites were operational in Australia and Singapore and five were "under development, targeting ready-for-service over the next 24 months". Its website also spruiks its relationship with US chip giant Nvidia, which has a 7.2 per cent stake in Firmus. Institutional investors raise doubts Today, after Firmus announced the IPO had been pulled, UniSuper chief investment officer John Pearce said it was disappointing. "The ASX needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," he said. Firmus tries to save mega share market float The company is reportedly having to price its shares lower as it closed its books to potential investors abruptly overnight. Ahead of the announcement, he had released an investment update detailing potential investors' doubts about the AI company and why the super fund would not directly invest in it. "Firmus is a neo-cloud company, and that means it provides cloud services, in very simple terms, to AI companies," he said. "The capital raise will be about $7 billion and that will give Firmus a total market value of around $44 billion." Mr Pearce said even though UniSuper was not directly investing in Firmus, UniSuper would own some shares if the float proceeded "because we have index strategies in our portfolios and Firmus will ultimately be a part of the major indices". He said the reason UniSuper was doubtful about investing was the high valuation. "At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation. "Furthermore, we're quite concerned that Firmus will have to keep coming back to the market for a lot more debt and more equity to fund its expansion plans." Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Holloway yesterday raised concerns over the company's debt levels. Lochlan Holloway is not convinced by the Firmus float. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "The neo-clouds are heavily geared," he wrote in an economic note. "The model is to borrow against customer contracts to buy chips, then use the rent to repay the loans." Once its data centres are built, Firmus expects to be carrying about $US30 billion ($43 billion) of debt, about six times the $US5 billion of operating earnings it forecasts for 2028. "Borrowed money alone does not make a bubble, and plenty of infrastructure is sensibly funded with debt. But credit is the common thread running through essentially every boom and bust cycle," Mr Holloway said. CDC was set to build data centres with Firmus but scrapped the deal.

events.title: US disrupts Chinese hacking tools as 7 govts warn of PRC spies stealing sensitive data worldwide
events.summary: The FBI announced that it has seized seven web domains linked to hacking tools allegedly operated by a Chinese security firm called Integrity Technology Group and used by Beijing-backed cyber operatives to scan a South Carolina power company's network and other critical infrastructure systems for vulnerabilities. In a subsequent advisory, the FBI and other government agencies in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, and Spain warned that Chinese government-linked attackers, enabled by Integrity Tech, are using botnets, malware, and other intrusion tools to target organizations worldwide and steal sensitive data, including from US critical infrastructure networks. “These actors exploit vulnerabilities by using scanning tools, cross-site scripting attacks, and password spraying on Microsoft Exchange servers, while establishing persistence through VPN software and exfiltrating emails and credentials using scripts,” according to the security alert. Based on this activity, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added five CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog: CVE-2015-3306 CVE-2015-5477 CVE-2016-3081 CVE-2021-3199 CVE-2023-22894 The court-authorized seizures are the latest in a long series of US law-enforcement attempts to disrupt a Beijing-backed cybercrew called Flax Typhoon and shut down its botnet. From 2021 until its disruption, Flax Typhoon allegedly used a version of this Mirai-based botnet to infect internet-connected devices with malware, scan networks for vulnerabilities, and launch additional cyberattacks, all while hiding the PRC government hackers’ true IP addresses and physical location. The feds allege Integrity Tech developed the botnet and a vulnerability scanner called Microscan, and operated a post-compromise tool called FishHub. The latter allegedly downloaded additional malware to the phishing victims’ networks and stole sensitive data. Court documents, unsealed on Thursday, allege Integrity Tech has contracts with the PRC government, and the feds have long linked Flax Typhoon to the private firm. “Flax Typhoon actors conducted successful computer intrusions against multiple victim entities which had been scanned using the Microscan tool,” according to the court documents. Victims include a university in Hsinchu, Taiwan, that Flax Typhoon compromised in March 2023, and a second university in Puli Township, Taiwan breached in August 2022. “On or about April 26, 2022, and on or about December 29, 2022, Flax Typhoon actors also used the Microscan tool to scan for vulnerabilities on the networks of a U.S. power company based in South Carolina, a multi-national Non-Governmental Organization, Japanese and Polish airports, and at least two Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies in the natural gas and power sectors,” the documents allege. Integrity Tech accessed Microscan through one of the seized domains, c0cc[.]cc. Meanwhile, five of the seized domains, 98aicai[.]com, 98aicode[.]com, outlook3650[.]com, youtubecard[.]com, and linkedinns[.]net, delivered the FishHub malware as recently as March, and infected about 20 Taiwanese universities. “Based on my training and experience I believe the tool was named FishHub because it facilitated phishing activity,” FBI special agent Adam James said in a seizure warrant affidavit. After FishHub downloaded a file onto victims' computers, that file used the five domains to retrieve additional malicious programs and code. The malware created a file listing, searched for specific files, compressed documents, and then exfiltrated the selected files to an attacker-controlled server. This gave Flax Typhoon remote access to compromised networks. In September 2024, the FBI said Integrity Tech and Flax Typhoon tore down their 260,000-device botnet after the FBI and its international pals went after them. As recently as this year, however, both private sector security researchers and Western governments warned that Chinese hackers continue to turn compromised routers and IoT devices into botnets and break into critical networks. In February, operational technology (OT) security provider Dragos said China’s state-sponsored spies haven't let up on their attempts to compromise America's critical infrastructure, and this includes a group whose activity overlaps with Flax Typhoon. This group focuses on gaining long-term access to OT engineering workstations and exfiltrating operational files, and it targets manufacturing, defense, automotive, electric power, oil and gas, and government organizations across the US, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region. In April, a 10-country joint advisory warned that basically every Chinese “Typhoon” group is using botnets “strategically, and at scale.” Some of these covert networks are built and maintained by Chinese infosec companies including Integrity Tech, which also controlled and managed the so-called Raptor Train network, the alert said. In late August, the FBI said that it had disrupted a different botnet and seized domains associated with two platforms that Chinese government-backed operatives allegedly used to target NASA, the US Senate, the Department of Energy, and several other government agencies and critical networks. The DOJ subsequently clarified that not all the named organizations had been compromised.®

events.title: Trump-tied firm helped organize political advisers’ Balkans travel
events.summary: The Scoop Continental, a Washington-based law and lobbying firm with close ties to President Donald Trump’s network, helped arrange a recent trip to Bosnia and Herzegovina by two Trump political advisers, three people familiar with the trip told Semafor. Republika Srpska, whose Russia-friendly Serbian leaders have sought to align themselves with Trump, agreed earlier this year to pay $35,000 monthly to Continental, which would organize “meetings and discussions and establish relationships with key stakeholders in the executive and legislative branches,” according to a Justice Department filing . Since then, former Trump campaign adviser Alex Garcia has helped arrange meetings with White House officials like Walker Barrett, Jarrod Agen and Richard Walters, according to another DOJ filing . A White House official told Semafor that Garcia, who was in Republika Srpska around the same time as LaCivita and Blair, also set up a recent meeting between Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles and a Serbian official from the region. The Balkan trip occurred after Garcia initially reached out to LaCivita, multiple people familiar with the situation said. LaCivita and Blair were there for 48 hours, one source said, to consult on voting equipment ahead of elections on Sunday. Trump on Wednesday signaled his displeasure with LaCivita and Blair’s trip, which was first reported by The New York Times , amid some intraparty criticism that his advisers aren’t as focused as possible on the midterms. But Trump wasn’t particularly harsh about the trip in private, two people familiar with the situation said. “If I’m the president … traveling the country every day and campaigning … I’m rightfully annoyed, right?” one of the people said. “With that being said, do I think James missed a second of work? No.” Two sources said that Trump and Blair had a call following the news, with one calling it “a good conversation.” And while the duo has faced criticism from some corners of the Republican party, others close to Trump are openly defending them. LaCivita and Blair’s trip focused on election integrity rather than political strategy, multiple people said; this year marked Republika Srpska’s first election using new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment. Asked for comment on whether Continental helped organize LaCivita and Blair’s trip, a spokesperson for the firm said only that Garcia was its only employee in Republika Srpska on Oct. 4 as well as its only employee to lobby the US government on its behalf. The spokesperson added that Wiles’ daughter Katie, who also works at Continental , traveled to Republika Srpska in August for a separate reason: helping a US-based company complete “a feasibility study.” Know More Republika Srpska voters on Sunday decided to keep former President Milorad Dodik’s nationalist party in power. The US last year lifted sanctions on Dodik, who was banned from holding office after violating his country’s peace deal. The Balkans isn’t the only place Continental is looking to cash in on the administration’s agenda abroad: The firm reportedly took on at least a dozen clients in Venezuela after the US captured its former leader earlier this year. Republika Srpska, for its part, has signed lobbying contracts worth at least $9 million since Trump was inaugurated in an effort to curry favor with the administration (though it’s never signed one with Ballard Partners, Susie Wiles’ former firm). So far, it seems to be working: Officials have yet to impose recently enacted sanctions on Serbian politicians despite Congress’ urging. House Democrats already have a plan, reported first by Semafor , to oversee the administration’s Balkans policy if they win a majority next month. Notable LaCivita has also advised another Continental client looking to ingratiate himself with Trump: Albania’s Sali Berisha . Trump this term has embraced a number of foreign governments who have moved to politically align themselves with the conservative or MAGA movement, as CBS and Reuters reported.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Commitment comes as GPUzilla prepares to fortify Uncle Sam's arsenal with at least seven AI-optimized supers Anthropic asks users to stop being mean to Claude 3 hours ago AI company moves to defend critical infrastructure and open-source projects from AI 13 hours ago There can be only one: Google Cloud casts Gemini as your enterprise AI hero 17 hours ago High-severity Nvidia bug could crash GPU monitoring on exposed servers 19 hours ago TSMC taps GlobalFoundries to bolster US silicon interposer production in $2B deal 20 hours ago Nvidia on Thursday scraped together some spare change to commit $1 billion — about 1/60th of its quarterly profits — to funding US scientific discovery over the next five years. The commitment , announced during an event in Washington, DC, aims to support the research and development of AI — or is it " super intelligence " now? — in fields including quantum computing, healthcare, and energy security. Nvidia's choice of technologies is not surprising as it has long aspired to fuse AI and high-performance computing. And while LLM training and inference pay Nvidia's bills, the GPU giant has continued to introduce new CUDA libraries specifically for AI-assisted quantum computing, healthcare, drug discovery, and physics simulation. The initiative is part of the US government's broader Genesis Mission , announced late last year by the Trump administration, which aims to use AI to drive the scientific discoveries necessary to ensure the country's continued technological leadership. The program marks Nvidia's return to US supercomputing in a big way. The Department of Energy's (DoE) last flagship supercomputers powered by Nvidia, Summitand Sierra, were commissioned all the way back in 2018. The A100-based Perlmutter system launched in 2021 is also notable, but fell far short of the older systems. And while Nvidia never stopped building supers for the US government, they tended to be significantly smaller than the massive AMD-based platforms like Frontier and El Capitan. That changed last year when Nvidia revealed it would supply the US government with no fewer than seven new supercomputers across the Argonne, Los Alamos, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratories. Argonne will house the 100,000 Blackwell-GPU-based Solstice system. Built in collaboration with Oracle, the machine is largely aimed at emerging AI workloads, which don't depend on ultra-high precision computation and instead can get by with 16, eight or even four bits of precision. That puts Nvidia in a strong position to meet the US government's goals under the Genesis Mission. Over the past few generations of GPUs, Nvidia has traded much of its accelerators' double-precision FP64 grunt in favor of higher throughput at precisions used by more lucrative AI workloads. In the case of its upcoming Vera Rubin platform, Nvidia relies heavily on an FP64 emulation capability based on the Ozaki scheme we looked at in more detail earlier this year . Los Alamos' upcoming Mission and Vision systems will be powered by these same chips and take advantage of Nvidia's Quantum-X800 InfiniBand. FP64 emulation comes with compromises, but for workloads that are predominantly AI-optimized and only occasionally need higher precision, it can be worthwhile for the additional matrix FLOPS. While Nvidia is playing a much bigger role in US scientific computing efforts, it's worth noting that the DoE's biggest super — at least for pure FP64 — will still be powered by AMD. Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Discovery system, which is expected to come online 2029 will be built by HPE's Cray division and feature The House of Zen's FP64-optimized MI430X GPUs and Venice CPUs. Discovery is expected to offer peak theoretical performance somewhere between 3.3 and 8.5 exaFLOPS depending on whether or not Oak Ridge gets a facility power upgrade. Meanwhile, China's LineShine leads the Top500 ranking of Earth's mightiest computers.

events.title: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring programme
events.summary: The White House has often made extreme claims regarding international workers and immigration Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa programme. Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H-1B visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents. Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable companies in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants." Microsoft said most of the H-1B visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff. "No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said. He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference. Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers. The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment. The total number of H-1B visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped , external at 85,000 per year. A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide. Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H-1B visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace US workers and "undercut" their wages. The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H-1B visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires. She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H-1B visa programme are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive. According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary , external for an H-1B worker at Microsoft is $155,000. "We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said. Satya Nadella, Microsoft's long-time chief executive, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump. Trump presented Nadella with a national medal of technology and innovation Introducing Nadella during the event, Trump said the White House was "honoured" to be awarding the medal to him and that it was "so well-deserved". Other tech industry figures to receive medals from Trump were Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Michael Dell. Nadella and most of the other medal recipients were also present at other recent White House events, including a lunch on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping. Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday. "Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said. He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US. Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating , external that grace period altogether. Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H-1B visa programme, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more. None of those companies were included in Vance's comments on Thursday. The programme has been aimed at highly skilled or specialised workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades. The PERM programme is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely. During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified , external more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories. events.title: Kushner, Witkoff to pitch "new ideas" to end Russia-Ukraine war
events.summary: Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet with Ukrainian negotiators and European officials in Miami on Friday to present "new ideas and proposals" to break the stalemate in the Russia -Ukraine war, U.S. and Ukrainian officials say. Why it matters: The Trump administration is hoping to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the midterm elections and before brutal winter weather grips Ukraine. One of the ideas is a partial ceasefire that halts attacks on energy infrastructure and grain shipments. While Ukraine has said it's willing to take that step, Russia has shown little willingness. "They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop. So the U.S. is trying to mediate with the sides, with the goal of creating a unified proposal," a U.S. source said. Driving the news: Witkoff and Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September. Since then, they've been working with the Russians and Ukrainians on an updated peace initiative. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at a press conference in Lisbon Thursday that the war is at a "stalemate." He stressed that the U.S. wants to prevent further escalation of fighting in the coming month and find a way to end the war. Behind the scenes: Witkoff and Kushner met with President Trump Thursday to present the latest U.S. proposal and receive his input ahead of the talks in Miami, which are expected to last two days, a U.S. official said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and deputy national security adviser Mike Needham also attended the meeting. Zoom in: President Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, Foreign Intelligence director Rustem Umerov, diplomatic adviser Sergey Kyslytsia and Member of Parliament Davyd Arakhamia will participate from the Ukrainian side. The U.S. also invited national security advisers from the U.K., France and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the EU. A U.S. source said the parties will discuss proposals for security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war prosperity plan and other aspects of the conflict. The other side: Zelensky told reporters on Thursday that Ukraine is discussing with the U.S. the possibility of an energy and grain ceasefire. "As for what might be realistic or more realistic, I am not ready to say yet. I do not want to say something and then have Russia, as always, do the opposite out of spite. So let's wait and see," he said. Between the lines: A Ukrainian official said that despite skepticism in Kyiv, the U.S. midterm elections and Russia's need for sanctions relief might lead Russian President Vladimir Putin to agree to a ceasefire of some sort. What to watch: Witkoff and Kushner might travel to Moscow later this month for more talks with Putin, a source with knowledge said.

events.title: Pete Hegseth says the public can watch Fort Hood shooter's execution
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that the public will be able to watch the execution of the Fort Hood shooter by firing squad. Why it matters: The U.S. hasn't held a public execution in 90 years , and Hegseth's remarks raise questions about how the military would allow people to watch. Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting , is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, near Killeen, Texas. What they're saying: Hegseth told Real America's Voice Thursday that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be." "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it's public. Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." The latest: The Pentagon says the execution will be livestreamed, AP reports, but did not name where specifically the stream will be hosted. The Pentagon currently posts speeches and videos on X and YouTube . State of play: The Department of Defense declined to comment on Hegseth's remarks, leaving questions about how the public could watch the execution. The Army has not shared how it intends to conduct the execution, AP reports. It's unclear if Hegseth's remarks mean the execution will be open to public spectators, broadcast on streaming or TV, or made available to select individuals. Zoom out: This would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 . The last U.S. military execution by firing squad was in 1945, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, according to NPR . Firing-squad executions are rare in the U.S. Only Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah authorize the method, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . Last year, South Carolina carried out the state's first firing squad execution — the first in the U.S. in 15 years. The last public execution in the U.S. was in 1936, when Rainey Bethea , a Black man convicted of raping a white woman, was hanged in Kentucky.

events.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
events.summary: Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . With Astra, Jebens explored computer-aided design and tooling revisions for robots informed by simulation. The agent measured the available space and designed a wrench the robot could use to reach the suspension’s bolts. Jebens reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. This connects design and tooling decisions to disassembly results, offering a starting point for robot policy training. Explore the Onshape importer guide . Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. events.title: Fears backpacker ballot will leave coastal towns short-staffed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Hospitality businesses seek designated area migration agreement to combat backpacker ballot There are concerns about how to fill jobs when the backpacker ballot begins. ( Flickr CC BY-NC-ND 2.0: Jo Christian Oterhals ) Hospitality experts say the backpacker ballot could create significant workforce shortages in holiday towns that rely heavily on seasonal workers. North Coast Hotel Group director Harry Barry says his business hires backpackers because of a local workforce shortage. Business leaders along the NSW coast are looking to negotiate a federal agreement to help fill roles in the regions. For publican Harry Barry, backpackers are the lifeblood of his business. But he says many of his employees are considering returning home after the federal government announced a backpacker ballot , which would effectively cap second-year backpacker visas. "The incentive was a guarantee they could extend their visas by another 12 months," he said. "A lot of them are deciding that there is no guarantee that [they're] going to be earning enough money to pay [their] way. Harry Barry says a designated area migration agreement could help the Coffs Harbour region. ( ABC Coffs Harbour: Claudia Jambor ) The new backpacker ballot will cap annual places at 45,000 for second-year visas if the standard 88 days of regional work are completed. Even fewer third-year places are available. About 57,000 people qualified last year . Mr Barry is among a number of business owners concerned about how the cap will impact their staff. The director of the North Coast Hotel Group runs pubs from Grafton to Taree that employed 80 backpackers over the past two years, with 20 still on his books. "If we're employing 80 backpackers, we're doing it for a reason , and the reason is we can't find local workers to fill the slots," he said. Harry Barry believes the new backpacker ballot will negatively affect the Mid North Coast. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claudia Jambor ) According to jobs website Seek, there were more than 130 vacancies in the Coffs Harbour region in the industry on Wednesday. To fill the gap left by backpackers leaving, Mr Barry is backing a push to establish the region as a priority area for semi-skilled migrants, also known as a Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA). The DAMA is an agreement between the federal government and a state or regional authority that assists regional areas to fill roles that would otherwise remain empty. It allows skilled migrants, in industries of need, to move to the area for work. Industries include skilled roles in hospitality, agriculture, engineering and more. The agreements are usually in place for five years before they are reviewed. Backpackers help pick fruit across regional NSW. ( ABC Rural: Stephanie Anderson ) There are 13 DAMAs in place across Australia, with one operation in New South Wales; two in South Australia; five in Western Australia; one in the Northern Territory; two in Victoria; and two in Queensland. Regional Development Australia Mid North Coast CEO Madeleine Lawler said the DAMA was not about filling jobs with migrants that could have otherwise employed locals. "The DAMA requires businesses to be able to substantiate that they have been seeking Australians for a long period of time and have not been able to fill these positions with Australians or people locally," she said. A similar agreement in Townsville, in Northern Queensland, brought in an additional 480 workers over three years to fill a skills shortage. Holiday hotspot Cairns has held a DAMA for the past seven years. The agreement, according to the Cairns Chamber of Commerce, was key to keeping the region thriving. CEO Patricia O'Neill said there was a hotel on Thursday Island, which was included in the Cairns agreement, that would shut down without DAMA workforce. Patricia O'Neill says the DAMA has been a lifeline for the Cairns region. ( ABC News: Conor Byrne ) "Government go to [Thursday Island] regularly; there is only one hotel in the place. If they weren't able to apply to attract a chef, that hotel would need to close [because] it can't feed anyone," Ms O'Neill said. "That's how critical a DAMA is to certain parts of an economy up here. "Without having the Far North Queensland DAMA, we would not have a thriving economy; we would not have a workforce to take up jobs." Each area with an agreement has a list of specific jobs, tailored to the region's needs, that can be filled by overseas workers.

events.title: The staggering cost of winning a Senate seat in 2026
events.summary: Source: AdImpact, Census.gov Note: AdImpact data includes dollars spent on video advertisements on broadcast, cable and social media as well as spending estimates on streaming platforms. Chart: Stef Kight/Axios Every voting-age Mainer could get a $167 voucher for home heating oil with what Democrats and Republicans are spending on ads in the Senate race, according to an analysis of AdImpact data. Why it matters: Every senator gets one vote, but Senate seats aren't created equal — and they don't cost the same. Zoom in: Like two years ago , the less-populated states have a dramatically higher dollar-per-voter ratio in 2026. Maine is in first place, followed by Alaska, which is scheduled to be hit with $76 million in ads — enough to suck up most of the state's inventory. Between the lines: Ohio is only in fifth place on the dollar-per-voter metric, but it's on track to host the most expensive Senate race in the country — for the second cycle in a row . Sherrod Brown's comeback bid is proving more expensive than his 2024 race, when he was ousted by now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). And in New Hampshire, where Democratic Senate nominee Chris Pappas has been warning that his race is actually quite close, both parties are spending heavily to reach the state's voters. Data: AdImpact Note: AdImpact data includes dollars spent on video advertisements on broadcast, cable and social media as well as spending estimates on streaming platforms. Chart: Stef Kight/Axios The big picture: Both chambers are likely to come down to a handful of races. All year, Republicans warned that Texas would get really expensive if Attorney General Ken Paxton won the primary. They were right. Outside GOP groups spent a mind-blowing $131 million in just 17 days trying to rescue Paxton. And tens of millions more could be on the way. But in North Carolina, where Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), predicted the race could cost $1 billion , the contest looks like it will come in under $200 million. Republican super PACs are abandoning the Senate race there as they reallocate money to redder states. The bottom line: Republicans have a spending advantage, especially when it comes to how many eyeballs they're actually reaching in Texas and Ohio . But neither side has really figured out how to play moneyball and find a way to reach voters with a dramatically smaller budget.

events.title: Pretend you’re sitting at Elizabeth Holmes’ desk on this weirdly detailed website
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. With over a thousand emails, slides, texts, and documents unveiled during the United States v. Elizabeth Holmes trial, Extend engineer Bo Lau created a website that simulates what it might have been like to be the chief executive of Theranos before everything came crashing down. (Every day, I am grateful to the American legal system for making the discovery process public.) i built a website where you can sit at elizabeth holmes’ desk open her macbook, scroll her iphone, run the theranos edison machine her texts, emails, slides, documents, and theranos machine records are real, sourced from exhibits in the united states v. holmes criminal trial pic.twitter.com/5At9T5m3UV — bo lau (@bolau_) October 8, 2026 The environment that Lau created is ambitiously detailed, taking you right back to 2016, a time when iPhones had home buttons, and you had to slide your finger across the screen to unlock it. Even the MacBook Air is running OS X El Capitan. You can click around the environment, which lets you look through the documents made public from the court case on Holmes’ iPhone and laptop screens. You can even run the Theranos Edison machine, the company’s ill-fated device that was supposed to be able to extract large amounts of health data from one drop of blood. The project seems like it was mostly made for laughs, but it’s actually an interesting way to peruse the documents from one of the most infamous court cases in tech history — it’s a lot easier to navigate this than to source thousands of PDFs from court websites. There’s another agenda, though. Lau is promoting a watch party that her company is throwing for Nathan Fielder’s upcoming documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, “ You Can See Everything .” Also, of course, she’s promoting the company itself. So, what exactly does Extend do? Apparently, it can “parse, extract, and split your hardest documents with unmatched accuracy.” (I’m not really sure what that means, but if it makes something like this Holmes desk simulator possible, then I guess that means I’m bullish on B2B SaaS.) events.title: 'Consumers should feel ripped off': How coffee brands have changed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coffee manufacturers quietly change marketing after price squeeze Coffee brands are changing their marketing due to price pressures. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) Major supermarket coffee brands have changed their marketing in response to bean prices surging to almost 50-year highs. Some companies no longer label their products as "100 per cent arabica" but instead as "coffee", or mix the more expensive arabica beans with cheaper robusta beans. Experts and consumers want companies to flag recipe changes to buyers. Major supermarket coffee brands have quietly changed their marketing in response to bean prices surging to almost 50-year highs. Labelling of premium arabica coffee beans, prized for their sweeter, more complex flavour, has switched in some cases from "100 per cent arabica" to being described as "coffee", or as a blend with robusta, a more bitter variety of the plant. While the change is legal and does not necessarily mean the coffee is worse, experts say consumers deserve to know when changes are made. Cairns pensioner Brian Rantzau said price was his most important consideration when buying coffee, but he also wanted clear information about changes to the product. "As a pensioner, you've got to mind every dollar," Mr Rantzau said. "It should really tell us what's in it, right?" Coles's Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee has doubled in price since 2024. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) The price of Mr Rantzau's preferred Coles's Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee has doubled since early 2024, jumping from $4 per 100 grams to $8. Earlier this year, the product's "100 per cent arabica" description was also changed to simply read "instant coffee". Both versions may appear on supermarket shelves at the same time as stores gradually phase out the old recipe. Coles is phasing out 100 per cent arabica from the label of its Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee. Its website currently shows the old and new labels. ( Supplied: Coles ) Gold Coast mother Vicki Jarvis said she stopped buying the product. "It just kept going up, and now it's $8 a jar, and I just would not pay that," she said. "[But] if they've gone and changed what is actually in it, it should be written on the front of the label to let people know." A Coles spokesperson said product formulations may need to change occasionally in response to ingredient availability and supply conditions. "We work closely with our suppliers to ensure our products continue to meet our quality standards and provide great value for customers," the spokesperson said. Australian food labelling rules do not require coffee companies to identify the species of bean unless they make a specific claim about it. University of Queensland sensory scientist Heather Smyth said consumers had every right to feel ripped off. Heather Smyth says robusta is not a bad bean, but it is more bitter. ( Supplied: UQ ) Professor Smyth said consumers should be told when a product they had previously chosen for a key ingredient had changed. Jason Lilienstein runs a specialty roaster in Toowoomba, Queensland, and has only ever used arabica beans, bought directly from Colombian farmers he has met personally. "Arabica has always been the preferred, high-quality bean," he said. Jason Lilienstein runs specialty roaster Six Of One in Toowoomba. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) Robusta is not necessarily bad, he said, but he has not found one good enough for his blends. "I haven't found it of sufficient quality to put in any of our coffee at this stage." He said his customers tended to focus less on the species of bean and more on its flavour and origin. Coffee prices have soared recently, with arabica prices reaching $15.40 a kilogram, while robusta hit $8.73 a kilogram — levels not seen since 1977 — piling pressure onto manufacturers. While prices have fallen about 35 per cent from their peak ahead of what is expected to be a record Brazilian harvest, some say consumers may not see lower prices as other costs continue to rise. Some coffee manufacturers have responded by adjusting the composition of their blends. Australian-owned coffee manufacturer Vittoria's website once prominently promoted its coffee as "100 per cent arabica", stating in 2020: "At Vittoria coffee, we make no excuses, all our coffee is 100 per cent arabica". The Vittoria website compares arabica to robusta beans in 2020. ( Supplied: Wayback Machine/Vittoria ) And in mid-2025, the company's website described robusta as an "inferior quality bean". But a few months later, that message had changed.

events.title: Average long-term US mortgage rate rises to highest level in nearly 3 years
events.summary: Mortgage rates marched higher for the seventh week in a row, driving the average long-term U.S. home loan rate to its highest level in nearly three years Mortgage rates marched higher for the seventh week in a row, driving the average long-term U.S. home loan rate to its highest level in nearly three years. The benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage climbed to 7.40% from 7.28% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.30%. The average rate is now the highest it’s been since Nov. 16, 2023, when it was at 7.44%. The housing market has been stuck in a rut this year in large part because of rising mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power and prompting many to put off buying a home. Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also rose this week. That average rate increased to 6.73% from 6.60% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.53%. Mortgage rates have been climbing in the months since the start of the U.S. war with Iran in late February. The recent run-up in rates also reflects heightened bond market volatility as surging oil prices due to the war fuel inflation worries. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen to its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation , big government debt loads and other factors. The yield was at 5.29% at midday Thursday on the bond market. That's well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran began. Man armed with gun, knife shot inside federal court by officers: Police Why are gas prices still high even as traffic improves in the Strait of Hormuz? Trump donor accuses Guilfoyle of asking him to pay her $100K credit card bill In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98%, its lowest level going back to late 2022. The 1.42 percentage point increase in the rate since then translates roughly into an additional monthly cost of $376 for a borrower financing a $400,000 home loan at the current average rate. Depending on a borrower’s income, credit and other factors, they may qualify for a rate on a 30-year mortgage that is below or above the current average. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. Last month, the National Association of Realtors said that existing home sales fell 2% in August from July to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.98 million units. That was their slowest annual pace in more than a year. The sharp rise in mortgage rates has many would-be homebuyers putting their home shopping plans on hold. Mortgage applications, which include loans to buy a home or refinance an existing mortgage, fell for the fifth week in a row last week as mortgage rates kept climbing, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Higher rates are also keeping many homeowners from refinancing their existing mortgage. Home loan refinance applications fell last week to their lowest level since January 2025 and were less than half last year’s pace, according to the MBA. events.title: There can be only one: Google Cloud casts Gemini as your enterprise AI hero
events.summary: Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said that Gemini will be "your new single, universal agent for work," a declaration as unassailable as Google's history of consistency, customer service, and long-term product support. Long-term here means a median lifespan of about 4.1 years and a mean lifespan of about 5.4 years across 308 discontinued products and services. That doesn't include enduring successes like Gmail and Search. Perhaps Gemini is destined for that level of longevity. In a blog post adapted from the prepared remarks he spoke at the Gemini at Work 2026 event – and what could be more appropriate for Google than to herald Gemini with a derivative work? – Kurian laid out his vision for an AI service known as Bard only two years ago. Gemini, he said, has your business context – which is to say, data – and thus can be used for various tasks like question answering, content creation, and coding. "It plans the work, uses skills and tools, connects to your systems, and brings back something finished — inside the documents, the inbox, and the developer environments you already work in," Kurian said. "It chooses the best model for the job, has built-in cost controls, and most importantly, has the security, administration, and governance required by your company." Kurian's actual remarks at the event were more succinct. "Today, Gemini became an agent," he said. "You give it objectives, not just instructions. It plans the work, uses custom skills and tools, connects to your systems and brings back something finished." You might wonder what role you play in all this as a Google Enterprise customer, when Gemini is planning, executing, and delivering. There's always Minesweeper and hunting for a job that involves physical labor and human dignity. Sundai Pichai, CEO of Google parent Alphabet, opened the Google Cloud event with the Recitation of Self-Reported Statistics, a common ritual in the technocratic liturgy. "Enterprise adoption is moving faster than most people realize," he said. "Nearly 80 percent of Google Cloud customers are using our AI products. And they are not just using it, they're using it intensely. Nearly 500 enterprise customers have each processed over 1 trillion tokens on our platform in the last year." Pichai took time to praise Google's latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, noting that it outperforms rival models Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra on the DeepSWE v1.1 coding benchmark with a score of 77.9 percent. And within Google, he said, Gemini 4 Argon has reduced post-submit code rollbacks by 30 percent while increasing agentic code submissions from employees by 35 percent. Kurian then continued the customer success report by citing various claimed productivity gains from Google Cloud customers. Japanese telecom biz NTT Docomo, he said, has saved 450,000 hours annually using data agents. Your mileage may vary. But Kurian's emphasis on the solipsism of Gemini isn't entirely accurate. Gemini is unified in theory. It works within Gmail, Dive, Docs, Slides, Sheets, Chat, and Calendar as a single surface. It can be accessed across iOS, Android, Windows, and Mac desktops, not to mention third-party applications where enabled or during headless operations. It resides in Google Cloud so it retains contextual info. But no agent is an island. Just like the stellar twins for which it's named, Gemini has more than one moving part. "It can dynamically create a roster of sub-agents — temporary, job-specific agents, each with their own identity — to tackle multi-step tasks," said Kurian, perhaps overestimating the appeal of naming spawned processes. And the Gemini agent is distinct from the various models it may call upon, even if one of those might be Gemini 4 Argon. "It runs each job on the model that fits best — orchestrating across our Gemini family of models and Claude models from Anthropic today, and other leading private and open models in the future — to deliver optimal quality and lower your costs," Kurian explained. During the event, Kurian highlighted how Gemini inherits existing enterprise controls. "Every Gemini agent has an identity of its own, separate from your identity," he said. "Your policies reach it the very same way they reach your people: set the policies once, apply them everywhere rather than agency by agent. You set its budget before it starts and that budget covers the whole cost of the work." That's the promise, but of course the very existence of enterprise cost control mechanisms suggests costs can get out of hand. It was only two months ago that Google introduced flexible billing and cost controls for agents. Managing AI spending, however, remains an unsolved problem. As noted by the Wall Street Journal recently, "Spending on AI Is Becoming Almost Impossible for Businesses to Budget." Back in July, AI cost management company Coworker AI observed there were two Gemini Enterprise products that could easily be confused. Now we're told there's just one. Enjoy it while it lasts. ®

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Space agency claims steady progress on lunar reactor plans, but offers little evidence to back it up Margaret Hamilton, software pioneer who helped put humans on the Moon, dies at 90 22 hours ago Google teams with nuclear power giant to give reactors a tune-up 2 days ago Scientists find planet made on new matter recipe, and it formed after a Red Giant ate a solar system 3 days ago Google launches first datacenter satellite and research that finds orbiting bit barns can work 7 days ago Boeing's Calamity Capsule gets another shot at the ISS taxi business 9 days ago NASA and the Department of Energy have agreed to expand their collaboration on the space agency's nuclear ambitions, as administrator Jared Isaacman pushes ahead with a tight deadline to launch a fission-powered spacecraft to Mars. “We are entering the ‘Nuclear NASA-era,’” Isaacman said at a signing ceremony where he and Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed a joint memorandum of understanding. The MOU, the full text of which doesn’t appear to have been published, establishes a framework for collaboration on space nuclear technology. Per NASA, the agreement “unites both agencies” in pursuing its objectives, with work to include research and fuel production, testing, launch integration, and operations. “Nuclear power will allow us to go farther, operate longer, and field more capable spacecraft and instruments than ever before,” Isaacman added. “The work we’re doing today is laying the foundation for the fission-poweuing NASA’s objred spacecraft of tomorrow and opening an entirely new frontier for exploration and discovery.” NASA has been making big plans to launch nuclear reactors into space since earlier this year when the agency paused work on the orbital Lunar Gateway station in favor of a base on the Moon’s surface. Those plans include a nuclear reactor to power said base , which NASA said on Thursday it intends to have ready for launch by 2030, giving the agency precious little time to meet such an ambitious goal. NASA has provided little evidence the initiative is on track, aside from noting in Thursday's announcement that it is “making steady progress” on Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1), the unit it wants to use to power its Moon base. Before then, however, NASA faces an even tighter deadline for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1), which it intends to use to power a nuclear-propelled spacecraft scheduled to launch in December 2028. That’s just over two years away, mind you, and NASA has provided little public evidence of progress on the spacecraft, which it has dubbed "Freedom." NASA provided details [PDF] for SR-1 back in March when it paused work on the Lunar Gateway, describing the spacecraft as being mostly constructed from a repurposed spacecraft bus that NASA had almost completed for a previous project. The reactor would produce more than 20 kilowatts of electricity to power Freedom's electric thrusters on its journey to Mars, where it would deliver three Ingenuity-class helicopters to survey potential future human landing sites. Whether that’ll happen on any sort of timeline that resembles the current one is anyone’s guess, but let’s face it: NASA doesn’t exactly have a great track record for getting things done on time. The Government Accountability Office has been watching NASA’s lunar return ambitions for years, and has been noting for nearly a decade that its timelines were more fantasy than reality. In the past couple of years, the GAO has noted that existing NASA timelines were tight enough that any one mishap could push them back considerably, and massive workforce reductions under the second Trump administration haven’t helped matters. The Artemis missions to return humans to the Moon have also suffered a few hitches. Artemis I and Artemis II faced multiple delays, and NASA has since changed Artemis III's objectives, turning the planned 2027 lunar landing into a demonstration mission in low Earth orbit, in part to address concerns about the readiness of lunar landing systems, including SpaceX's Starship.

events.title: 'Cheaper to buy everyone new TVs' as regions lose terrestrial channels
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Regional audiences facing a range of impacts from loss of Network 10 Rosy Smith says it is unfair people in regional areas are losing terrestrial TV channels. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) Regional audiences in parts of SA and NSW have mixed reactions to hearing that they will lose Network 10 channels. An expert says advertisers are spending online instead of on broadcast TV, creating an uncertain future. The channels are expected to go off air at midnight. An expert says it would be cheaper for television networks to buy Australians a smart TV with streaming capability than continue to broadcast terrestrial television. WIN Network has announced it will cease broadcasting Network 10 channels, including 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy, in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area markets, after the two networks failed to reach a new broadcast deal . WIN said it was providing the service in these markets was no longer viable, something that reflected "the realities of regional broadcasting". Network 10 says people can still stream its channels online. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) University of Sydney professor of digital communication and culture Terry Flew said TV licences used to be considered "licences to print money", but streaming had up-ended the model. "Traditional broadcasters around Australia and around the world are feeling the pinch," he said. "The cost of delivering the terrestrial service is now greater than the returns that are coming from the advertising share, and that is impacting on regional areas." Network 10 said audiences could continue to access its content online and via its app. WIN Network says the infrastructure costs of maintaining regional terrestrial TV are high. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) Professor Flew said commercial broadcasters had already seen about 20-30 per cent of their audience move to streaming platforms. He said audiences would need to adapt to the changing landscape. Terry Flew says the economics of broadcast TV have changed significantly. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) "You would then need to connect up all those homes with a modem, and people would need to become familiar with how to use the television in a different way. "There may be an opportunity for local or state government to get involved in providing services in that way." For some, the decision will not have much of an impact on how they consume media. Limestone Coast resident Talie Teakle, 54, said she had not had an aerial connected to her TV for about 17 years. Mount Gambier's Talie Teakle streams her shows, but worries about what losing terrestrial channels will mean for others. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) She said for many people, the flexibility of on-demand streaming was preferable to scheduled broadcasts. "Life is so busy, if I've got free time I want to be able to watch what I want, when I want to watch it," she said. "I don't want to be at the whim of a schedule where you're waiting for a weekly show to come on." Rosy Smith says she and other seniors will not move to streaming their shows. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) However, Mount Gambier's Rosy Smith said she was a regular free-to-air TV watcher, and it was an "absolute shame" to lose channels. She said the majority of people she had spoken to at the city's senior citizens' club would be impacted by the "unfair" decision. "There's a lot of people that don't want to go down that track," she said. "It's just another blow to the regional community, having had things and then it's taken away from you. events.title: Fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute misconduct claims, warn of chilling effect
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, the three safety researchers that OpenAI fired last week , have published an open letter denying the firm’s claims that they mishandled sensitive information outside of established company procedures and warned that their dismissal signals a chilling effect that will have ripple effects across the company’s culture. “We have become concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI,” the researchers wrote Thursday in an open letter to OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee, Safety Advisory Group, and Mission Advisory Council. The researchers were dismissed last week after allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization. OpenAI said they violated the company’s policies by “accessing and handling sensitive company information.” “AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” Wang, Korbak, and Balesni wrote. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.” They said that their firing represents a broader shift in the culture of OpenAI, one that used to encourage workers to “raise safety concerns and disagree openly.” They said employees are now “unclear on where they stand” when behavior that was allegedly normal a month ago is now suddenly grounds for dismissal. “Given the significant safety concerns surrounding the development of AI, employees must not be left working in an environment where fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work and weaken third-party accountability,” they wrote. “Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.” In the letter, the three denied involvement in a leak to The Information about less monitorable architectures in OpenAI’s newest models that make chain-of-thought reasoning more difficult to monitor. They also denied engaging with external parties outside the mandates of their jobs. OpenAI has not formally responded to the open letter, but shared with TechCrunch an internal memo attributed to a research leader, praising the three researchers’ contributions to AI safety and denying that they were fired in retaliation. “I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out,” the memo reads. “We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns.” Separately, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch the three were fired after an investigation revealed a “pattern of misconduct” in “clear violation of our policies of mishandling research information” that goes beyond sharing information with an outside AI evaluation group. OpenAI did not directly address TechCrunch’s questions about specifically which policies the researchers allegedly violated, the circumstances of their dismissal, or how the company protects employees who raise safety concerns and collaborate with external evaluators. The firings have fueled speculation about their circumstances, particularly as OpenAI faces scrutiny over recent safety incidents involving rogue agents and leaks about its models. The letter also addresses the researchers’ response to the Hugging Face incident , in which a swarm of agents broke out of their sandbox and breached external systems. The letter says that the incident and investigation was “without precedent,” meaning “internal policies were being developed in real time.” Due to the sensitive nature of the investigation, Korbak believed he was acting within OpenAI’s policies and norms by communicating closely with outside safety evaluators to build trust, per the letter. At the same time, Balesni was also working internally to address the growing AI monitorability problem, an effort the researchers say in their letter “can only succeed through extensive communication with external parties.” According to the letter, Balesni coordinated with and was supported by OpenAI board members and executives throughout his work. “Throughout, Mikita checked in with his reporting line and took care to remove sensitive details from materials before sharing them,” the letter reads. “He acted throughout in good faith and within the company’s norms as they stood at the time.
