events.title: Singapore’s cheque cut-off: Why this property player is switching to e-payments now
events.summary: With banks set to stop processing Singapore dollar corporate cheques from Jan 1, 2027, City Developments Limited has adopted the electronic deferred payment option that has made collections faster and more reliable CDL’s early adoption of e-payment methods like EDP+ has made payment collection for its property sales faster. Buying a property in Singapore has traditionally meant homebuyers writing physical cheques, while developers manually verify and match each one against the sale – a slow, paper-heavy process on both sides. City Developments Limited (CDL) has moved away from it, and with much success. The developer’s e-payment journey began as early as 2018, when it introduced FAST (Fast and Secure Transfers) for homebuyers at The Tapestry development in Tampines. That early move set the stage for CDL to become one of the early adopters of the Electronic Deferred Payment (EDP and EDP+) system when it launched in 2025 – a transition that, as it turns out, was also well-timed. With e-payments growing more convenient and widespread across the economy in recent years, cheque usage has also seen a sharp decline. As such, all banks in Singapore will stop processing Singapore dollar-denominated corporate cheques from Jan 1, 2027. Ahead of that deadline, businesses and consumers here are being encouraged to switch to e-payment alternatives such as EDP and EDP+. Both let payers make deferred payments instead of using future-dated cheques, for instance, to fulfil contractual requirements such as buying a home for individuals or making supplier payments for businesses. The two solutions were introduced to give individuals and businesses the option of making deferred payments with notifications to recipients, complementing existing options such as PayNow, GIRO (General Interbank Recurring Order), FAST and MEPS+ (MAS Electronic Payment System). For CDL, the shift to the latest e-payments has already created a win-win for the company, its clients and partner banks. The developer now uses EDP+ for sales bookings and progressive payments on its property transactions. “EDP+ provides a sustainable, more efficient alternative to cheques, which have traditionally been used for property sales collections,” says CDL’s group general manager Chia Ngiang Hong. “It improves payment collection, reduces the manual administrative effort associated with cheque handling, while enhancing payment tracking and reconciliation.” EDP vs EDP+: What is the difference? EDP and EDP+ are two e-payment solutions introduced on July 28, 2025, that let businesses and individuals make deferred payments in place of cheques. They complement existing options such as PayNow, FAST, GIRO and MEPS+. The key difference between the two lies in when funds are deducted from the payer’s account. EDP: Funds are deducted from the payer’s account only when the payee requests payment, that is, upon presentment of the EDP. EDP+: Funds are deducted immediately from the payer’s account upon issuance of the EDP+, ensuring the amount cannot be used for other transactions. This reduces the risk of non-payment due to insufficient funds in the payer’s account, providing greater assurance to payees as compared to EDP. The challenges and benefits of switching to EDP+ CDL’s move to EDP+ builds on its digital payment journey that began in 2018. Chia called it a “natural progression”. By working closely with its banking partners, CDL was able to align operational processes for successful implementation. One key challenge was adapting to the different ways banks process incoming EDP+ payments. As collections must comply with CDL’s existing banking controls and mandate requirements, the company collaborated with its banking partners to ensure the smooth collection of funds while maintaining appropriate governance and oversight. Homebuyers can opt for e-payments via EDP+ for Lucerne Grand, CDL’s new launch at Lakeside Drive. That groundwork paid off in three ways. The first is lower risk with less hassle. Because EDP+ funds are deducted and set aside upon issuance, CDL gets greater assurance of payment, reducing the risk of insufficient funds and unsuccessful collections – while also saving the time and effort of having to chase clients for replacement payments. The second is easier tracking and matching. With payment details captured electronically, CDL can more easily identify who made a payment and match it to the correct transaction, improving the accuracy of its bank reconciliation and giving the finance team better visibility and control over incoming payments. EDP+’s presentment feature, accessed through the bank’s digital banking platform, enables CDL’s finance team to receive incoming EDP+ payments while providing clear visibility of the payer, payment amount and payment purpose. The third benefit reaches beyond the balance sheet: moving away from paper cheques complements CDL’s sustainability and digitalisation goals.

events.title: An air-con firm building AI, a hygiene business going regional: How home-grown SMEs are turning decades of expertise into new revenue
events.summary: With guidance from Enterprise Singapore and SME Centres, these firms are packaging their know-how into AI tools, overseas ventures and services they can sell Innoflex founder and managing director Kelvin Gan (centre) is turning two decades of engineering know-how into digital tools that could open up new service and revenue opportunities. Twenty years ago, this home-grown firm was merely a five-man air-conditioning contractor. Today, Innoflex has close to 100 employees, takes on multimillion-dollar projects – and is developing its own digital and AI tools. Its ZEGGO CoolHub brings equipment records, maintenance history and fault reports onto one platform, while ZEGG-BOT, an AI-enabled assistant, helps technicians retrieve information and identify possible causes of faults using everyday language. It is a significant shift for the company, and reflects its ambition to turn two decades of engineering know-how into a new source of growth. The innovations were developed as a means to address a challenge that emerged as the company grew. As Innoflex took on larger and more complex projects, manual reporting, fragmented records and reliance on individual employees’ experience became increasingly difficult to manage. These projects included maintenance work across SBS Transit’s interchanges, transport hubs and depots; air-conditioning and ventilation works at SMRT stations; and servicing about 700 units across CapitaLand’s portfolio. That pushed the company to look beyond fixing internal inefficiencies and reconsider the role it wanted to play for customers. Innoflex founder and managing director Kelvin Gan says: “Instead of being a contractor, we want to be a solutions provider, using technology to solve our customers’ problems.” Technology offered a way to do that. But coming up with the idea was easier than putting it into practice. Innoflex initially envisioned its digital transformation as one large project, with multiple AI and digital functions developed simultaneously. Gan soon realised that this would demand substantial money and manpower – many a hurdle that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often face. To help SMEs navigate such challenges, Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) works with trade associations and chambers to strengthen and build capabilities of business advisors at SME Centres, enabling them to provide more effective and personalised support for companies. Business advisors at these SME Centres work with companies to assess their needs and growth plans, and extend support in areas including capability development and internationalisation too. Such support would enable businesses to be connected with relevant expertise, partners and support programmes. “As a small and open economy, Singapore can stay relevant and competitive only if our businesses continue to build capabilities, innovate and internationalise. SMEs anchor growth and create good jobs, which is why strengthening them is key,” says Audrey Lok, executive director of Enterprise Experience at EnterpriseSG. “Through the trade associations and SME Centres, our partners amplify EnterpriseSG’s efforts by bringing industry expertise, trusted networks and on-the-ground insights to SMEs. This multiplier effect allows us to reach more businesses and deliver more targeted support, enabling our SMEs to stay competitive and seize opportunities for growth.” Building new capabilities for the next stage of growth For Innoflex, the way forward came after it approached the SME Centre at the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEC@ASME) in 2024. Business advisor Steven Wong helped Innoflex break down its plans into steps to better manage its digital transformation. This involved assessing what could realistically be executed and implemented, and also helped the company identify where to start. The first phase focused on digitalising analogue data and signals, human servicing procedures and error codings. Phase 2, which is now under way, involves merging all digital data onto one platform. At Civil Service Club @ Tessensohn, Innoflex’s digital tools help facility teams monitor equipment, spot faults earlier and plan maintenance more efficiently. Innoflex’s head of sustainability Dr Ng Kong Jee, who worked closely with Wong, says: “Because of Steven’s advice, we managed to get Phase 1 working and already implemented on site, and now we’re on Phase 2.” EnterpriseSG’s Enterprise Development Grant (now streamlined into the EDGE Grant) also supported the company in engaging technology partners, organising its operational data and testing the system in practice. What started as a solution to Innoflex’s own operational challenges could eventually become a new source of revenue. Managing director Gan wants to offer services such as energy optimisation and predictive maintenance throughout a building’s operations, and eventually take these solutions to regional markets.

events.title: Coca-Cola looks to sell Costa Coffee
events.summary: The Scoop Coca-Cola is seeking to unwind its $5 billion acquisition of a British coffeehouse, months after a sales process faltered earlier this year. The American beverage conglomerate is once again exploring a sale of Costa Coffee, according to people familiar with the matter. Coca-Cola acquired Costa for $5.1 billion in 2018 , but has struggled to grow the business meaningfully. It explored selling Costa in late 2025, before calling off the sales process earlier this year after a tepid response from private-equity bidders, the Financial Times reported in January . At least one strategic acquirer mulled what a deal for Costa would look like before passing due to valuation and strategic issues, one of the people said. It couldn’t be determined what price Coca-Cola might seek for the asset were it to market it more actively again. Coca-Cola’s on-again, off-again efforts to sell Costa mean it might again choose to wait. Coca-Cola did not return a request for comment. Know More Costa Coffee has 2,700 outlets in the UK and Ireland and employs 20,000 people. The coffee chain is targeting younger consumers by adding more iced drinks and matcha to its menus. Coca-Cola bought Costa from British hospitality company Whitbread. The business lost nearly £20 million in 2023 and 2024 combined. Costa reopened a number of its revamped high street outlets in early 2026, around the same time as Coca-Cola reportedly abandoned its plans to sell the chain. Costa’s chief executive Philippe Schillee told the Guardian that the company’s new Hertfordshire headquarters, which will open in January 2027 with capacity for 300 workers, “really signals our confidence in the business.”

events.title: She Designed Meta’s New AI Logo. Then Came the Hate
events.summary: Bay Area lettering artist Jesscia Hische knew that when she took a freelance gig to design the M logo for Meta’s new AI assistant Muse , it was bound to make some people angry. “AI is such a third rail, and Meta is such a third rail,” she tells me. Still, as a small business owner who relies on client work to keep her two brick-and-mortar art and stationary shops in Oakland afloat, she says she needed the money. “New Work! (Don’t be mad at me),” Hische wrote in her newsletter last month. “I worked with Meta on an icon and logotype for their latest release: Muse, which just launched! It’s Meta’s foray into the AI agent / personal assistant world. I know folks have big feelings about both AI and Meta, but this has been a really fun project for so many reasons.” The news quickly went viral on Threads, where dozens of fellow designers criticized Hische for selling out. She responded to the haters by trying to explain the decision: “For the past year, I pretty much have 2-4 payrolls in my account at any given time, which if you own a small business, you know is pretty precarious,” she wrote . She added that she had also invested $100,000 in Studioworks, an admin platform she runs for creatives, and $30,000 in Drawling, her art shop for kids in Oakland, where she hosts classes and workshops. “I have 4 people on payroll including myself, my mom, and two shop employees,” she added. Nothing she said seemed to help. “Disgusted,” wrote one user. “It’s not about money, it’s about ethics.” Another person responded saying, “Doing this job is like doing a hit for the mob, and being surprised later when the mob takes you out too.” Other users posted photos of Hische’s house and speculated about her wealth and finances. Hische had expected some pushback from the artist community, but the level of vitriol caught her off guard. Even if people didn’t like Meta, she felt the company should be commended for hiring an independent artist rather than using generative AI. But the backlash made it clear just how unpopular generative AI has become in some circles, to the point that working for one in any capacity is seen as a betrayal. We spoke on the phone last week about the backlash, her design process, and whether she was instructed to not make the Muse logo look like a butthole. This interview has been edited for clarity and length. Zoë Schiffer: In your newsletter, you acknowledge that people have complicated feelings about Meta and about AI. Did that make it hard for you to take this job? Jesscia Hische : The last year or two, my client work has been really slow, and my client work is what supports the other things I do, because the brick-and-mortar businesses are not hugely profitable. My margins are razor thin. I think between the two shops, I had like $10,000 in profit last year. I can't sustain myself on $10,000 a year. So when the Meta project came around, it was like, alright! Let's get some money in the account so I can pay my staff and I don't have to feel so stressed out every time I have to run a pay cycle. What were you hired to do, specifically? I specialize in logo refreshes. I did the redesign of Squier from Fender, I redesigned Jeni’s Ice Cream a few years ago and did Southern Living magazine. When I work on logos, I want them to look like they went to the spa for a weekend—not that they went and got a ton of plastic surgery, you know? Just fresh and new, where you're like, “Oh, something's different. I can't tell what, but I like it.” The [Meta] team had done an exploration of the M internally. They knew it wasn't quite right. It’s just a bunch of product designers and engineers designing type. Some of them are very skilled at typography, but it's just such a super unique thing to be able to draw letterforms. They wanted to refine what they had already done in terms of the M. It was a huge sprint for that M. I did the work in two days. There were 32 different versions. The logotype took another two weeks. What did the team tell you they wanted to change? They had drawn the M as a single stroke, a vector stroke. It was the same width all the way around. When something is just a mono-weight stroke with no adjustments, there's not a lot of subtlety around the shape. This is where the fun happens with type design. As strokes touch each other and join, it creates this heavier pocket, visually. You get these little inky moments. And what type designers often do is sort of play with subtracting and adding bits of weight. Their big ask was, “We want this thing to feel inspiring and creative and to get people thinking that Muse is a fun thing you can play with, not that it's like this very rigid, engineered, cold thing.” How much do you get paid for a project like this? I charged what I thought was an amazing fee for a two-day sprint for a big company, which was like $12,500. That’s an amazing amount of money to make in two days, but it’s not life-changing.

events.title: The Footscray Club prevailed for 132 years, but it couldn't survive this moment
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts The pale faded blue of Gary Tomlins's eyes is an almost perfect chameleonic colour match for the dusty pool cue tip he has spent so much of his life peering over. For 45 years, the limber 78-year-old has held court at the pool table by the windows of the Footscray Club. Gary Tomlins is rarely without a pool cue in hand. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) As the light waned on Sunday afternoon, he tried to eke out just a few more games before the club shut its doors for good. "It's sad. It's 132 years of history," Tomlins said. "It's a wonder I haven't got tears running down my eyes. Maybe those will come later. I'm just hiding them at the moment." Tomlins says he doesn't know where he'll go now the Footscray Club is closed. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) The Footscray Club has survived in some form since 1894. Like so many community cornerstones around the country, the working-class members' club, perched atop 33 narrow steps in Melbourne's inner west, has become overwhelmed by the new economic reality . Neil Lewis says the club is closing out of necessity, not choice. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) "We've been holding on to all this for as long as we can," the club's 73-year-old president Neil Lewis said. "We've tried everything. We're not closing because of choice." An old stamp for the Footscray Cycling Club, first founded in 1894. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) Lewis recently found an old stamp that gives a clue to the club's origins. A picture of a bicycle with the letters F.C.C. — Footscray Cycling Club — harks back to its earliest 1890s iteration, before it broadened to an (initially male-only) members' club. Do you have a story to share about your community? Email Jeremy Story Carter at storycarter.jeremy@abc.net.au or his secure email jstorycarter@protonmail.com . What that has meant in more recent times is a club for people — typically in their 50s-70s — to gather, grab a soft drink or $7 schooner and feel some sense of belonging. An archival photo of the Footscray Club found in an old magazine. ( Supplied: Footscray Hotel ) "It's a family sort of thing," Lewis said. "There's not many pubs around where you can leave your wallet on the bar or table and walk away and come back and [it's still there]." It is, by no means, a model business for modern times. The Footscray Club has prided itself on being welcoming to all. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) The room is unremarkably furnished. There used to be cheap plates of hot food, but that had to be wound up. "We kept getting hassled by the health department and the council. It just wasn't worth it," committee member Steven Bartlett said. Steven Bartlett used to work as a bartender at the club and has been a member for decades. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) The club instead relied on drink sales to remain viable, but found itself pinched at both ends. As inflation has nudged the word "recession" back into public debate , recent ABC analysis found the cost of beer has risen 23 per cent since the COVID-19 pandemic . The tension of soaring costs and a shrinking member base with less money to spend has become unsustainable. An older member and former service member at the Footscray Club. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) "We don't put the price of beers up or the price of drinks up because if we do that, we're going to lose those members," Lewis said. The steep stairs to the club have become a problem for some older members. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) Club regular and local Cameron, a comparatively younger member at 49 years old, can feel the cost-of-living crisis changing the community around him. "Sometimes you've got to cut things out that you can't afford," he said. "This shouldn't be one of the places." Long Huynh used to pay rent to the Footscray Club to run a bakery in the space beneath it. Long Huynh at the Footscray Club on the last day of trading. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) When the club badly needed an injection of funds, it sold to Huynh, who has rented it back to it for almost two decades. "I want to keep this club," Huynh said. "But at the moment, Footscray is very bad." Community safety has become a major issue in Footscray. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) In an economically depressed moment, signs of disadvantage — of homelessness and drug use — are visible from the club's doorstep. In August, amid growing concerns about community safety, Mayor Mohamed Semra was threatened with a knife in the nearby mall, remarkably while waiting to meet the minister of police.

events.title: Trump Administration Cuts Off Access to a Major Immigration Program for Workers at Microsoft and Adobe
events.summary: The Trump administration will no longer allow Microsoft and other tech companies to participate in a program that allows H-1B visa holders to apply for green cards, one of the most common pathways for skilled foreign workers seeking permanent residency in the United States. In addition to Microsoft, administration officials said on Thursday that software giant Adobe and IT companies including Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata will be suspended from the PERM program, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification program. PERM is a key step for H-1B visa holders to gain permanent residency, requiring employers to prove that there are no American workers who would be suitable for the applicant's permanent job opportunity. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said that the agency is investigating whether these companies committed fraud, undercutting American workers by hiring foreign employees. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, singled out Microsoft. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said during a press conference. In a statement provided by Microsoft representative Kaitlin Haskins, the company said it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," adding that it develops its workforce by "strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world." Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment. The suspension marks a victory for tech workers who have complained about unfairly losing out on jobs to immigrant workers. Jobs Now, an advocacy group composed of US citizens working in big tech, celebrated Vance’s announcement on its X account with a video of dancing crabs. The group publicizes otherwise difficult-to-find PERM job postings and says it helped Americans apply to nearly 500,000 jobs across 7,000 employers between last January and this past July. The organization and its members have also filed complaints against tech companies about alleged abuse of the PERM system, and have called for a number of changes to the employment immigration system. “Every job in America should be offered to an American first, no exceptions,” the group told WIRED in an unsigned statement. This isn't the first time tech companies have been targeted over PERM. Earlier this year, OpenAI and a company it acquired agreed to settle accusations from the Trump administration about violating rules for the program. Apple reached a similar deal in 2023. The administration's disparagement of H-1B visas—one of the most common work visas in the US—has sent waves of panic through Silicon Valley since Trump's reelection. Tech companies are some of the H1-B program's biggest users: So far in the fiscal year 2026 , the top three employers with the most visas approved are Amazon, Tata, and Infosys. Microsoft is No. 5, with 3,688 visas approved in 2026; in 2025, 6,258 visas were approved. According to the company, 80 percent of last year's visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees, not to hire new people. "The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our US workforce," Microsoft’s statement said. It's unclear if Thursday’s announcement would affect the ability of employees at these companies to apply for H1-B visas themselves. The Office of the Vice President and the Department of Labor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for clarity on if the suspension would impact those seeking H-1B visas. "It's one thing if you want to bring in someone like Elon Musk" who aims to "build something great in America," Vance said on Thursday. He equated the current state of the H-1B program to bringing "indentured servants" into the US, taking jobs away from American workers. (Musk, who was born in South Africa, came to the US via Canada to pursue a bachelor's degree at the University of Pennsylvania.) The announcement came shortly before Trump was set to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. When asked about the upcoming event, Vance said, "We’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.” Vance also said that the administration is investigating nine universities to see if they might be committing fraud with the J-1 visa program, which allows international candidates to study and conduct research in the US.

events.title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
events.summary: Jorge Moreno (left) says "vulture funds" are hiking up rents, while Pierina Nicuray points out that there is "a lack of homes" in Spain Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis , she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause. "It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes." She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb." Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees. "There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own. "They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home." His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government. On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate". Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month. Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay. Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday . Protesters at Pueta del Sol have been paying tributes to Maricarmen Abascal Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market. Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years. When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent. "When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security." Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista. In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%. Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern. A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market. Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes. Carmen Pérez says high rental costs have affected her health However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation. He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies. Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain. "When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years." The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes. The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million. There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs. Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.

events.title: Veterans sue government over 'mass and routine' medical data sharing
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Veterans sue Australian government over sharing of medical data Alan Ashmore said he was "staggered" by the volume of information transmitted to UniSA. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) A new class action alleges the federal government breached privacy laws by disclosing thousands of ex-ADF members' medical records to an Australian university. The MATES healthcare program was shut down by the Veterans' Affairs Minister in 2024. The case will be heard in the Victorian Supreme Court and the Department of Veterans' Affairs declined to comment while proceedings are underway. A class action has been launched against the federal government over allegations of "mass and routine sharing" of veterans' medical records over 20 years. On Wednesday, Gordon Legal served the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) with a privacy breach claim, following a two-year investigation into a health program which accessed thousands of Australian military veterans' data. Medicines Advice and Therapeutics Education Services (MATES) was administered by the now-defunct University of South Australia (UniSA) under contract from 2004 to 2024, when the Veterans' Affairs Minister shut it down after an ethics review. Gordon Legal partner Seb O'Meara, who worked on the Robodebt class action settlement, said anyone who used a DVA healthcare card while MATES operated — around 300,000, including bereaved spouses – could register for the lawsuit. Lawyers for the plaintiff will alleged most veterans were "not aware of the MATES program" and "did not provide consent … for the disclosure of their personal information". The firm will seek damages for breach of confidence in the Victorian Supreme Court. Gordon Legal estimated more than 300,000 veterans and family members with DVA healthcare cards had been auto-enrolled in MATES. ( AAP: Tracey Nearmy ) Case about 'what government can do with our information' DVA's website said MATES was about "preventing adverse health outcomes, such as hospitalisations or unwanted side effects, for veterans who take multiple medications". Their DVA healthcare card payments — equivalent to Medicare data — were periodically sent to UniSA, including their name, address, accepted medical conditions and treatments. The patient's identity was initially obscured, but if health risks were found, "a restricted and small number" of staff identified them and contacted their GP. "In these instances, the data accessed was limited to the veteran's name, address and targeted patient feedback … this may have included prescribed medicines, prescriber details and potential risk factors," the website said. Mr O'Meara said the legal issue was that DVA enrolled participants without seeking their informed consent about who would see their personal information and where it would be stored. Seb O'Meara said at least 6,000 people have expressed interest in joining the class action. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) "At the heart of this case is what our own government can do with our personal information, and in particular … of a reasonably vulnerable cohort of people," Mr O'Meara said. "A lot of these people have pretty complex medical histories. "They include complex psychiatric and psychological conditions, and for many of them, learning of the disclosure … has caused them pretty significant distress." A DVA spokesperson said it was aware of the class action but it would "not be appropriate to comment" while the matter is before the courts. "Throughout its operation, the program was conducted under ethics approvals and formal contractual arrangements, including data security requirements," they said. "As this matter is the subject of active legal proceedings, it would not be appropriate to comment further on questions relating to program governance, consent arrangements, data handling processes, or allegations made by parties." DVA previously said MATES prevented 930 hospitalisations and 140 deaths. Adelaide University, an institution created during a merger between UniSA and University of Adelaide, declined to comment. Vietnam War veteran Alan Ashmore, who has "significant health issues" stemming from deployment, is among at least 6,000 who have expressed interest in joining the action. Mr Ashmore, of Melbourne, is helping others use Freedom of Information to access their MATES files, following a recent swell of interest. Alan Ashmore was sent to Vietnam as part of his national service. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) He was "staggered" to discover his own contained 25 pages, including health conditions and prescribed medications.

events.title: 'Got to be more careful': Paxton leaks prompt Republican handwringing
events.summary: The News Three is a trend, and the leaks about Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton’s campaign have more than hit that threshold. On Thursday the Texas Tribune published audio of Paxton saying the US needs to “suck it up” and cut federal programs, more drips from the same fundraiser that elicited Paxton’s complaints about gas prices , lack of control over his own campaign, and the Republican midterm convention depressing his numbers. “Paxton has always relied on his base and a strong statewide ticket to carry him across the finish line. He’s never played anywhere near this level and doesn’t understand the magnitude of effort being expended on his behalf to try to win this race,” Steven Law, former leader of the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC, told Semafor. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, said of Paxton: “Got to be more careful when you run with the big dogs.” Republicans don’t see any of Paxton’s remarks as politically fatal to Paxton’s campaign, but the leaks are not helpful — they only contribute to perceptions of GOP disarray in a tight Senate race. National Republican Senatorial Campaign spokesperson Joanna Rodriguez told Semafor that Republicans need to “put your jersey on and fight with us or go sit in the stands enjoying tofu with the Talafreakos.” Know More Polls this week have continued to show Democratic nominee James Talarico with a slight lead or tied with Paxton, a harrowing result for the GOP in the home state of the modern Republican Party. President Donald Trump rallied with Paxton on Wednesday night, then offered Paxton up for a debate with Talarico — prompting the Democrat to quickly agree and say: “I agree. Ball’s in your court, Ken.” Republicans saw all this coming from a mile away, of course, spending huge sums to help Cornyn defeat Paxton in the primary, reasoning that the general election would be a relative layup for Cornyn. But that didn’t happen, Trump endorsed Paxton, and now Republicans say they need to act like the entire majority is on the line in Texas — because it very well might be. “There are only two teams fighting for Texas’ future: the one with vegans and radicals who want to ban meat, reopen our borders, and transition your kids or the Republican team with a proven record fighting everything the other stands for,” Rodriguez said.

events.title: Exclusive: Anthropic's plan to protect critical infrastructure
events.summary: Anthropic is launching a new cybersecurity initiative designed to bring its most powerful AI models and engineers to companies protecting power grids, water utilities and other critical infrastructure, the company first shared with Axios. Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are struggling to secure aging, complex systems as AI threatens to make cyberattacks faster and cheaper to execute. Driving the news: Under its new Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, Anthropic will provide its frontier AI models, on-site engineers and threat research to companies already responsible for securing critical infrastructure systems. Participating companies will use these resources to identify and fix vulnerabilities in their customers' systems. The program's founding partners include Accenture, Booz Allen Hamilton, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC and Rockwell Automation. Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same. Zoom in: Anthropic is also launching a free AI-powered vulnerability scanning service for open-source software projects, called OSS Scanner. Participating projects will receive periodic scans from Claude, along with automated reports detailing vulnerabilities, how they could be exploited and suggested fixes. The reports won't undergo human review before being sent to software maintainers, meaning some findings could be inaccurate. The big picture: Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI developers are looking for ways to put their most powerful models in the hands of cyber defenders as hackers gain access to similar capabilities . Anthropic's new initiative builds on lessons from Project Glasswing, which gave vetted organizations access to its most capable AI models to identify security vulnerabilities. The company said the project demonstrated how quickly AI can uncover vulnerabilities, but also how difficult it remains to verify and fix them. Yes, but: It's unclear how participating companies will safely test and deploy fixes without disrupting utilities' operations, one of the biggest challenges in securing critical infrastructure. Anthropic also didn't specify whether partners will receive free model access or who will cover the computing costs associated with using its AI tools. events.title: Trump: Anyone saying "AI" is "THE ENEMY!" The White House uses it
events.summary: President Trump on Thursday called anyone who uses "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" "THE ENEMY!" — even as the White House continues using the term "AI." Why it matters: Trump's push to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" clashes with established terminology in the technology industry. Trump's branding blurs the distinction between AI and super intelligence , a hypothetical version of AI more advanced than human intelligence. What they're saying: "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday. Zoom out: Trump's executive order from September doubled down on using "SI" over "AI," though it did not offer a penalty for using the term. The order specifically defines "Super Intelligence" using the existing federal legal definition of AI. The order calls on federal agencies to change how they describe AI in official communications. The State Department already ordered diplomats to use the term after Trump's United Nations speech on Sept. 22. Yes, but: The White House still uses "AI" as a term, including on its AI-focused website, AI.gov . The White House's Office of Science and Technology Policy also makes reference to "artificial intelligence." But when an Axios reporter asked the America.gov chatbot about AI, the bot responded: "The executive branch uses Super Intelligence (SI) for this topic, not the older term you used." What we're watching: Whether the White House could update its websites to reflect Trump's preferred terminology. The White House did not respond to Axios' request for comment Thursday.

events.title: Ben Affleck is an AI nerd, and the internet is impressed
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. They cast the wrong lead in “Good Will Hunting,” apparently, because it’s Ben Affleck who is the secret genius, as it turns out. The actor who earlier this year sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix for a reported $587 million has gone viral this week for demonstrating his understanding of AI technology, neural networks, machine learning, and the like, across multiple video clips of his recent interviews. He can even write a little Python, he says. The movie star delved into his interest in technology most recently on an episode of GQ’s “One More Question” series this week, where he humbly started with “I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young,” before nerding out on the development of AI as it relates to filmmaking, while using AI terminology like machine learning, neural networks, transformers, tensors, GPUs, inference, and more. In a clip that’s making the rounds, Affleck explains to the impressed interviewer, Zach Baron, that he got into the space when analog film moved to digital. As he spoke, he kept defining terms so the interviewer could understand what he was talking about. “I became more interested in that aspect of it, and the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning,” Affleck began. “So I can write, like, pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that. Because with convolutional neural networks — which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do — which is just much more computation simultaneously — you would do things like, look at what’s called a tensor — which is just the numerical translation of a visual image, in numbers like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame, and how many? It’s just that simple, right?” No, Ben Affleck, it is not just that simple, which is why this video is going viral. The actor then went into how neural networks were used to identify patterns and do edge detection or feature extraction, which he described as “identifying patterns enough to know — like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.” He also admitted he used his status as a Hollywood star to get a peek at emerging AI technology, at times. OpenAI was among those he visited, Affleck said in a separate clip, which ultimately led him to understand how he could get more directly involved in the AI space. As the interviewer continued, Affleck explained how AI can help with filmmaking while not replacing it, leading to the development and sale of his own startup in this space. (He claims the $587 million figure is “not right,” noting that he didn’t own the whole company.) “I gambled on this notion that in order to do this in an ethical way and in a way that could take this technology and actually make it work hand in glove with artists in this community where there are very fixed, long-standing relationships around likeness and so forth, we had to create our own dataset,” he said. “So I raised the money. I shot for about eight months with a lot of cameras and a lot of equipment, and created a dataset that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks, sort of where the training code, the inference code, were related to one another and geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value,” Affleck said. In a separate clip, also going viral, Affleck spoke to Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw at the Screentime 2026 conference in LA, where he talked about how he fine-tuned AI models by taking open source models, unfreezing the weights, then teaching them to meet certain cinematic standards. In the process, the filmmaker retains their proprietary work, while benefiting from the learning they create by training their own unique model for the movie they’re making. Ben Affleck (Hollywood star & Artists Equity CEO) talks about how he fine-tunes open video models by unfreezing weights and trained only the last cinematic layer so a film crew can hit real production standards. for context, Ben Affleck founded InterPositive in 2022, a 16-person… pic.twitter.com/xIOvD0xMyt — Rohan Paul (@rohanpaul_ai) October 1, 2026 The actor used the technique himself in his movie “Animals,” where AI aided in the post-production process. At one point, he also weighed in on the concerns around AI and its world-ending potential . His worries, however, were much more rational. “When I worry about AI, I worry about my kids in school. I worry about the 30% rise in the number of A’s given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use. I don’t worry about Skynet, and I don’t think that it’s going to take over [the movie] business in any meaningful way.

events.title: Popular AI leaderboard Arena nearly doubles valuation to $3.1B valuation in 10 months
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Arena , which originated in 2023 as a research project at UC Berkeley that crowdsourced rankings of AI models, has raised a $200 million Series B round at a $3.1 billion valuation, it said on Thursday. This comes after the company said it reached $100 million in annualized run-rate revenue in June. The round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures, with Salesforce Ventures, 01 Advisors, Dell Technologies Capital, Endeavor Catalyst, a16z, Felicis, and others joining in. Arena previously announced a $150 million Series A in January at a $1.7 billion post-money valuation. At the time, its annualized revenue was $30 million , it said. So that means its valuation has nearly doubled in about 10 months. Arena provides a crowdsourced platform that is free for consumers to use. People enter prompts or request vibe-coded projects and then rate which model does it better. Arena claims it has tens of millions of monthly visitors. In September of last year, it introduced its commercial product, AI Evaluations , a service that provides model labs and enterprises with detailed performance analytics based on its community feedback. The timing proved impeccable. This year, AI labs realized that their models were gaming benchmarking tests, finding ways to rack up good scores without truly earning them. At the same time, enterprises wanted help determining which model works best for their own internal needs rather than relying only on standardized benchmarks. “AI is advancing faster than our ability to evaluate it, and static benchmarks break down once models recognize they’re being tested,” the company said in its funding announcement. “The world needs a neutral third party to measure how safe and aligned AI actually is once it’s in the hands of real people. Arena is stepping into that role today,” it added. To that end, Arena has also added a new category to its leaderboard: alignment . This is where it ranks models based on issues like unauthorized action (taking actions it wasn’t asked to take); false attribution (wrongly crediting statements or facts to the wrong source); and what it calls “deceptive completion” (lying about completing tasks that it didn’t do). Currently, a slate of OpenAI’s models are at the top of its preliminary alignment leaderboard, with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable in sixth and ninth place, respectively. events.title: Google brings agentic AI to Gemini, starting with businesses
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface. The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work. Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these. Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future. The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others. It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network. Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person. The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers. Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters The GPU giant released a fix for the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-47483 Nvidia found $1B under the couch to help secure American scientific computing dominance 16 hours ago Microsoft N1Xes Intel in favor of Nvidia's shiny new SoCs in Surface Laptop Ultra 1 day ago The question you would ask HPE and NVIDIA if nobody was recording 3 days ago Californian accused of shipping $300M worth of Nvidia chips to China without Uncle Sam’s approval 6 days ago Nvidia debuts $4,999 DGX Spark with half the RAM and storage, amid memory crunch 7 days ago Researchers found thousands of GPU servers exposing Nvidia's DCGM Exporter to the internet, with hundreds potentially vulnerable to a high-severity flaw that could let unauthenticated attackers crash the GPU monitoring service and disrupt AI workloads. DCGM Exporters read telemetry from the GPUs on a host, including its hardware, utilization, memory usage, power consumption, and error events. Each GPU has its own unique ID, or UUID, and all of these metrics are exposed in plaintext over HTTP. This exposure provides would-be attackers with detailed information useful for reconnaissance, including mapping GPU infrastructure, identifying potentially vulnerable systems, and monitoring workload activity. Michael Katchinskiy, a researcher at datacenter security startup Lava, found and reported the bug in the GPU health and performance monitoring service. In September, the GPU giant Nvidia released a fix for the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-4748 3, and gave it an 8.2 CVSS high-severity rating. “Once we realized how much these endpoints revealed, the next question was: How many of them are exposed to the internet?” Katchinskiy said in a Thursday blog. So the researchers started scanning the internet for exposed DCGM Exporters. And the scale of exposure proved “especially significant,” he wrote. Over the course of four scans between March and May, the threat hunters found about 2,100 GPU servers exposing DCGM Exporter metrics to the open internet. These included 12,000 GPU UUIDs. None of these required authentication. The hosts belonged to about 300 organizations, according to Katchinskiy, and nearly half - 5,274 of the exposed GPUs, or 44 percent of the total - were located in the US. These GPUs represented about $100 million in hardware, and included Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs, H200s, and H100s - used to run large-scale AI workloads - plus consumer RTX 5090 and 4090 systems. While investigating the exposed systems, the Lava team found that about 25 percent of the exposed DCGM hosts also revealed data from Go’s /debug/pprof/ built-in profiling tool. The profiler collects and exposes runtime performance data such as CPU and memory usage for running Go applications. This includes CPU usage, memory allocations, goroutine states, and blocking events. “With enough concurrent unauthenticated requests, the exporter could run out of memory and crash, cutting off visibility into GPU health and activity,” Katchinskiy wrote. The CPU and memory pressure could also affect AI training or inference workloads. Nvidia fixed the issue in version 4.8.2, and operators should upgrade to that version or later. In addition to GPU telemetry, Lava looked into Prometheus Node Exporter, which monitors server hardware and operating systems, and also exposes metrics over HTTP. The team found 12,096 public Node Exporter hosts exposing data on server models, operating systems, firmware versions, hostnames, storage paths and networking hardware commonly used in GPU clusters. This information reveals how environments are built and configured, which could also be used by attackers for reconnaissance, matching the system to known vulnerabilities. The publicly exposed monitoring services affected customer infrastructure across neocloud and GPU cloud providers including Nebius, Voltage Park, Lambda, Northern Data, and DigitalOcean. Lava reported all of this to the affected providers, and Katchinskiy says that these providers worked with customers to address the exposures.

events.title: U.S. Lawmakers Launch Sexual Abuse Probe of Youth Sports Giant AAU
events.summary: Left image: A scene from an Amateur Athletic Union-affiliated volleyball game in 2026. Right image: Rep. Brett Guthrie, R-Ky., left, chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and ranking member Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., D-N.J. Collage by ProPublica. Photos by Sarah Blesener for ProPublica and Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images. What Happened: Bipartisan leaders from the powerful House Energy and Commerce Committee launched an inquiry on Wednesday into the Amateur Athletic Union, criticizing the sprawling youth sports organization for its handling of child sexual abuse allegations and demanding answers, citing reporting by ProPublica and The Washington Post . What They Said: “It is unacceptable that AAU is failing to implement standard reforms to protect child athletes, and is misleading the public, parents, and athletes about preventative measures in place within AAU sports,” the letter reads . The committee chair, Kentucky Republican Brett Guthrie, called ProPublica and The Post’s reporting “deeply disturbing” in a statement on Thursday, saying it “raises serious questions about the organization’s actions over the past decade.”  “Our Committee is seeking information on how the AAU’s policies have potentially fallen short, and what needs to be done in order to protect young athletes,” Guthrie said.” The members of the committee, which in 2018 investigated systemic failures surrounding sexual abuse by former USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar and others, said in the letter that they were “seeing parallels” between its past investigation and “what is being uncovered within the AAU today.” The letter is addressed to Jo Mirza, the AAU’s president, and asks detailed questions about the organization’s operations, taking the extra step of demanding a briefing from Mirza to the committee by Oct. 21. Among questions about its safety policies and coach training, the committee asks Mirza to lay out how many sexual abuse allegations the nonprofit receives each year and how many coaches it disciplines, information that has long been shrouded in secrecy. The AAU declined to provide the data to ProPublica and The Post. The AAU does not publish a list of banned coaches like many other youth sports groups do, and ProPublica and The Post found that it has used confidential arbitration clauses to keep lawsuits from child sexual abuse victims from being heard in open court. The letter is signed by Guthrie, ranking Democrat Frank Pallone Jr. from New Jersey and representatives in charge of oversight and investigations. Read More A Youth Sports Giant Promised Reforms to Protect Kids From Sexual Abuse. Most Never Happened. Background: ProPublica and The Post found that the AAU, which has some 760,000 athletes and coaches nationwide, is failing on nearly every level to adequately protect young athletes from sexual abuse — breaking pledges it made in the wake of a 2011 sexual abuse scandal involving its CEO and young basketball players. The investigation found that the AAU has become a haven for coaches suspected of abuse, according to a review of public disciplinary lists and interviews with current and former executives from six national sports governing bodies and other key stakeholders. The AAU, the investigation found, does not offer child abuse prevention training, though it claims to the public that it does. And ProPublica and The Post found that it has suppressed allegations of sexual misconduct, including against another top executive in 2018. Why It Matters: The committee is one of the key congressional groups charged with overseeing the federal youth sports safety system. It has the power to push for changes in child safety law — and to force transparency from organizations like the AAU, which has repeatedly failed to deliver on past promises of reform. In 2018, in the wake of the allegations against Nassar, scrutiny from Congress led to the passage of a law known as the Safe Sport Act. It created the U.S. Center for SafeSport, an oversight group, to investigate allegations of sexual misconduct and gave it the power to suspend or ban coaches for life. But SafeSport has jurisdiction only over national sports governing bodies, like USA Gymnastics and USA Volleyball, that are overseen by the Olympic and Paralympic Committee — meaning much of the law does not apply to the AAU. The law does require “all amateur sports organizations” — not just governing bodies — to “offer and provide consistent training to all adult members … regarding prevention and reporting of child abuse.” The Energy and Commerce Committee’s letter cites that provision of the law and demands that the AAU explain how it complies. Response: In a statement, the AAU said, “As always, we will cooperate fully and respond appropriately to any questions or requests from congressional committees or U.S. government agencies.” Previously, the AAU told ProPublica and The Post that it is “committed to protecting its athletes through comprehensive protection policies overseen by our Compliance Department,” and said it has an “ongoing commitment to providing a safe, secure, supportive, and trusted environment where athletes can thrive.” The post U.S. Lawmakers Launch Sexual Abuse Probe of Youth Sports Giant AAU appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: OpenAI’s math solutions aren’t meeting the field’s standards yet
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When OpenAI released hundreds of claimed solutions to some of the world’s hardest math problems this week, the frontier lab said that it had consulted an advisory group of elite mathematicians to avoid the controversy that came with the last time one of its models solved a long-standing problem in the field. But OpenAI fell short of those standards, particularly where the mathematicians emphasized the need for human understanding of a mathematical result. That’s especially concerning after a new paper highlighted gaps between the natural language and formally expressed solution to a million-dollar problem ostensibly solved by OpenAI’s models. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), hosted by Princeton University’s Institute for Advanced Studies, is made up of nine prominent researchers at institutions around the world. The organization released guidelines for frontier labs solving math problems at the end of September. In a statement on the latest set of proofs, the AGMAI said that “it is ultimately up to the mathematical community to assess the extent to which our recommendations were followed successfully.” However, the organization’s first request was “to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.” OpenAI’s release explicitly says that it is evaluating its proprietary models using open research problems in mathematics. The advisory group did not respond when asked by TechCrunch for a more thorough evaluation of OpenAI’s latest proof release. The lab clearly followed some of its principles, including releasing results as soon as possible and including information about how the models reached their conclusions. But not for all of them: Just 10 of the 719 manuscripts included releases of the model’s chain of thought. For papers that people don’t understand, the mathematicians suggested the proofs should be formalized — but just 42% of the proofs released by OpenAI had not undergone this process. Ultimately, it’s still not clear that OpenAI is taking “responsibility for ensuring that human understanding will follow” when releasing its proofs, in accordance to the AGMAI principles. AGMAI suggested that OpenAI should help fund the work of human mathematicians who will be required to make the lab’s solutions meaningful in any real way. “Problems are being solved autonomously by AI prompters who have no interest in the broader field itself once their initial target is ‘solved’, and do not understand the AI output well enough to answer questions on the result, give talks, or otherwise interact with the rest of the field,” Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician who has criticized OpenAI’s approach, wrote on social media after the release. That problem is exemplified by a paper released this week by mathematicians at the University of Cambridge and King’s College in London that questions the way frontier labs are approaching these challenges. When AI models solve mathematical problems, they first create a “natural language” explanation, then try to express that result in Lean, a programming language that in theory confirms the accuracy of the proof by compiling it as code. However, there may be problems with the way the models translate their natural language proofs into code; this paper documents at least two discrepancies between the natural language proof and the Lean code behind the solution OpenAI has offered to a problem derived from the Navier-Stokes equations that describe the complex behavior of fluids. These discrepancies don’t necessarily disprove either solution, but they do raise questions on whether we can simply rely on models to formalize their own solutions without human involvement. That’s one reason that AGMAI asked OpenAI to “include machine-readable metadata correlating the natural language and formal artifacts,” something that the frontier lab did not do with these releases. “Because of the phenomenon of mistranslations — as highlighted in this paper — the NL proof by OpenAI and other autoformalised Lean proofs should not prima facie be trusted without the same peer review process and scrutiny that other proofs are subjected to,” the authors of the “lost in translation” paper conclude. Mathematicians stress that when new results are discovered by humans, they take responsibility for them and engage with the broader community through papers, talks, and seminars. That process increases understanding of the solutions, finds strategies that can be used to solve other problems, and allows the new knowledge to be applied in practical fields.

events.title: Trump's foreign worker crackdown comes for Microsoft, Adobe, IT firms
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the Trump administration is suspending Microsoft , Adobe and several other IT firms' ability to hire foreign-born workers for permanent residency in the U.S. Why it matters: The move will affect hundreds of companies owned by the tech giant, escalating the Trump administration's crackdown on immigrant labor. What they're saying: " We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector," Vance said during a Thursday news conference. "We're the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers." "And so our message to Microsoft is, you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants." Zoom in: The permanent labor certification program , which is administered through the Department of Labor, allows a company to hire foreign workers to live permanently in America. It's typically the first step in receiving an employer-sponsored green card. It's also separate from H-1B visas, which allow workers to live and work temporarily in the U.S. H-1B visas primarily go to highly skilled workers in specialized occupations. Technology companies are among the program's biggest users. The Trump administration has made reducing the number of foreign workers in the country a rallying cry, and accused foreign-born workers of taking jobs that could — and, in its view, should — go to Americans. Driving the news: Vance specifically singled out Microsoft, slamming them for laying off 6,000 workers last year. Vance said Thursday that "[a]t the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. Now that is a scandalous system that we've allowed in this country for far too long." Microsoft owns hundreds of companies, including LinkedIn, Skype and gaming studio Activision Blizzard . Adobe and IT outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini are also suspended from the program. The other side: "We believe in the strength and talent of the American workforce," Microsoft said in a statement . "That is why the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans. We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information." "For example, of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country." Microsoft also said it only files H-1B petitions for people who "meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and that they pay H-1B workers comparable compensation to other employees." Worth noting: Trump will award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House today. Microsoft did not respond to Axios' request for comment. events.title: Trump: U.S. won't attack Iran before midterms
events.summary: President Trump said Thursday the U.S. will not attack Iran ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Why it matters: Trump had been considering for several days resuming major combat operations before the midterms. However, his past statements about his intentions in Iran haven't always matched what he ultimately did. If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include large-scale strikes on Iranian energy facilities, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say. Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterms, in part because oil prices might rise in response. It could also influence Israel's elections, which are scheduled for Oct. 27. What he's saying: "I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait ... we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Flashback: In June 2025, before Operation Midnight Hammer, the White House said Trump would decide "within two weeks" whether the U.S. would join Israel's war against Iran. When he made that statement, he had already decided to attack Iran's nuclear sites. On Feb. 27, less than 24 hours before Israel and the U.S. launched the war against Iran, Trump claimed he hadn't made a decision on going to war. In reality, Trump had already decided to authorize the attacks. Driving the news: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran , Axios reported on Wednesday. Behind the scenes: On Tuesday, Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke with senior U.S. officials who briefed him on the U.S. military's preparations for the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a U.S. official and another source briefed on the call. Zamir said during the call that resuming the war within that timeframe could lead to the postponement of the Israeli elections, given the assessment that Iran would respond by launching missiles at Israel, the sources said. The IDF declined to comment on conversations between Zamir and his U.S. counterparts. Between the lines: It's unclear whether Trump's statement will reassure Iranian leaders that an attack is not imminent. U.S. and Israeli officials say Iranian leaders are deeply suspicious of Trump's statements. The officials said Iranian leaders were surprised twice and want to avoid a third surprise attack. What to watch: Trump said the U.S. and Iran "are having productive discussions." But there are no signs that the major differences between the two sides have narrowed.

events.title: Trump administration blocks tech companies from visa program
events.summary: The News The Trump administration on Thursday suspended more than a half-dozen tech companies, including Microsoft, from the program that allows permanent hiring of foreign workers — escalating its long-simmering clash with the tech industry over immigration. “The H-1B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers,” Vice President JD Vance, who helms the administration’s fraud task force, told reporters. “Unfortunately, the program has become rife with fraud.” The administration has tangled with tech companies since President Donald Trump returned to office over its interest in reining in H-1B visas for highly skilled workers. That tension has resulted in a partial pullback of some attempted policy shifts, such as May’s clarification of an announcement that H-1B holders would have to start applying for permanent residency from outside the US. The administration has also recently moved to charge more than $100,000 for a single H-1B visa. Thursday’s announcement formally bans Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and four other companies from the permanent labor certification process. Representatives for Adobe, Cognizant, and Infosys did not immediately return requests for comment. Microsoft said in statement that “we look forward to providing the Administration with additional information.” The company added that it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category. Notably, Trump plans to award a medal to the CEO of Microsoft later on Thursday. In addition, the administration announced it had served subpoenas for a new investigation into multiple universities over their use of J-1 visas for exchange students. Among the educational institutions targeted by the probe are Pitt, Yale, Harvard, Stanford, Brown, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and MIT, officials said at a press conference. “We will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research,” said the Labor Department’s inspector general, former Republican member of Congress Anthony D’Esposito. Know More Foreign workers made up almost a quarter of the US’ STEM workforce in 2023, according to the American Immigration Council . Businesses, which challenged the proposed H-1B fee in court, say they need visas to overcome worker shortages that stem in part from lagging workforce development . Thursday’s announcement marks a continuation of Vance’s focus on fraud heading into the midterms and 2028. The vice president has portrayed the issue as bipartisan — though Trump, when he announced the task force earlier this year, suggested it would focus “primarily” in blue states. Asked Thursday to explain his allegations of visa fraud, Vance pointed to “a couple of certifications” companies must make to receive the visas, including “that the person that you’re bringing in has a specialized, hyper-capable skill set.” “That’s clearly not the case if you’re just replacing one American worker with a foreign indentured servant and undercutting their wages in the process,” Vance said. “So the fraud is that they’re making representations when applying for this program that are fundamentally illegitimate and therefore ultimately illegal.” Notable Vance declined to directly address a Wall Street Journal report that US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle requested a donor pay off debt in exchange for access to government officials, though he told reporters he doesn’t “love that.”
