events.title: CPO Testing Faces A Moving Target Problem
events.summary: Key Takeaways: The industry is busy developing different connector designs and laser sources, while massive data centers with the first levels of CPO are being built. In the absence of design-for-test, companies have to test each individual waveguide, resonator or photodiode, which is inefficient and does not scale. Optical components are much more sensitive to slight offset than electronic components, making issues like thermal and warpage particularly troublesome. Experts At The Table : The steep data center build-out contains an increasing amount of near-packaged optics (NPO) and co-packaged optics (CPO), putting pressure on test manufacturers to produce high-volume manufacturing tooling. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at Teradyne ; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at Advantest America ; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of ASE Group ; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at Keysight Technologies . Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal. SE: Some people liken the testing of optical devices to testing electronic devices several decades ago. What are the most significant challenges associated with testing photonic devices? Griffin : There are two key changes we’re making to the test cells to support co-packaged optics. One is the optical instrumentation itself at the wafer, optical engine, or package level. The second is the automation. So how do I optically interface with the device under test (DUT)? That could be a fiber alignment at wafer, a connector alignment, or receptacle alignment at the package or optical engine level. This is what needs to change to enable high volume. Some of the photonics engineers will say, ‘Well, what’s the big deal? I’ve been testing optical transceivers for 20 years. I’ve been designing optical transceivers for 20 years.’ The difference is the scale of going to high-volume manufacturing, where you’re deploying many testers on a test floor. You want to support high-volume software, data analysis, and test programming capabilities, so it’s not as simple as bringing rack-and-stack instrumentation onto a test cell or designing your own custom optical alignment system like you would in your characterization lab. That is really where the challenges lie. Leventhal : It really comes down to maturity level, and if we wind the clock back 40 years, with each generation of electronics, there’s some new capability being added. In the beginning of my career, ATE was strictly digital test. But we kept getting greater levels of integration, bringing together digital, analog, mixed-signal, RF, and now millimeter wave, in a single package. Photonics is yet another progression of new technology. There’s a less mature ecosystem for the optical part of the test content, and that needs to mature to enable us to truly bring up this technology at scale. For example, customers are still trying to determine which connection technologies they’re going to use and what laser sources they’re going to use. A lot is still evolving. I don’t see this as a fundamentally different challenge, but the signal is optical and not electronic, so electrical engineers are looking at things like polarization extinction ratio, for example, so it takes that next level of learning to evolve this to HVM. Armstrong : Ira hit on an important point. A lot of what we’re doing harkens back to the old days of digital logic before we had scan test. At that time, a lot of people were trying to take rack-and-stack or bench equipment and use it for production test, which tended to be clunky, cumbersome, and slow. Then we got design for testability (DFT) integrated into the logic. We haven’t done DFT for optical. People are trying to deploy some PRBS (pseudo-random binary sequence) type approaches, which have existed in logic devices for a while, but in large part we don’t have DFT, so we have to test each waveguide component, ring, modulator, etc., one at a time, and it is slow and laborious. There’s a lot of different perspectives on what needs to be tested and how to test it, and I’d say one of the biggest challenges is, as Matt alluded, we don’t have a hybrid engineer. We’ve got two different camps of people (those optically trained and those electrically trained) who have a hard time learning each other’s core capability, so we have to get people on the same page, educated similarly both for electrical and optical, with similar standards in place. Yamaguchi : Optical alignment must be extremely precise and can slow down testing. For this reason, using an optical probe card would be ideal but is difficult — not only because of the non-contact mechanical implementation, but also because optical calibration is needed to make reliable and traceable measurements. The multi-channel optical connectivity with the FAU has design variation from unit-to-unit and channel-to-channel, resulting in channel-performance uncertainty. For example, a measurement on channel 1 of a waveguide is different from the same measurement on channel 2. A slight offset due to pitch and x,y mismatch causes an optical alignment offset, which is more impactful than a similar offset at electrical probe. SE: How does the addition of photonics change test flows? Armstrong : We all share a very similar view of insertions. Insertion one is for PIC (photonics IC) testing. Insertion two is wafer-level optical engine testing. Insertion three is die-level optical engine. Insertion four is module test, and insertion five is system-level test. You can add insertion 1.5, wafer-level burn-in, a stability bake of your optical components, and it’s a must for lasers to get rid of infant mortality. PIC testing is certainly done broadly today, although some people who have the most experience in the market say it may not need to be done in the future. Optical engine testing is a must, and that’s where most of the effort is. Optical engine is also what’s quite new vis-a-vie logic device testing. Insertions 2, 3 and 4 feel like a must for the hyperscalers, which feels like a follow-on effort to what hyperscalers have been doing for years with a large ATE high-power test of the heterogeneous integration. Griffin : I’ve been working in this space for about ten years, and almost every insertion has felt like the most important one at some point, depending on which customer or which part of the market you’re talking to. Our goal is to provide test solutions across all insertions and give our customers the flexibility to shift coverage as they gain more insight into the volume manufacturing flow and where they need to optimize. events.title: It's a bird, it's a plane...well, more of a spinning parachute, but really it's a droppable robot boat
events.summary: The ALBATROSS, a sailboat drone prototype developed by researchers at Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), lacks the aerial grace of its avian namesake. It doesn't so much fly as plummet – an unsettling start to a sea launch, more so because it's designed to spin like a maple leaf seed as it descends. The sailboat drone's rotation slows its fall and minimizes its impact with the water. This eliminates the engineering challenge of implementing hardware for two modes of mobility. There's no need for landing gear, actuators, or sensors to manage both flying and floating. Watch and download graphics and videos of ALBATROSS here. Developed by SUTD researchers Shane Kyi Hla Win, Danial Sufiyan, Brian Leonard Suhadi, Luke Soe Thura, Xinyu Cai, Wei Jun Ang, and Shaohui Foong, the ALBATROSS represents an achievement in both acronym construction and engineering. The Airborne Lander with Buoyant AuToROtating Sailing Sensor is described in a Science paper as a hybrid robotic system that combines a bio-inspired design for controlled aerial descent with autonomous sailing. Beyond the bio-inspired operation of the rigid wingsails for creating aerodynamic lift during descent and propulsion on the water, the ALBATROSS further cribs from nature's bag of tricks with a rudder that acts like a caudal fin – it moves side to side like a tailfin to generate thrust. And it does so with just three actuators and three primary sensors. Practically, the boat drone, which weights 1.107 kg, was built to fill the gap between expendable aircraft-deployed ocean instruments and floating robots deployed from ships or shore. Its light weight and adaptability make it well suited for rapid aerial deployment followed by energy-efficient persistence on the water, as might be required to monitor an oil spill or time-sensitive weather events. It is intended to be an alternative to large automated sailboats like Saildrone and Sailbuoy that may require ground- or ship-based management. And it has far greater deployment range than hybrid aquatic micro aerial vehicles: more than 100 km, compared to about 7 km for SailMAV, or so its makers claim. "Building on prior work on guided autorotation, ALBATROSS is designed to be released from an aircraft or UAV, passively enter autorotation for a controlled, low-impact water landing, self-right without actuation, and seamlessly transition into a wind-powered sailboat," the researchers explain. "Unlike many hybrid aerial-marine systems, ALBATROSS eliminates the need for aerial propulsion, complex mechanical reconfiguration, or active stabilization during the air-water transition and can sail back to shore at the end of a mission." The prototype takes flight amid a market doing the same. Last year, PwC's Strategy& consultancy issued a report [PDF] that forecasts a sea drone market worth €18.9 billion (~$21.2 billion) by 2030, based on a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.5 percent. By the end of the decade, most of that (84 percent) is expected to be for civilian uses like scientific research, commercial, recreational, and engineering applications, and search and rescue operations. ®

events.title: ICANN reveals bids for new top-level domains
events.summary: ICANN has revealed the applicants for new generic top-level domains (GTLDs). As The Register reported in August, this is just the second time ICANN has accepted applications for GTLDs, strings like “.com” or “.net”. For years, only ICANN could decide on new GTLDs. The governance body changed that policy and in 2012 allowed over 1,200 new GTLDs. The organization decided to repeat the process this year and on Wednesday announced it received 1,615 applications. A process is now under way to confirm those applications are viable. ICANN has made information about all of the applications available in a searchable form here along with a downloadable list that The Register has pored over to bring you news of the following applications. OpenAI wants 15 GTLDs, among them .chatgpt and .agi – the latter likely the acronym for artificial general intelligence. Six other entities also want that string. The AI upstart also wants .mcp, which probably refers to the open source Model Context Protocol. Google bid for this GTLD, too, as have three other entities. The Big G, through its subsidiary Charleston Road Registry, is in an eight-way tussle to score .api. It has applied for over 30 new names, most pertaining to its products. Anthropic wants only its own name and .claude. Microsoft is another that hopes for just a pair of names: .copilot and .msft. Meta will have to fight another contender to control .superintelligence, but is the only entity trying to claim .wearables. 13 entities hope to claim .agent, with Meta and Google among the contenders. Salesforce wants its own name, plus .force, .slack, and .tableau. An outfit named Fomalhaut Exploration wants .intel. That could be Chipzilla acting through a third party, or the beginning of a legal tussle. Three contenders want to be the home of .drone, while nine are fighting over .brand. Ten applicants want to build their own .hub, while two hope to take GTLDs to .mars. Seven operators hope to run .official, the kind of domain that brands buy defensively so they end up with [companyname].official before someone cynical nabs the name. North America was home to most applicants – 864 – followed by 506 Europeans, 218 from Asia Pacific, 16 from Africa, and just 11 from Latin America and the Caribbean. When multiple parties apply for the same GTLD, ICANN first applies a “community priority evaluation” process that tries to find the most appropriate home for a string. If that fails, rights to the GTLD go to auction. All applications must be decided by November 17, aka String Confirmation Day, after which successful applicants can start the work to establish a registry for their new GTLDs. Readers will likely be able to register domains using the new GTLDs next year. ®

events.title: Biggest coal-producing state fears impact of High Court emissions decision
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Queensland mining sector worried by implications of High Court emissions ruling The Queensland government says the state is the biggest producer of coal. ( Supplied ) The High Court on Wednesday ruled planning authorities in New South Wales needed to consider overseas emissions when approving a mine expansion. It's sparked concerns from the mining sector in Queensland – the country's largest coal-producing state. The industry says it's working through how the decision will impact the state, while the government says the laws are already strong and will strengthen them if needed. A High Court ruling that planning authorities needed to take overseas emissions into account when approving projects could spook investors, the industry fears. Yesterday, the High Court ruled in favour of a New South Wales community group which had been fighting the expansion of a coal mine in the Hunter Valley region. The court ruled the state's planning body had failed to consider the emissions of coal burnt overseas when approving the project. The High Court yesterday ruled in favour of a community group which fought to block an expansion of a coal mine in New South Wales. ( Supplied: Zoe Lonergan ) Speaking to the ABC, federal industry minister Tim Ayres was quick to downplay broader impacts, saying it was "squarely a NSW decision", which would be worked through by the state government. He stressed there would not be implications for either jobs or investment in the sector. "It is a High Court decision, but it's absolutely confined to the provisions of the New South Wales Act and the way … the planning authority did their work," he told the ABC. Resources minister Madeline King agreed it was a "pretty technical ruling" which she believed would not impact other states unless their planning legislation contained similar provisions. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli says the state is "open for business" when it comes to investment in mining. ( ABC News: Brendan Mounter ) Premier says Queensland laws 'bulletproof' In Queensland, Australia's largest coal producing state, Premier David Crisafulli sought to allay industry fears, saying the state's "already bulletproof" laws would be amended if needed in response to the ruling. "We have the best laws in the country, and we have the highest environmental standards and we are the most pro-mining government in the nation," he said. The state's peak industry association for the resources sector feels the ruling could have further-reaching impacts. Overseas emissions, known as 'scope three' emissions, are already considered by regulators, according to the Environmental Protection Act. National Coordinator at Lock the Gate Alliance Ellen Roberts welcomed the New South Wales ruling. She said it was important for decision makers to take these emissions into account because they impacted not only people overseas but people in Australia. But Queensland Resources Council chief executive Janette Hewson said she was concerned by any changes to the interpretation of laws and regulation because it increased risk in the sector. Janette Hewson is the chief executive of the Queensland Resources Council. ( ABC News: Erin Byrnes ) "We are very concerned that our international partners, whether they're investors or customers, will look at what's been happening in Australia," she said. Those concerns were echoed by the Minerals Council of Australia — the group going as far as to say the ruling would send "shudder's down everyone's spine" in the industry. Qld parliament to debate mining law changes Proposed laws in Queensland would restrict who can object to a mine. Its chief executive Tanya Constable described herself as "very concerned", and although she conceded the decision affected New South Wales, said it would set a "bad precedent" in other jurisdictions. The MCA's concerned the decision would spook investors, leading them to fund overseas projects rather than in Australia. Queensland senator Matt Canavan was even more scathing, imploring "all governments" to overturn the High Court's decision by passing laws through state or federal parliaments. He said it was "ridiculous" to have a situation where the viability of Australian mining projects, as well as jobs, were threatened because of emissions created overseas. Professor John Rolfe said it could be hypocritical for Australian mining projects to have to take overseas emissions into account.

St Andrew's Hospital has reported a data breach "affecting a group of individuals". It says the individuals affected and federal privacy and cyber security agencies have been notified. SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said he is expecting to be briefed on the breach later on Thursday. An Adelaide private hospital has notified individuals and cyber security authorities of a data breach of personal information. In a limited statement, St Andrew's Hospital on Thursday morning confirmed it had been investigating a breach of personal information affecting "a group of individuals". The precise number of people impacted, and the circumstances around the breach, are currently unknown. St Andrew's Hospital did not confirm the numbers or nature of the breach in response to questions from the ABC, however its chief information officer Nathan Crettenden said an internal investigation "identified that a subset of data from our servers was downloaded". "As soon as the incident was identified, our team took our systems offline as a precaution, worked to secure our environment and strengthen our security protocols, and engaged specialist forensic experts to conduct an investigation," said Mr Crettenden. "We are taking all reasonable steps to limit the impact of the incident and improve our security posture in response to the incident." Agencies, affected individuals notified In the statement, the hospital's CEO Angela McCabe said an "investigation into the nature and extent of the incident has now progressed to the point where we can communicate directly with affected individuals, in line with our regulatory obligations". She said affected individuals were provided information and support as to how they can protect their personal information. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) and the Australian Cyber Security Centre have been notified of the breach. Ms McCabe said the hospital was working with government agencies to "apply additional protective measures, to help detect and prevent suspicious and fraudulent activity". St Andrew's Hospital says it has notified affected individuals ( ABC News ) Under Australia's Privacy Act, entities covered by Notifiable Data Breach scheme are required to report breaches to the OAIC that are likely to result in "serious harm" to affected individuals. According to the OAIC, information breaches that could carry serious harm can include the exposure of information about a person's health, documents commonly used for identity fraud and financial information. South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said the state government expected to be briefed on the matter later today. "We expect to be updated on exactly what's occurred here and whether or not things have occurred of a criminal nature that might be subject of the South Australian criminal code," Mr Malinauskas said. "That will be of interest to us. The cyber security dynamic globally is clearly under challenge and under threat and it will be important that our law enforcement agencies assess the situation.

events.title: Oil prices rise on potential US strikes on Iran before midterm elections
events.summary: Oil prices jumped on Thursday after reports about Pentagon plans for US strikes on Iran that could be launched before the midterm elections amid continued Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, climbed nearly 3.86 per cent to $104.1 a barrel at 1.49pm UAE time, after falling below the $100 mark earlier this week. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, rose 3.78 per cent to $91.62 a barrel. Crude prices have been hovering above the $100 per barrel mark despite a lull in the US military campaign. US President Donald Trump, who is facing domestic backlash over the war, earlier indicated that the US would resume strikes only after the midterms. However, rising Iranian attacks in recent weeks on oil and gas tankers in the strait may force Mr Trump’s hand. The Atlantic on Tuesday reported that the US Defence Department was identifying targets for attacks in Iran. The size of potential strikes, if the US administration were to proceed with hostilities ahead of polls, was still being discussed, it said, quoting unnamed US officials. The US may choose to conduct a limited military campaign and follow it with a larger operation after polls conclude next month, The Atlantic reported. Axios quoted officials as saying potential operations could involve extensive US-Israeli strikes on Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets. “President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States,” the US news outlet quoted a White House official as saying. Israeli officials said the chances of renewed combat before the elections remain low but could rise significantly afterward, with escalation potentially triggering a major Iranian missile response, according to the report. "Renewed tensions — or, rather, the increasingly crowded headlines surrounding existing and persistent Middle East tensions — weighed on market sentiment," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. "Oil fluctuated, and Brent is extending gains above $102 per barrel." Thin traffic Traffic through the strait, the narrow waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil and gas flowed before the conflict broke out, has remained thin. The number of vessels transiting the strait fell to the lowest in more than two ⁠months, according to shipping data from analytics firm Kpler. Seven commodity ships passed through the strait on Tuesday, the ⁠lowest figure since July 23, data showed. Strikes on tankers climbed to their highest weekly rate since the conflict began on February 28. In the latest attack, a tanker north of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, causing casualties, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Wednesday. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's civilian and energy infrastructure are also adding to market jitters. Saudi Arabia's maritime blockade in the Red Sea by the Houthis and consistent strikes on Saudi Airports, ports and oil pipelines as well as refining facilities are stoking fears as an all-out war that would further crimp supplies energy supplies through the Bab El Mandeb strait. "The risks of multi-front escalation in the region and the war heading toward further fragmentation are boosting the risk premium in pricing," Samer Hasn, senior market analyst at XS.com said. "Nothing suggests a possible return to diplomacy; rather, all signs point to the situation in the region heading toward further deterioration at existing flashpoints and expanding into new ones."

events.title: WA treasurer surprised by High Court outcome and seeking advice
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts What a High Court decision on a NSW coal mine could mean for WA gas projects Industry bodies in WA have raised concerned about a High Court ruling relating to a NSW coal project. ( ABC News: Chris Lewis ) A landmark ruling in the High Court has found planning authorities in New South Wales are required to consider global climate change impacts when approving local fossil fuel projects. Industry bodies and consultants are concerned the ruling could have a broader impact on investment in the resource-rich state of WA. WA Premier Roger Cook said his government would need to look closely at the implications. A High Court ruling in New South Wales has Western Australia's energy industry "deeply concerned" about future investment in the resource-rich state. The ruling stymied the planned expansion of MACH Energy's coal mine after it had already been approved by NSW planning authorities in 2022, after three out of five judges ruled in favour of a community group, Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG). The ruling found the planning authorities were required to take into account the emissions caused by using the coal MACH would export, otherwise known as the project's scope 3 emissions. While the ruling is an interpretation of NSW planning laws, the energy industry is concerned effects could be felt on the other side of the country. In WA, Woodside's $30 billion Browse gas proposal, which would produce more than 11 million tonnes of gas per year, is still being considered by state and federal environmental bodies. WA Treasurer Rita Saffioti said the High Court's assessment came as a surprise, and said the government was seeking urgent legal advice. Rita Saffioti says the High Court decision in New South Wales came as a surprise. ( ABC News: James Carmody ) "Everyone was slightly shocked by the decision, [particularly] a state like WA, which continues to develop significant resources to help our trading partners deal with their emissions," she said. "I'm no legal expert, but it was made in relation to a planning decision in NSW. "The question for us is under what guidelines the High Court made their decision, and whether that impacts every state or just the NSW planning framework." Ms Saffioti said it was likely the decision would require a federal government response. "The whole nation will need to look at work we can continue to support resources development," she said. Independent oil and gas consultant Jeanette Roberts said the decision affirmed industry fears of "lawfare". "One of the issues that concerns the industry in general is this lawfare of an approval being given, and then an opportunity for it to be challenged, and the approval rescinded," she said. "International investors will come because they believe that there's certainty and a rule of law and understanding what the rules and ground rules are. "That certainly swings the pendulum away from that." Aaron Morey says the implications of the decision need to be taken seriously. ( ABC News: Kimberley Putland ) Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive Aaron Morey said it was "deeply concerning". "If we shoot ourselves in the foot and we don't allow the development of these sorts of projects, then what you'll find is that new projects will spring up in other countries with lower environmental controls and standards," Mr Morey said. Mr Morey said it was important that everyone took the implications of the decision as seriously as possible. "Those are the sorts of issues that we need to more deeply understand," he said. The Conservation Council of WA executive director Matt Roberts said it was common sense for all the environmental and climate impacts of a project to be considered in the approvals process. "Australia can't wash its hands of the emissions caused when coal, oil or gas that is extracted here ends up being burnt overseas," he said. "Gas export projects like Woodside's Browse proposal at Scott Reef risk massive climate damage because of their scope 3 emissions. "We've always said that state and federal governments need to consider these scope 3 emissions when assessing these projects." Johnson Legal director Elaine Johnson said while it was an interpretation of NSW laws, the decision would be relevant to courts in other jurisdictions. "The High Court of Australia has issued its first climate ruling, so obviously the content of that decision is going to be relevant to other courts in different jurisdictions around the country, including, I would assume, Western Australia," Ms Johnson said.

events.title: Hormuz traffic hits lowest level in two months as tanker attacks surge
events.summary: ​The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz fell to the lowest in more than two ⁠months after attacks on tankers in the key waterway reached their highest last week since the start of the ​ Iran war , shipping data showed. Seven commodity ships passed through the strait on Tuesday, for the ⁠lowest figure since July 23, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. “Crude crossing the strait fell ​27 per cent ⁠from a wartime high the week ‌before, to at least 10.1 million barrels a day,” Kpler analysts Emmanuel Belostrino and Yui Torikata ​wrote in a note on October 6. “That is back to its September average, but 74 per cent of its prewar level.” Most of the fall was in ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, where cargoes move between tankers, they added. However, exports from the Gulf of Oman coast and the Red Sea rose to 6.7 million bpd, more than twice prewar levels, analysts said, making up for lost supply from Hormuz. This helped keep overall exports of Middle East crude at the prewar level, they said. The number of vessels transiting the strait edged up to 10 on Wednesday, but was well short of the daily tally of more than 20 on Sunday and Monday, the data showed. More vessels entered the strait than exited in the past two days. The figures exclude vessels crossing with their ​Automatic Identification System transponders turned off to avoid detection. LSEG data of all ‌vessels crossing the strait showed eight ⁠on Tuesday, evenly divided between entries and exits, ​down from the previous day's 14. These included five oil tankers and the liquefied ​natural gas tanker ‌Al Mafyar which loaded at Ras Laffan in Qatar and was set to head for Port Qasim ⁠in Pakistan, LSEG added. Attacks on tankers sailing through Hormuz hit their highest last week of ⁠any week since the Iran war began, maritime security sources tracking incidents said, as Gulf producers made a bigger export push. In the latest incident, projectiles struck a tanker 94km north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal, with casualties reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said ​on Wednesday. Before the February 28 start of the Iran war, about 125 large commercial vessels went through the strait each per day, comprising tankers, gas carriers, bulkers and container vessels. Their cargoes accounted for a fifth of global supplies of crude oil and liquefied natural gas.

events.title: Major share market float in trouble as interest in Firmus wanes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Data centre company Firmus tries to save its mega share market float as interest underwhelms The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston. Its data centres require a lot of energy and expansion plans have been described as ambitious. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) The $44 billion Australian float of data centre operator Firmus appears to be in trouble. But Firmus is not currently listed on the ASX's "upcoming floats and listings" webpage, and analysts who spoke to the ABC have raised concerns over the firm’s debts and the wild increase in its valuation over a short period of time. The company is scheduled to float on the ASX on October 23. It was touted as the biggest float since Telstra in the 1990s, but the share market debut of data centre operator Firmus is in trouble before it has even hit the share market. Investment banks stopped taking bids for the initial public offering (IPO) today and will now determine at what price the company lists on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX). But Firmus is not currently listed on the ASX's "upcoming floats and listings" webpage, and analysts who spoke to the ABC have raised concerns over the firm's debts and the wild increase in its valuation over a short period of time. Adding to concerns, Goldman Sachs was reportedly tapped to rescue the float from collapse at midday today. The ABC has contacted several industry players directly connected with Firmus's fundraising, including Wilson Asset Management, Bank of America and Goldman Sachs. The investment bank told the ABC it had no comment. Fund manager Roger Montgomery said there had been inconsistencies in the messages given to market participants about the capital raising. "Investors were previously told that indicative orders were already above the size of the offer at $11 a share," he said. Indicative orders are what investors suggest to brokers they are willing to pay for a stock before orders are formally taking for a public listing. "If that were true, why has the price been cut to get the deal away?" Mr Montgomery said. "Warren Buffett said you want to invest with people who are energetic, intelligent and honest." The ASX told the ABC it does not comment on individual companies. The floats and listings webpage, however, makes it clear that "it only records new listings for which ASX has received a formal listing application". "A formal application would typically only be made late in the listing process when the entity has made all necessary preparations to list in the near term (i.e. within four to six weeks)," it says. This would suggest a formal application has not been made by Firmus to the ASX within 15 days of its expected listing. The caveat to this is that the ASX webpage also states that is "usually updated within three business days of receiving a formal application", meaning the official application may have been lodged. Firmus was set to hit the boards of the ASX at $11 per share, but reports suggest that price may have been set too high. Market participants have been underwhelmed by the float's roadshow, with some criticising it for having an "unprecedented lack of detail" and others concerned about its debt and energy needs. The float, or total number of shares on issue, is reportedly having to be revalued down because of the lacklustre interest, with reports it could drop to about $8 per share. Late on Wednesday, the company's representatives also pulled out of an appearance before a parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence today, with reports the troubled IPO was the reason for the no-show. Is Firmus here for a good time or a long time? Data Centre operator about to float on Australian share market. Firmus is a so-called neocloud technology company. It builds, owns and operates upscale data centres or so-called "AI factories", used to run and train artificial intelligence models. The firm is raising cash from investors to build an AI factory in Launceston and plans for two more in Tasmania. But its ambitions extend across Australia and into South-East Asian markets as well. Reports suggest Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion from institutional and retail investors in its IPO, which could value the company at more than $50 billion. But the conclusion of a $73 billion partnership with data centre firm CDC and community backlash for proposed suburban data centres has caused concern for investors. Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis was also jailed for 12 months in 2016 for a 2007 insider trading scheme.

events.title: Ransomware fixer claimed he could decrypt files, allegedly defrauded clients instead
events.summary: The United States Department of Justice has charged a man with fraud after he allegedly told clients he could decrypt files locked up by ransomware but actually paid ransoms – and seemingly got away with it for years. The Feds allege that Zohar Pinhasi – aka “Zack Silver” and “Zack Green” – ran a Florida company called “MonsterCloud” that advised ransomware victims not to pay because it had a way to recover encrypted data. “The charges relate to Pinhasi’s claimed ability to decrypt ransomware without paying cybercriminals, purportedly using ‘proprietary tools’ and ‘advanced decryption techniques' on behalf of distressed business owners who came to his company,” according to a DoJ press release. “In fact, Pinhasi allegedly used a portion of his clients’ fees to pay off the ransomware attackers, and then kept the rest, often extracting a substantial markup.” In one case, Pinhasi allegedly charged his client $150,000, paid the $8,200 ransom, and pocketed the rest – but didn’t admit he had paid the ransom. That scheme allegedly worked so well that Pinhasi charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million in ransom payments. The DOJ’s indictment [PDF] says MonsterCloud’s website mentions its use of “advanced decryption techniques and cutting-edge technology” – the same language found on this monstercloud.com page. The site also contains this claim: “At MonsterCloud, we are not a team of IT Experts. We are the most sophisticated Counter Cyber Terrorism team in the world.” The indictment suggests MonsterCloud was nothing of the sort, and that its claims rang hollow for years. “MonsterCloud's website included ‘testimonials’ and other promotional content, including from at least one compensated spokesperson,” the indictment states. “In May 2019, one such spokesperson – an individual who had provided a paid testimonial for the MonsterCloud website – contacted the defendant Zohar Pinhasi with questions about Pinhasi’s business practices and truthfulness.” “Among other things, the spokesperson asked Pinhasi whether MonsterCloud actually had any proprietary software that would allow MonsterCloud to decrypt encrypted data. Pinhasi responded: ‘MonsterCloud doesn't hold any proprietary technology [to] decrypt the ransomware data.’” Pinhasi faces two counts of wire fraud, and one of wire fraud conspiracy. He could do twenty years on each count, if convicted. events.title: 'Enough is enough': Alan Jones emails to schoolboy read in court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Complainant denies deceiving Alan Jones for financial assistance, trial hears Veteran broadcaster Alan Jones denies all allegations against him. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Complainant A is giving evidence in the Alan Jones trial in the New South Wales Local Court on Thursday. The complainant, who is now an adult, is accusing Mr Jones of kissing him and touching his buttocks when he was a 17-year-old. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. A man accusing Alan Jones of kissing him when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy has denied he and his mother tried to deceive the veteran broadcaster to obtain as much financial assistance as possible before he came forward with his allegation. The now-adult, known as Complainant A, alleges Mr Jones kissed him, put his tongue in his mouth, and touched his buttocks when he visited the radio host at his farm on the Southern Highlands as a 17-year-old. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexually touching relating to five male complainants between 2003 and 2020. Mr Jones is facing 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Complainant A said he first reached out to Mr Jones when he was 13 years old, sending the 2GB host a letter asking for help with his family's serious financial struggles. Emails read to the court showed Mr Jones had extensive correspondences with the young boy over a three-year period and used his influence to help the boy's mother re-negotiate a more favourable home loan, which included $600,000 being wiped off her initial debt. The trial heard Mr Jones also provided more than $100,000 of his own money to help with the completion of the boy's family home and to help with their legal fees. The court is hearing from Complainant A, who is the fifth and final male complainant. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Under cross-examination, defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC raised an email sent by Mr Jones to the boy, three years after they started communicating with each other, and a year before the alleged indecent assault occurred. The court heard Mr Jones informed the boy in the email about how he had provided his family more than $100,000 in support, writing "enough is enough" and "there must come a point where I have to say, no more". Complainant A said he believed Mr Jones's email expressed frustration but told Ms Bashir he did not believe the email meant the end of the broadcaster's financial support to him and his mother. "Isn't it that the case that your intention was on obtaining as much financial assistance from Mr Jones as you possibly could?" Ms Bashir suggested. "That is not true," the complainant replied. "It's the case that your mother had the intention of obtaining as much financial assistance from Mr Jones as she possibly could?" Ms Bashir asked. "That is a lie," the complainant said. The court heard the boy replied to the email, writing that his family was "happy to make arrangements to make repayments", with Mr Jones's reply asking about when a legal matter would end and that "he was not a mobile bank". Ms Bashir questioned the complainant about whether he had drafted specific emails to Mr Jones or whether his mother also had some level of involvement. Complainant A repeatedly told the court he could not remember who may have drafted specific sections of emails but said there was certain information contained in correspondence that he would have only been able to obtain from his mum. "You were you trying to deceive Mr Jones about the author of the email when you sent emails signed off just from [your name] that your mother had input into?" Ms Bashir suggested. "I suggest that you were, what do you say to that?" Ms Bashir said "[I say] that you're wrong," he answered. The trial heard Mr Jones and the boy met in person on several occasions, including at his Circular Quay apartment, at the boy's home and alone at a pub. It is alleged that after many invitations over several years, the boy agreed to spend two nights at Mr Jones's Fitzroy Fall's property when he was 17 years old. Complainant A said the alleged indecent assault occurred on the second day at the property and that it left him feeling "violated". The court heard, the boy later wrote a letter to his mother saying, "something happened at Fitzroy Falls" and took his allegation to police the next year.

events.title: Singapore’s central bank wants all FinTech AI use cases subject to independent review
events.summary: Singapore’s Monetary Authority, which acts as both central bank and finance industry regulator, wants all local industry players to seek independent review of AI use cases before deployment. The island nation’s combination of strict regulation and low taxes have made it one of the world’s premier finance hubs. One of the roles of Singapore’s Monetary Authority (MAS) is ensuring the nation retains that status, but in its first Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions, published on Wednesday, warns that AI increases risk. “The use of AI can improve performance across business and functional areas but its complexity and probabilistic nature can lead to greater uncertainty, as well as unexpected or more biased behaviour that is harder to identify compared to the use of simpler methods,” the guidelines state. And that’s MAS’s view of old-school AI: it rates generative AI as even riskier. “The greater complexity of Generative AI gives rise to even greater uncertainty and unexpected behaviour compared to AI,” MAS warns, citing “noise that is inherent in training data, training data that may not be representative, or when the model encounters scenarios that are not present in its training data” as sources of risk. The regulator fears agentic AI “could further amplify these risks.” MAS therefore calls for financial institutions (FIs) to expand their risk management frameworks to cover AI and expects board and senior management to make that happen. The regulator also wants all AI use cases to undergo independent review before going into production. “Prior to deployment, an FI should subject the AI use case, including its underlying systems or models, to reviews by parties not involved in its development to ensure that the relevant controls, such as evaluation and testing, have been adhered to,” the guidelines state. MAS also wants regulated entities to run technology and cybersecurity reviews “to ensure that AI can be deployed into the production environment in a controlled and secure manner.” If an AI project survives those reviews, MAS wants ongoing monitoring of both the FI’s own systems and any third-party AI powering an application. “Given the uncertainties associated with AI, their dynamic nature and the potential for model staleness and performance degradation due to data or model drifts over time, ongoing monitoring is critical to ensure that deployed AI operates as intended and remains fit for purpose over time,” the guidelines state. MAS does not see failings by third-party AI suppliers as an acceptable excuse for AI problems at entities it regulates, and it wants FIs to monitor their suppliers’ products and services to ensure they remain stable and secure. “FIs remain accountable for AI used in the services they deliver, including AI developed, operated or provided by third parties,” the regulator explained. “FIs should obtain sufficient assurance from third-party providers, assess whether third-party AI is suitable for their intended use, and apply compensating controls where practical constraints or assurance gaps arise. If the risks cannot be brought within the FI’s risk appetite, it should consider limiting, suspending or replacing the use of the third-party AI service.” The regulator also wants Singaporean FIs to maintain up-to-date inventories of all AI used in their business. If that’s not possible due to third-party services using AI without revealing it, financial institutions need to find ways to manage the risk of unknowable AI contributions. Another of the guidelines calls for FIs to develop contingency plans and fallback options for AI used in high-risk applications. Those plans should include “alternative systems or manual processes, to ensure business continuity in case of AI failure or unexpected behavior.” The guidelines come into force on October 7, 2027. ®

events.title: Africa launches credit rating agency
events.summary: The News Africa’s long-planned credit rating agency launches in Mauritius on Wednesday, the continent’s most concrete answer yet to years of complaints that the world’s biggest agencies overstate African risk and drive up borrowing costs. The creation of the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) comes as global agencies face growing criticism for relying on offshore models that some African leaders and policymakers say misread local realities — a debate sharpened this year by Afreximbank’s public break with Fitch . AfCRA will rate governments, cities and companies, and it is meant to complement the three US firms, which control 95% of global ratings markets. The new ratings agency “ will add another opinion in the market place of opinions ,” said Marie-Antoinette Rose-Quatre, head of the AU body that incubated it. She called it “a very tangible outcome of our aspiration to build our own financial institutions”. Only three African sovereigns hold investment grade ratings, according to a background note from the AU’s African Peer Review Mechanism (ARPM). Thirteen are rated at very high risk or in default, and 23 have no rating from the big agencies, which cuts them from international bond markets. The AU has also said the continent’s external debt service costs climbed from roughly $60 billion in 2010 to more than $160 billion in 2024. Know More The launch is part of a wider push by developing countries, at the G20 and the UN, to change how global finance prices their risk. South Africa used its 2025 G20 presidency to put borrowing costs on the agenda. In an op-ed published in Africa Renewal, the UN magazine, Rose-Quatre and Ahunna Eziakonwa, the UN secretary-general’s special adviser on Africa, said unfair ratings cost Africa $74.5 billion a year — an estimate which was first published by the UN Development Programme in 2023. Key details of the new agency remain unclear. The APRM describes it as privately owned and self-funded but has not named its shareholders, chief executive, or board. Mauritius Commercial Bank and the pan-African lender Afreximbank took part in a 2025 meeting to raise support for the project. According to the APRM note, AfCRA “will require a licence” from Mauritius’ financial regulator. People close to the project say trust will take time. “Credibility in credit rating is accumulated rather than declared,” said Daniel Cash, a UK-based law professor who has advised the APRM on credit ratings. The real test, he told Semafor, will come when AfCRA issues a rating that a member state, “particularly an influential one” strongly dislikes. “Independence is demonstrated at the point of disagreement.” The launch also comes as global agencies expand on the continent. Moody’s owns GCR, the largest issuer of ratings in Africa, and in July S&P agreed to buy a majority stake in Nigeria’s Agusto & Co. S&P Global declined to comment, while Moody’s and Fitch did not respond to requests for comment. Tiisetso’s view For half a century, the cost of African borrowing has been set largely in New York by three firms that rate the 55 countries from a distance. AfCRA is the continent finally taking a seat at the table where its risk is priced. Every 10 basis points shaved off a $1 billion Eurobond saves an issuer $1 million a year. Twenty-three states have no rating from the big agencies at all, which locks them out of mandates that require one. That’s the prize. True, AfCRA has no track record and no named shareholders, but the quickest route to credibility runs through pain: an early, well-argued downgrade of one of the governments that cheered the launch. Room for Disagreement Critics question whether investors will trust any agency created by the governments it rates. David Lubin of UK think tank Chatham House asked whether AfCRA amounts to Africa “marking its own homework,” adding that fund managers compare African borrowers with the rest of the world and an African agency “does nothing” for them. Misheck Mutize, AfCRA’s chief architect, acknowledged that the agency’s main role would be to steer Africa’s $4 trillion savings into African assets rather than changing how foreign investors see the continent. “The challenge here is that this is the bare minimum disclosure required before international investors can even begin to take AfCRA seriously,” said Bright Simons, head of research at IMANI, a think tank based in Accra, writing on public policy platform Katanomics Society. Notable Nigerian President Bola Tinubu made the case for an African rating agency , arguing that the Big Three misjudge African risk and that a homegrown agency could spot progress early, which the global firms would later confirm.

events.title: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
events.summary: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran , U.S. officials said. Why it matters: The directive didn't include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump hasn't made any final decisions. But U.S. and Israeli sources say it could happen before the U.S. midterm elections and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier. The big picture: If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say. Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterm elections, in part because oil prices might rise in response. "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told Axios. A White House official said Trump has all options available at any time. "The U.S. is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." The Atlantic reported earlier Wednesday that Trump is weighing striking Iran before the midterm election. Driving the news: On Friday, Trump's national security team met at Camp David for several hours to discuss the war and other issues. An Israeli official told Axios that part of the meeting focused on a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that it focused on "long-term" foreign policy planning. Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran haven't made any progress. Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian response to a U.S. counterproposal that included demands for nuclear concessions. "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out. After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly," a second Israeli official said. Behind the scenes: President Trump spoke Wednesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was their second call in days , after barely speaking for many weeks. A U.S. official said Trump and Netanyahu spoke about "remembrance and respect for the victims of the October 7 massacre." The call took place after Netanyahu held a meeting with his national security team about Iran, the first Israeli official said. Netanyahu spoke to Rubio on Monday. If major combat operations resume, they will most likely be with the U.S. and Israel working in tandem and with the Israeli military participating. The two Israeli officials said the Iranian regime is desperate and paranoid, which might lead it to strike first. They said the Iranians have suffered two surprise attacks and don't want to experience a third. Between the lines: Resumption of the war could also affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. A renewed escalation — or even a heightened state of tension or emergency — could benefit Netanyahu politically and prevent his opponents from attacking him in the final stretch of the campaign.

Please enter a search term. The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will represent UK wildlife and feature as the central images on our next series of banknotes. The decision comes after nearly 500,000 people responded to a public consultation asking which native wildlife they would like to see on our banknotes. They chose from a shortlist of 18 options across three categories – mammals; birds; and amphibians, insects and fish – developed in collaboration with a panel of UK wildlife experts. The Bank used the feedback from the consultation to decide on the four animals, one for each denomination of banknote. The selected animals meet the Bank’s objectives for a distinctive set of banknotes that can support counterfeit resilience and are representative of the UK. The barn owl (Tyto alba), buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) and European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) were the most popular animals in their respective categories. The Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica) was selected because it was the most popular marine animal. The inclusion of a marine animal will add variety to the series, making the denominations easier to distinguish and will provide an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline. The decision on which animal will feature on which denomination will be made in due course and announced closer to launch. While the selected animals will feature as the central imagery for the next series, the banknotes will also feature other elements from nature to complete the designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The next series will continue to include a portrait of the monarch. It takes a number of years to design, test and print banknotes, to make sure they are high-quality, resilient and accessible. The expectation is, therefore, that the first denomination from the next series will be launched over the next few years. Victoria Cleland, Bank of England Chief Cashier, said: ‘I am delighted that nearly half a million people responded to our wildlife imagery consultation, showing that cash still matters. I would like to thank everyone who engaged, including those who I met at our events. With their support, we have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes.' Rhys Phillips, the Bank’s incoming Chief Cashier who will be responsible for delivering the new series of notes, said: 'It’s fantastic to see how engaged the public have been in this choice. With these animals as the focus for the design we can deliver a new series of banknotes that are secure and represent the UK at its best. We’ll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we’ve announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science’. 1. In July 2025, the Bank announced that work would begin on designing the next series of banknotes, with the important goal to increase counterfeit resilience. As part of this, it also launched a consultation on the theme for the new images for the notes. The July 2025 theme consultation received over 44,000 responses and in March 2026, the Bank announced that nature had been chosen as the theme for the next series of banknotes. Nature received the highest proportion of nominations in the July 2025 consultation, with 60% of respondents nominating it as one of their preferred themes, as well as support in focus groups commissioned by the Bank. 2.

events.title: Seafood shop owners fear being forced to close due to gillnet ban
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gillnet ban will lead to seafood shop closures and fishers retiring, businesses warn Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Neil Green says the ban might see him out of the industry. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) A couple running a seafood restaurant say they may be forced to close if commercial fishers leave the industry when gillnets are banned in the Great Barrier Reef Zone. In 2023 the state and federal governments made the commitment to phase out gillnets in the zone. Temporary gillnet licences are set to expire on June 30, 2027, with the state government running trials with fishers to find alternative fishing methods. Business owners in north Queensland are concerned about the economic flow-on effect of the looming Great Barrier Reef gillnet ban. Some commercial fishers fear they will have to leave the industry and seafood shops may be left with no other option than to close. Peter and Heather Bradford are worried about the future of their business. ( ABC News: Brooke Tindall ) In Ayr, Heather and Peter Bradford serve locally caught seafood to about 150 families a week and say their business will not survive without gillnet fishers on the water. "Next year we'll have to probably close the shop," Mr Bradford said. "Cut out the netting, there's 80 per cent of our business, so we've got no other option but to close." Gillnets are used to catch certain species of fish, including barramundi, by their gills. In 2023 the Queensland and federal governments made the decision to phase out the use of gillnets in the Great Barrier Reef fishing zone by June 30 2027. The governments provided financial assistance to licensed fishers at the time of the decision and established the temporary NX licence, which allowed fishers to use gillnets under strict on-board camera monitoring. The state government has been working with fishers to find an alternative fishing method in the last three years, such as trapping and line fishing. Barramundi is largely caught using gillnets. ( ABC News: Brooke Tindall ) But as the expiry of the NX licences approach, no solutions have been rolled out to fishers. South of Townsville, Alva Beach commercial fisher Neil Green said the other options trialled had not been successful so far. "The intent was to have alternative gear running by 2027. That's been a failure," he said. Neil Green is one of 25 NX licensed fishers in Queensland. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) Mr Green said without change he would probably be forced to retire, but he was worried about more than his own future. "It's not about me — it's about the next generation of fishers that are coming on that we're talking about," he said. Mr Green is among several fishermen in the industry pushing for a three-year extension to the ban, which has the support of Shadow Minister for Northern Australia Susan McDonald. "It will allow [the fishers] to demonstrate that gillnet fishing is incredibly targeted on the species that the fishermen are taking," she said. Susan McDonald supports the seafood industry's call for a three-year extension on NX licences. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Senator McDonald said the 2027 deadline would increase reliability on imports. "If we allow more seafood to be imported from offshore, we are handing over seafood production to countries that don't have the same high standards that Australia does," she said. Back in Ayr, Ms Bradford said importing seafood had not worked for her and her husband's business in the past. "We couldn't compete with [the major supermarkets] price-wise, so it's not going to be viable for us at all," she said. Ms Bradford said other small seafood businesses were in the same boat. "Fish and chip shops will be gone, especially all up along the north coast," she said. Not everyone agrees that putting off the eventual gillnet ban is a viable option. Australian Marine Conservation Society (AMCS) Great Barrier Reef fisheries campaign manager Simon Miller said a three-year extension of the NX licences would come at a cost to wildlife. "The current gillnet fishery, the NX fishery, is still catching thousands of threatened species each year," he said. "We do urge the Queensland and Australian governments to fully deliver their commitment to phase out gillnet fishing from the reef by June 30 next year." The AMCS is against extending temporary licences but Mr Miller says there is support for finding alternative fishing gear. "We need to be looking to the future for genuinely sustainable ways to catch these fish and put them on Queenslanders' plates, but without this impact on threatened species," he said.

events.title: GitHub Copilot brings on-device AI coding to new Windows PCs
events.summary: Bringing local models and sandboxed tools to Windows and GitHub Copilot Coming soon, GitHub Copilot will determine when a task is best handled by on-device intelligence and when it should leverage cloud-scale models. When leveraging agents, developers need both choice and control. They need technologies that offer clear boundaries for their agents and make it easy to choose the model with the right speed, performance, and cost profile for each task. That’s why GitHub offers frontier models from major model providers, as well as options like Project HydraFusion , an orchestrator choosing one or multiple models for each task while balancing performance, cost, and latency. It’s also why Windows has developed Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) to help secure interactive and non-interactive agentic coding sessions. Coming by the end of the month, GitHub Copilot will determine when a task is best handled by on-device intelligence and when it should leverage cloud-scale models. Rather than forcing developers to manage infrastructure decisions themselves, GitHub Copilot automatically coordinates local and cloud inference behind the scenes. For NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows PCs like Surface Laptop Ultra, that means we are enabling local coding in GitHub Copilot with powerful local inference models and hardware capable of delivering a great experience at the edge. The result is poised to be the next step in the HydraFusion vision: intelligent orchestration that spans not just multiple models, but multiple compute environments including the edge. GitHub Copilot can run commands in these environments with controlled access to files, networks, system capabilities, and credentials. Developers can automate with confidence and security in mind. Why memory matters for a local coding agent Local inference starts with a memory budget. Surface Laptop Ultra is built around NVIDIA RTX Spark, with up to 128 GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of AI compute. With a discrete GPU, dedicated video memory is an important constraint: moving model data between system memory and the GPU can add overhead. Unified memory gives the CPU and GPU access to a shared physical pool. That makes more capacity available to the workload, but it doesn’t make all of it available to model weights. The operating system, your applications, and the inference runtime need memory, too. So does the key-value cache, which stores attention state for tokens the model has already processed. As an agent reads files and receives tool results, its context can grow, increasing memory use and the work needed to process the next request. Keeping a model loaded between requests can avoid repeated loading work. However, it doesn’t guarantee constant response time; context length, memory pressure, and the rest of the workload still matter. That’s why the useful question isn’t just whether a model fits, but how it behaves over a complete coding task. Introducing MAI Code 1.1 Flash for local coding To bring this local-development experience to life, Microsoft AI developed a local version of MAI Code 1.1 Flash, a coding-optimized mixture-of-experts model with 137 billion total and 6.8 billion active parameters. The on-device work applies quantization and speculative decoding to reduce the model footprint and improve end-to-end responsiveness while preserving the task completion and tool-use quality that matter in an agent loop. Quantization reduces the precision used to represent model weights and activations, lowering memory requirements. Because code doesn’t degrade gracefully, the release evaluation must measure coding-task success as well as footprint: a single incorrect token can produce a syntax error, wrong identifier, malformed tool call, or broken diff. Speculative decoding trades additional working memory for higher decode throughput and lower end-to-end latency. A drafter proposes candidate token blocks and the target model verifies them. For a coding agent, the important tradeoff is whether the smaller model can still complete the same tasks. A smaller footprint is useful only if changes in code quality and tool use are understood. With our first shipping version of MAI Code 1.1 Flash on Surface Laptop Ultra we achieve the following performance at different context lengths, with peak memory usage of 75.5GB at 256k context. At 64k and 128k context, prompt-processing throughput reaches 923.5 and 769.8 tokens per second, respectively. The quantized version of MAI Code 1.1 Flash we use on device retains capability impressively compared to the Bfloat16 cloud variant, coming in at 53GB, an 80% reduction in size. Two ways to use local models in GitHub Copilot GitHub Copilot is adding two ways to use local models across the GitHub Copilot CLI, Copilot app, and VS Code. Developers can let Copilot’s intelligent Auto orchestration choose when to use local or cloud inference, or they can explicitly select a local model for workflows that require direct control. With Auto, developers do not need to decide where each task should be run. Across a multi-turn session, Copilot can consider task context and cache state as it routes work between local and cloud models, preserving useful, cached work as the session evolves. This orchestrated experience complements direct model selection, giving developers a choice between letting Copilot optimize model placement and choosing a specific local model themselves. Explicit local-model selection supports workflows that need a specific provider, model, or endpoint. Developers can select MAI Code 1.1 Flash through the Windows ML provider or connect GitHub Copilot to OpenAI-compatible local endpoints and choose from the models those endpoints expose. How sandboxes help secure tool execution An agent’s shell commands normally inherit the access of the account running them. Moving inference onto the device doesn’t change that. Sandboxing applies a policy to the processes and local services the agent launches, controlling access to files, networks, credentials, system capabilities, and execution paths regardless of which model requested the work. GitHub Copilot uses Microsoft Execution Containers , or MXC, an open-source library from the Windows team that translates policy into native operating-system controls. On Windows, GitHub Copilot uses the BaseContainer tier of the ProcessContainer backend. On macOS, it uses Seatbelt. On Linux, it uses bubblewrap . These local backends don’t require a separate virtual machine or container image, but we plan to make them options available through MXC in the future. When sandboxing is enabled, shell commands and, by default, local Model Context Protocol servers and language servers run inside the process boundary. Built-in file tools run inside GitHub Copilot itself: the agent harness checks their requests against the effective policy, but those checks aren’t OS-enforced child-process isolation.

events.title: Microsoft is about to let Copilot loose on your file system
events.summary: If you thought Windows Recall was creepy, buckle up. Microsoft is about to shoehorn even more AI into its desktop operating system, giving Copilot access to every file on your PC. But don't worry, Redmond insists it's totally secure and safe since the agents powering the functionality will run entirely on your PC — some of the time. Microsoft describes the new functionality, announced alongside a new Nvidia N1X powered Surface Laptop, as "hybrid intelligence." Built atop Microsoft's HydraFusion model router, Windows apps and Copilot features will soon be able to use local models when it makes sense and cloud-based models when it doesn't. For example, Windows might use a local model for simple or privacy-sensitive tasks, or decide complex or performance-sensitive requests need OpenAI's GPT-6 or Anthropic's Claude. Local agents will run in Microsoft's Execution Containers (MXCs), agent sandboxes with fine-grained permissions applied at runtime. According to Microsoft EVP of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri, MXCs mean Windows is now "the most secure platform for agents." (That claim will surely age well because models never escape their sandboxes and routers never misbehave.) To support this hybrid intelligence functionality, Microsoft is extending support for Windows ML, its inference framework built on the ONNX runtime, to Llama.cpp – one of the highest-performing inference engines for local AI inference. By adding support for Windows ML, Llama.cpp should be able to take advantage of a broader range of accelerators. Microsoft is rolling out its hybrid intelligence functionality to GitHub Copilot — its AI code assistant — next week and its Copilot app over the next few months. The new Copilot features look and sound suspiciously like OpenClaw in a business suit. Copilot's agentic functionality will now have access to your entire file system, opening the door to advanced search functionality and productivity tasks through integrations with Microsoft Office. In a demo, Microsoft showed how Copilot could be used to find and organize a user's tax documents, then draft an email with those files attached, addressed to an accountant. Microsoft insists it'll only go snooping through your docs if you ask it to. Windows is also getting AI-enhanced search functionality enabling users to surface settings like dark mode. The OS will also get a conversational interface to perform tasks like sending a text message to a friend. Finally, for those interested in coloring outside Microsoft's agentic lines, the company is rolling out a new onboarding experience to make deploying agent harnesses like OpenClaw a bit easier and more secure. Keeping sensitive tasks on device may help to assuage anxieties over privacy, which have dogged Microsoft since the first Copilot+ PCs arrived in 2024 alongside Qualcomm's Snapdragon X Elite SoCs. It should also help to reduce the load on Microsoft's servers by keeping low-priority, low-complexity requests on devices. That said, the impact of running these models locally on battery life, fan noise, and workload quality could prove a turnoff for many users. ®

events.title: Brazilian students in Rio de Janeiro march against the prospect of another Bolsonaro presidency
events.summary: Thousands of Brazilian students have marched in Rio de Janeiro against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro winning the presidency RIO DE JANEIRO -- Thousands of Brazilian students marched in downtown Rio de Janeiro on Wednesday to protest against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro winning the presidency, after the far-right candidate received more votes than incumbent and left-leaning Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election . A sea of red-clad demonstrators made their way between two historical squares in Rio’s center, chanting and holding signs referencing Brazil’s sovereignty and democracy in the South American country , which they said were under threat. “We’re fighting for Brazil, not for Lula,” said Talita Amaral, a 19-year-old environmental science student at a nearby university. She was wearing Brazil’s yellow and green soccer jersey, often worn by supporters of Bolsonaro, which she said was a gesture aimed at reclaiming the national colors. “We don’t have time to be sad, we need to be doing this, occupying the streets, sending messages in WhatsApp groups, trying to convince people,” Amaral said, as the chant “Olé olé olé ola, Lula Lula” rang out across Cinelandia square. Neither Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup, nor Lula received more than the required 50% of the vote needed to become Brazil’s leader on Sunday. Therefore, they will face each other in an unpredictable runoff on Oct. 25. But Flávio Bolsonaro has at least two advantages: He received 2 million more votes than Lula on Sunday and the candidates who placed third, fourth and fifth are all on the right of the political spectrum. They gathered more than 8 million votes between them. Bolsonaro is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion because of his ties to the failed Banco Master — a case that many protesters in Rio made reference to on Wednesday. Some pointed to Jair Bolsonaro's handling of the coronavirus pandemic , during which 700,000 people were reported to have died from the disease, while others held signs emblazoned with messages such as “Brazil isn't anyone's backyard” and “I don't vote for someone who sells Brazil.” Many on the left fear a Flávio Bolsonaro presidency would fully align the Brazilian government with the United States because of the proximity in ideologies between U.S. President Donald Trump and the Bolsonaro family. Last year, Trump imposed a 50% tariff on Brazilian goods and imposed sanctions on a Brazilian Supreme Court justice, citing Jair Bolsonaro’s trial, which he called a “witch hunt.” Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer ISIS-inspired mass shooting plot at Mall of America thwarted, FBI says Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys “If Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become a colony of the United States,” said João Victor Vieira, 20, who studies literature. He said that Bolsonaro represented a threat to minorities such as people of color, women and the LGBTQ+ community. Bolsonaro's father was notorious for homophobic remarks. Vieira said that while he was initially dispirited following the results on Sunday, he has since regained hope. “This protest shows that social movements are still very much alive,” he said. “We will resist.” This story corrects a previous version that stated the candidates who placed third, fourth and fifth gathered 6 million votes. The correct number of votes is more than 8 million.
